0verkill.title: 0verkill
0verkill.description: Bloody 2D deathmatch in ASCII art: run, jump and shoot against friends or bots
0verkill.provenance: Brainsoft (Brain, Clock and others) released 0verkill 0.16 in 2000; hackndev fixed it for newer compilers from 2008 to 2010, and ravener revived it on GitHub from 2021.
0verkill.page:
A bloody 2D deathmatch drawn entirely in ASCII art. Run, jump, creep and
climb through the levels, pick up weapons, armor and grenades, and frag
everyone else in sight. Started from Asciiverse, it opens a game on your
machine against two bots; friends on your network can join the same game.

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: run
- **Up**: jump (with a direction, jump aside)
- **Down**: creep; **C** toggles creeping
- **D**: climb down ladders and drop through platforms
- **Ctrl** or **Z**: fire
- **1** to **5**: change weapon
- **Enter**: chat

## Playing with friends

One player starts the game; everyone else joins it with
`0verkill -i <that player's address>`.

## History

Brainsoft, a Czech group at Charles University in Prague, released 0verkill
in 2000. Its code has been kept alive since: hackndev fixed it for
newer compilers (2008 to 2010), and ravener's revival (2021 to 2026) fixed
its network checksum and a memory bug.

## Credits

- Game: Brainsoft (Brain: code, design, graphics, levels; Clock: idea, AVI
  editor, graphics)
- Fixes: hackndev (Marek Vasut, Jonathan Neuschäfer), ravener and lumidify
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0

2048.description: Slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 board, merge equal pairs, and try to build a 2048 before the board fills up
2048.provenance: Maurits van der Schee wrote 2048.c in 2014, a console version of Gabriele Cirulli's game of the same year, in one C file that draws with ANSI escape codes.
2048.page:
The puzzle that took over 2014, in a plain terminal. Every move slides
all the tiles on the 4x4 board as far as they go in one direction, and
two tiles of the same number that run into each other merge into one
with their sum. After each move a new 2 (or now and then a 4) appears
in an empty cell. Keep merging up through 4, 8, 16 and on to 2048; the
game ends when the board is full and no move is left.

Each merge adds the new tile's value to your score, and a tile merges
only once per move. The usual plan is to keep the biggest tile in a
corner and build towards it, but the new tiles have a way of turning up
in the wrong place.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **WASD**, **h j k l** or **4 8 6 2**: slide the tiles
- **r**: start again (asks first)
- **q**: quit (asks first)

At game over, **r** plays again and **q** quits.

## Options

- `2048 blackwhite`, `2048 whiteblack`, `2048 bluered`: other colour
  schemes for the tiles
- `2048 test`: runs the built-in tests of the sliding rules

## History

Gabriele Cirulli made 2048 in 2014 as an open-source web game, after
earlier games of the same kind. Maurits van der Schee wrote this
console version, 2048.c, the same year, in a single C file that draws
with ANSI escape codes and needs no libraries; it is packaged by Debian
and others. This edition waits at game over so the final board stays
in view, and is built for Windows as well.

## Credits

2048.c is by Maurits van der Schee, under the MIT licence.

all-things-devours.title: All Things Devours
all-things-devours.description: Break into your own lab to destroy a time machine before anyone can use it
all-things-devours.provenance: Toby Ord wrote All Things Devours, as half sick of shadows, for the 2004 Interactive Fiction Competition.
all-things-devours.page:
It is 4:17 in the morning. The plan is simple: get into your lab, plant the bomb and run, so the prototype is destroyed and nobody dies. The guard is out securing the grounds and you have six minutes. Then time itself starts to fold back on you, and every move you make has to fit with the ones you have already made.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/all-things-devours`.

## Credits

- All Things Devours: Toby Ord, writing as half sick of shadows; IFComp 2004
- License: Public domain, by the author's statement in the game and its source
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

andromeda-apocalypse.title: Andromeda Apocalypse
andromeda-apocalypse.description: The last survivor of a dead world drifts through space on a strange vessel
andromeda-apocalypse.provenance: Marco Innocenti's Andromeda Apocalypse won the 2012 Interactive Fiction Competition.
andromeda-apocalypse.page:
Korhos is setting over the shore, a storm is coming in from the south, and Uncle Oren is waiting by the water. What follows takes Ektor Mastiff, the sole survivor of a world, across the cosmos on a strange vessel. The second part of the Andromeda series; the first is not needed to play.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/andromeda-apocalypse`.

## Credits

- Andromeda Apocalypse: Marco Innocenti, 2012; title song by Wade Clarke
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

angband.title: Angband
angband.description: Go down a hundred levels of dungeon beneath Angband and defeat Morgoth, Lord of Darkness, in the classic Tolkien roguelike
angband.provenance: Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand wrote Angband at the University of Warwick in 1990 from the code of Umoria, and a line of maintainers, now the Angband Dev Team, has kept it going since.

upstream.name: Angband Dev Team, after Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand (1990)

angband.page:
Somewhere beneath the fortress of Angband, a hundred levels down, waits
Morgoth, Lord of Darkness. You choose a race and a class, start in a
small town with some gear and a little gold, buy what you can, and go
down. Every level is made afresh each time you enter it, full of
monsters out of Tolkien's Middle-earth and far beyond, traps, treasure,
unique foes and legendary artifacts. Death is permanent, and the game is
long and deep: a win usually takes many characters.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or the **number keys** (1 to 9): move; walk into a
  monster to attack it
- **.** and a direction: run along a corridor
- **<** and **>**: take stairs up and down
- **g**: pick up, **i**: inventory, **e**: equipment, **w**: wear or wield
- **q** quaff a potion, **r** read a scroll, **E** eat, **a** aim a wand,
  **u** use a staff, **z** zap a rod, **f** or **v** fire or throw
- **m**: cast a spell, **b**: browse a book
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors, **R**: rest
- **C**: character sheet, **l**: look around, **M**: map of the level
- **=**: options (a roguelike keyset with hjkl is there too)
- **?**: help, **Ctrl-S**: save, **Ctrl-X**: save and quit

## Saving

Your game is saved in your data folder (`~/.local/share/angband`) when you
quit with Ctrl-X, and Angband carries on from it the next time you start.
Character dumps, options and the score list are kept there too.

## History

Angband grew out of Moria, Robert Alan Koeneke's VMS game of 1985, by way
of James E. Wilson's Umoria (1989). Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand wrote
Angband 1.0 at the University of Warwick in 1990; Ben Harrison's rewrite
from 1995, Robert Ruehlmann, Anna Sidwell and the current maintainer, Nick
McConnell, have carried it on, and dozens of other roguelikes are its
variants.

## Credits

- Game: the Angband Dev Team (maintainer Nick McConnell), after Alex
  Cutler, Andy Astrand, Ben Harrison, Robert Ruehlmann, Anna Sidwell and
  many others; based on Moria by Robert Alan Koeneke and Umoria by James
  E. Wilson
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0 (Angband is also offered under its own non-commercial
  licence)

aquest.title: AQuest
aquest.description: Mark Mackey's XQuest in the terminal: steer a drifting ship round the arena, grab every crystal, dodge the mines and leave through the gate, fifty levels deep
aquest.provenance: Mark Mackey wrote XQuest for DOS in Turbo Pascal and released it as shareware from 1994 to 1996. David ported version 1.3 to C and SDL2 as xquest-sdl, and AQuest carries that port's game logic line by line into Rust and Ratatui for the terminal.
aquest.page:
You're a jolly little ship dingus which shoots around a rather abstract
landscape collecting little gem thingies, while avoiding mines. Pick up
every crystal on the level and the gate at the top opens; fly out through
it to the next one. Fifty levels, each with more crystals, more mines, a
narrower gate, and from level 33 a gate that won't keep still.

Every level has a par time, counting down in the corner. Beat it and
each second left is worth 500 points; overstay it and the whole game
starts to speed up. An extra ship comes every 15,000 points on the first
levels, every 100,000 later.

Your ship steers by thrust and drifts on when you let go, so brake before
the wall: on every difficulty but Wimp, the wall is as deadly as a mine.
Your shots fly the way you do, as fast as you do. Enemies come in through
the side gates, eighteen kinds of them: Grungers wander, Zippos curve,
Zingers and Snipes shoot, Miners lay mines, Meebies follow you,
Retaliators fire back when they die, Tribblers burst into five, Clusters
into fifteen shots, and the Repulsor shoves you away. Catch a Supercrystal
for a power-up (Shield, AimedFire, RapidFire, MultiFire, AssFire,
HeavyFire or Bounce; a banner says what you got and what it does, and the
status bar shows all seven, lit while they last), and keep a smart bomb
for the moment it all goes wrong.

The game is the original, rule for rule: the same physics, levels, enemies
and sounds, and Mark Mackey's sprites drawn in Braille dots and half
blocks, cell by cell, so even a small terminal shows them in fine detail
and full colour; at full size, his own status bar.

## Controls

- **Arrows**, **WASD** or the numpad: thrust
- **Space** or **Enter**: fire (hold it with RapidFire)
- **Shift**, **Z** or numpad **5**: brake
- **B** or **X**: smart bomb
- **P**: pause; **Esc**: quit the game; **V**: graphics (Mixed, Blocks
  or Braille); **M**: sound
- Mouse: move to thrust, left button fires, right bombs, middle brakes
- Gamepad: stick or d-pad to thrust, **A** fires, **B** bombs, **X** or a
  shoulder brakes, **Start** pauses

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm,
Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others), with the mouse or with a gamepad;
elsewhere a held key stutters until the terminal's repeats start.

## Options

- `--mixed`, `--blocks`, `--braille`: how to draw
- `--demo`: watch the built-in demo
- `--record FILE`, `--play FILE`: record and play back demos in the
  original `xquest.dmo` format
- `--difficulty N`: 0 Wimp to 4 Inhuman
- `--mute`: no sound

## History

Mark Mackey wrote XQuest in Turbo Pascal for DOS, a Mode X game at
320x240, and released it as shareware from 1994 to 1996. Make it to
Inhuman, the manual promised, and he'd send you a UUencoded GIF of a
tenner.

Thirty years on, David, who played it as shareware in the mid-90s, ported
version 1.3 to C and SDL2 as xquest-sdl. AQuest
carries that port's game logic over to the terminal line by line: a demo
recorded in either one plays back in the other, frame for frame. The Hall
of Fame and the demos keep the original file formats.

## Credits

- **XQuest**: Mark Mackey, 1994 to 1996
- **xquest-sdl**: David, the C and SDL2 port this edition is built on
- **AQuest**: the terminal edition, for Asciiverse

Free to play and share, never sold.

armoured-commander-ii.title: Armoured Commander II
armoured-commander-ii.description: Command a tank and its crew through ten campaigns of World War II, from Poland in 1939 to Germany in 1945, in the tank commander roguelike
armoured-commander-ii.provenance: Gregory Adam Scott wrote Armoured Commander II in Python and libtcod between 2016 and 2020, and Asciiverse ported it to Rust and Ratatui for the terminal.
armoured-commander-ii.page:
You command a tank and its crew in one of ten campaigns of World War
II, from the invasion of Poland in September 1939 to the last weeks of
the war in Germany in April 1945. Fight for Germany, Poland, the Soviet
Union, Finland, France, the United Kingdom, the United States or
Canada, in tanks from the TKS tankette and the T-26 to the Char B1 bis,
the Panzer IV and the Sherman.

Each campaign is a calendar of combat days. Each day is a map of zones
to take and hold: travel, scout ahead, call in air and artillery
support, resupply, and deal with whatever the zone holds. Each
encounter is a battle on a hex map round your tank: spot the enemy,
give every crewman his orders, turn the turret, choose the shell, and
let the dice decide each to-hit, penetration and firepower roll, all of
them shown. Crewmen gain experience and skills, get wounded, spend time
in the field hospital and are replaced; refits bring new tanks. One
saved game per campaign, so several can run side by side.

## Controls

- In battle: **W/S** choose a crewman, **A/D** change his order,
  **H** open or close his hatch, **F** the crewman's menu;
  **Space** ends the phase
- Moving: **W/S** forward or reverse, **A/D** pivot, **H** try for a
  hull-down position, **R** reposition
- Shooting: **W/S** choose a weapon, **A/D** choose a target, **Q/E**
  turn the turret, **C** change the shell, **R** use the ready rack,
  **F** fire; **Enter** goes on after each roll
- **Tab** in battle: your tank in full
- On the day map: **1** to **4** for Supply, Crew, Travel and Group;
  **Q E A D Z C** choose a direction, **Enter** move, **R** recon,
  **W** wait or defend, **I** abandon the tank
- On the calendar: **1** to **4** for the day's mission, crew and tank,
  journal and field hospital; **Enter** starts the day
- **Esc**: the game menu with sound, volume, message pause and keyboard
  layout (QWERTY, AZERTY, QWERTZ, Dvorak), and Save and Quit

## Options

- `--battle [campaign]`: straight into one battle with a fresh tank and
  crew, to try the battle rules (nothing is saved); campaigns are named
  as `poland_campaign`, `pattons_best`, `winter_war_finland` and so on
- `--art`: browse the game's pictures

## History

Gregory Adam Scott made Armoured Commander II in Python 3 and libtcod
between 2016 and 2020 as free software, the sequel to his Armoured
Commander; later versions went to Steam. This edition ports the free
version to Rust and Ratatui: the same rules,
campaigns, art, sounds and theme tune, with every screen laid out for a
terminal of 100x30 and the maps growing with a bigger one. Its README
lists the few places where it plays or looks different.

## Credits

- Armoured Commander II: Gregory Adam Scott, 2016 to 2020
  ([github.com/sudasana/armcom2](https://github.com/sudasana/armcom2))
- Terminal port: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

armoured-commander.title: Armoured Commander
armoured-commander.description: Command a Sherman and its five-man crew through the campaigns of 1944 and 1945 in the World War II tank commander roguelike
armoured-commander.provenance: Gregory Adam Scott wrote Armoured Commander in Python and libtcod between 2015 and 2017, and Eric Normandeau maintained it from version 1.04. Asciiverse ported it to Rust and Ratatui for the terminal.
armoured-commander.page:
You are the commander of a Sherman tank and its crew of five, from the
breakout in Normandy in the summer of 1944 to the end of the war in
Europe. Two campaigns: Patton's Best with the US 4th Armored Division
from July 1944, and Canada's Best with the First Canadian Army from
August 1944.

Each combat day is a map of the front to fight your way across, area by
area, calling in artillery and air support and dealing with what you
find. Each encounter is a battle on a hex map round your tank: spot the
enemy, give every crewman his orders, choose the ammunition, and let the
dice decide each to-hit and to-kill roll, all of them shown. Crewmen gain
experience and skills, get wounded, win medals and are killed;
refits bring new tanks; and when your commander falls, his name goes on
the stone on the title screen.

## Controls

- **W/S** or **Up/Down**: choose a crewman; **A/D** or **Left/Right**:
  change his order; **O**: the full list of orders
- **H**: open or close a hatch; **R**: the next shell to load;
  **T**: use the ready rack
- **Space**: on to the next phase
- **Enter**: fire; **Tab**: next target; **A/D**: turn the turret;
  **M**: next machine gun; **F**: area or direct fire with HE
- On the day map: **Tab** and **Enter** to pick an area and move in;
  **W/S** to scroll
- **F1** help with every key, **F2** tank, **F3** crew, **F4** settings,
  **F5** campaign stats, **F7** sound on or off; **Esc**: menu, save and
  quit

## Options

- `--encounter advance`, `battle` or `counterattack`: one encounter with
  a fresh crew, to try the battle rules

## History

Gregory Adam Scott wrote Armoured Commander in Python 2.7 and libtcod
between 2015 and 2017 as free software; Eric Normandeau maintained it
from version 1.04. Scott went on to make a sequel, Armoured Commander II.
This edition ports it to Rust and Ratatui: the same rules, art and
sounds, every screen
laid out for a terminal of 100x30 and growing with a bigger one. Its
README lists the few places where it plays differently.

## Credits

- Armoured Commander: Gregory Adam Scott, 2015 to 2017, maintained by
  Eric Normandeau
  ([github.com/sudasana/armcom](https://github.com/sudasana/armcom))
- Terminal port: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

arogue.title: Advanced Rogue 5.8
arogue.description: Bell Labs' Rogue of 1984 and 1985 with character classes, over a hundred monsters and a quest for one of the dungeon's unique artifacts
arogue.provenance: Advanced Rogue was made at AT&T Bell Labs in 1984 and 1985, by a group that seems to have included Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka, from Rogue 3.6 with parts of Super-Rogue. Nicholas J. Kisseberth restored it in the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Michael Morgan, Ken Dalka and AT&T (1985); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

arogue.page:
Rogue grown into something bigger at Bell Labs. Before you go down into
the Dungeons of Doom you choose to be a fighter, a magic user, a cleric
or a thief, each with abilities of its own: spells, prayers, turning
the undead, stealing from monsters. Over a hundred monsters wait below,
many of them clever, and you are on a quest for one of the unique
artifacts some of them carry. Experience, not gold, is your score.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **z**: zap a wand or staff
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **P**: pick up
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off
- **C**: cast a spell, **p**: pray, **a**: affect the undead, **^**:
  set a trap, **D**: dip something in a pool
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `arogue -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Advanced Rogue was developed by a group at AT&T Bell Labs between 1984
and 1986, among them apparently Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka, and AT&T
distributed it for a time through its Toolchest. Version 5.8 grew from
Rogue 3.6 with parts of Super-Rogue. Nicholas J. Kisseberth (Yendor) restored
it in the Roguelike Restoration Project (5.8.1 in 2005, 5.8.2 in 2006).
This edition keeps your files in your data folder and has fixes for
64-bit machines and the score file. It is part of the Roguelike Restoration
Project in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Michael Morgan, Ken Dalka and their Bell Labs colleagues, after Rogue by
Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold and Super-Rogue by Robert D.
Kindelberger; restoration by Nicholas J. Kisseberth. BSD licence with
clauses on the names Advanced Rogue and ARogue.

ascii-fluid.title: ASCII Fluid
ascii-fluid.description: Water poured, dropped and splashed in ASCII: Yusuke Endoh's fluid simulator from the IOCCC, running its scenes one after another
ascii-fluid.provenance: Yusuke Endoh wrote this smoothed-particle fluid simulator for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest in 2012, where it won "Most complex ASCII fluid" (2012/endoh1).
ascii-fluid.page:
Fluid in plain characters. Columns of water collapse and slosh, tea pours
out of a cup, water runs down rice terraces and through funnels, and an
hourglass empties, all computed live by a real fluid simulation and drawn
with slashes, dots and hashes, coloured by how dense the fluid is. The
first scene is the program's own source code, which melts into a puddle.

There are eighteen scenes, each playing for as long as it stays lively,
round and round. Warning: the picture changes quickly and may flicker on
some terminals.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `ascii-fluid -m` shows the original black-and-white
version, `-t 20` gives every scene 20 seconds, `-l` lists the scenes, and
naming scenes plays only those (`ascii-fluid tanada clock`). A text file
of your own works as a scene too: `#` is a wall, any other character is
water.

## History

Yusuke Endoh wrote this for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest
in 2012, where it won "Most complex ASCII fluid". The whole simulator,
smoothed-particle hydrodynamics done in complex numbers, fits in 23
lines of C. The colour version came after the contest, at
the judges' suggestion. Asciiverse runs the entry as the IOCCC publishes
it, inside a small launcher that plays the scenes in turn and quits
on any key.

## Credits

- 2012/endoh1 by [Yusuke Endoh](https://github.com/mame/), from the [IOCCC](https://www.ioccc.org/2012/endoh1/index.html); clock scene by HAMANO Tsukasa, other scenes by the author and the IOCCC judges
- Copyright Landon Curt Noll, licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) ([the IOCCC's summary](https://www.ioccc.org/license.html))
- Asciiverse edition: the launcher, scenes in turn, any key quits; changes listed in PATCHES.md

ascii-patrol.title: ASCII Patrol
ascii-patrol.description: Roll a moon buggy through alien country, hopping craters, blasting rocks and shooting saucers out of the sky, in a love letter to Moon Patrol
ascii-patrol.provenance: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix) wrote ASCII Patrol in C++ from 2017, after Moon Patrol, his favourite arcade game as a child; 1.7 came out in 2019.
ascii-patrol.page:
"Be careful, they come with mega bombers fleet. Their bombs make huge
craters in the ground. Good luck cadet!"

So says the Commander, and off you roll: one cadet, one moon buggy, and
a whole planet's worth of aliens between sector @ and sector Z. The
ground never stops coming. Craters open in front of your wheels,
boulders sit in the road, saucers swing overhead dropping bombs that
punch fresh holes where the road used to be. Your cannon fires two ways
at once, straight ahead to crack the rocks and straight up to pop
whatever is hovering, and your jump has to land on all three wheels or
the suspension goes and so do you.

It is Moon Patrol, lovingly rebuilt in ASCII art by someone who grew up
on it: a parallax sky of mountains and cities, a thumping tracker
soundtrack, and between sectors a radio drama with your Commander about
minefields, missiles, alien eggs and plants that may not be as friendly
as they look. Two full missions, Mission One and The Lowering, five
sectors each. Make it through the minefield and the Commander may even
call you sergeant.

And it is your face on the radio: build an avatar from hair, eyes, nose
and chin in the Player Profile before you set off.

## Controls

- **Right** or **D**: speed up (hold)
- **Left** or **A**: brake (hold)
- **Up** or **W**: jump
- **Down** or **S**: duck (hold)
- **Enter** or **L**: fire, forward and up at once
- **Esc** or **Q**: leave the level
- **Tab**: save a screen shot to the data folder

The letters can be changed under Keyboard Input in the menu. Holding
keys needs a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, Ghostty, foot,
Alacritty, the Linux console); elsewhere the keys are sticky: tap Right
to speed up, Left to slow back down. The Control Panel sets music and
effects volume and the colour mode.

## Credits

- ASCII Patrol: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix),
  [github.com/msokalski/ascii-patrol](https://github.com/msokalski/ascii-patrol),
  2017 to 2022, C++; XM player slides and vibrato by Tom Hargreaves
  (hexwab); CMake build by Michael Hirsch
- Inspired by Moon Patrol (Irem, 1982)
- stb_vorbis by Sean Barrett (public domain); miniaudio by David Reid
  (public domain or MIT-0)
- License: GNU GPL version 3

ascii-wars.title: ASCII Wars!
ascii-wars.description: A boss rush bullet hell: ten bosses in phases of rings, rain, walls, homing swarms and sweeping beams, and you only fire while you move
ascii-wars.provenance: Carlos Alvarez (VikingosTeam) made ASCII Wars! in Rust and Bevy in 2025, ten bosses of glyph rings and aimed shots in a graphical window. Asciiverse brought it to the terminal and grew it into a fuller game.
ascii-wars.page:
Ten bosses, one after another, each a glyph with a grudge. You fire at
the boss whenever you move, and only then: standing still is safe from
nothing, so every dodge is an attack.

Each boss fights in phases. It opens with its old attack, then starts to
move and brings out new ones: aimed fans, rings that turn into spirals,
shots raining from the top, walls with one gap, bullets that curve, speed
up, bounce off the edges or home in, and lasers that show as a dotted
line before they burn. Break a phase and every shot on screen turns into
points; break it without a scratch for a bonus.

Hold focus to move slowly through the tight spots, drop a bomb to clear
the shots round you, and brush past bullets to graze them for points and
the next bomb. A hit makes you blink for a moment; the sixth one ends it.

## Modes

- **Arcade**: all ten bosses in a row, with one score and your health
  carried from fight to fight
- **Practice**: any boss you have reached, with your best time
- **Classic**: the original game as it was, rule for rule
- Easy, Normal and Hard; a demo plays itself when the title is left alone

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **WASD**: move (and fire)
- **Shift**, **Z** or **J** (hold): focus
- **X**, **K** or **Space**: bomb
- **Esc** or **P**: pause; **M**: sound on and off
- **Enter**: choose; the mouse works in the menus
- Gamepad: stick or d-pad to move, **A** or a shoulder button to focus,
  **B** or **Y** to bomb, **Start** to pause

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm,
Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others) or with a gamepad; elsewhere a
move runs on a little after the key is let go.

## Options

- `--level N`: start Arcade at boss N
- `--classic`: the original game
- `--demo`: watch the computer play
- `--mute`: no sound or music

## History

Carlos Alvarez made ASCII Wars! in Rust with the Bevy engine in January
2025: ten bosses drawn with a CP437 font in a graphical window, each
firing rings and aimed shots at a ship that fires back while it moves.
This edition brings it to the terminal and builds a fuller game around
it, with phases, moving bosses, new attacks, bombs, grazing, a score,
colour, sound and a chiptune for every boss. The original lives on
unchanged as Classic.

asciicker.title: Asciicker
asciicker.description: A whole 3D island drawn in characters: walk it, turn it, jump, swing a sword and fill your pack, in Gumix's ASCII action RPG
asciicker.provenance: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix), who also made ASCII Patrol, built Asciicker from 2019 to 2024 as a 3D ASCII game concept that plays in the browser at asciicker.com.
asciicker.page:
Let's kick some ASCII.

Asciicker is a real 3D world made of characters. Hills rise in blocks of
green and dotted grass, pines stand in dark teal stacks, a grey boulder
the size of a house sits by the path, and when you press Q or E the whole
island swings around you, mountains, lake, fences and all. Nothing is
painted on: it is a terrain and mesh renderer that happens to draw with
CP437 instead of pixels.

You wake on a forest path with two armoured companions who follow you
wherever you go. From there the island is yours: wander up the slopes,
jump the rocks, meet the bands of armed strangers, and pick up what you
find. Giant's maces and hammers, an alpha sword, a crossbow, a flail,
light and heavy armour, helmets and shields, unidentified rings in four
colours, meat, eggs and water. Equip a weapon and Enter swings it. Drink
the grey potion and you are riding a wolf; drink the gold one and it is a
giant bee.

Be warned that this is a concept, not a finished adventure: Marcin
Sokalski (Gumix, of ASCII Patrol) built it as a showcase of what ASCII 3D
can do, and the world has more to explore than to accomplish. As a piece
of terminal engineering it is astonishing.

For the curious, it is also scriptable: open the chat with Tab, start a
line with a backslash, and the rest runs as JavaScript against the game,
with `ak.getPos()` and friends.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **WASD**: walk
- **Q** / **E**: turn the view
- **Space**: jump
- **Enter**: attack (with a weapon equipped)
- **I**: open and close the inventory; **1** to **9** pick up the item
  shown under you, **0** drops the highlighted one
- **Tab**: chat; Tab again sends it (a line starting with `\` runs as
  script)
- **Esc** (or **\\**): the game menu (video, sound, controls, main
  menu, exit); Esc again closes it
- A gamepad works too (checked with an Xbox 360 pad)
- Mouse: hold the left button toward where you want to walk, right
  button to jump, drag with the right button to turn the view

In terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol (kitty, Ghostty, foot,
WezTerm) held keys walk and turn smoothly; elsewhere a held key is
followed through its key repeat, so walking starts after your keyboard's
repeat delay. **H** or **?** shows the keys in the game, and the menu's
Controls has a page for the keyboard and one for the mouse.

## Credits

- Asciicker: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix),
  [github.com/msokalski/asciicker](https://github.com/msokalski/asciicker),
  2019 to 2024, C++; [asciicker.com](https://asciicker.com)
- QuickJS-ng by Fabrice Bellard, Charlie Gordon and the QuickJS-ng
  authors (MIT); miniaudio by David Reid (public domain or MIT-0);
  stb_vorbis by Sean Barrett (public domain)
- License: MIT

atc.title: ATC
atc.description: Air traffic control at the terminal: steer jets and prop planes by typed commands, and never let two of them touch
atc.provenance: Ed James wrote ATC in 1986 and 1987 and contributed it to UC Berkeley, where it became one of BSD's games; Mike Sharov later modernised it in his bsd-games.
atc.page:
You are the air traffic controller. Planes enter the radar from the
edges and take off from the airports, and each one has a destination: an
exit on the edge, which it must leave through at 9000 feet, or an
airport, where it must land facing the right way at altitude zero. You
give every order by typing it, while the clock keeps ticking.

The game ends when a plane runs out of fuel, leaves by the wrong way, or
comes next to another plane at the same height. There is no winning,
only lasting longer: the score is the number of planes you brought home
safely.

Prop planes are capital letters and jets lower case, with their altitude
beside them in thousands of feet. Jets move every tick, props every
other tick.

## Controls

A command is a plane's letter, then what it should do, then Enter. Type
`?` at any point to see what can come next, and Backspace to take back
the last part.

- **a** and a number: climb or descend to that altitude in thousands of
  feet; **a+** and **a-** (or **ac** and **ad**) change it by that much.
  At an airport, climbing means take off
- **t** and a direction: turn to that heading, with **w e d c x z a q**
  for 0, 45, 90 and so on round to 315 degrees; **tl** and **tr** turn 45
  degrees left or right, **tL** and **tR** 90
- **tta**, **ttb**, **tte** and a number: turn towards that airport,
  beacon or exit
- **c**: circle, clockwise; **cl** circles the other way
- **ab** and a number, after a turn or circle: wait until the plane
  reaches that beacon
- **m**, **u**, **i**: mark, unmark or ignore a plane on the radar
- **Enter** on its own, or **Space**: let time pass
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw the screen

From the manual: `atlab1` turns plane A left at beacon 1, `gtte4ab2`
turns plane G towards exit 4 at beacon 2, `ma+2` climbs plane M by 2000
feet, and `stq` turns plane S to 315 degrees.

## Options

Started from a shell, `atc -l` lists the scenarios (Default, Atlantis,
Killer, OHare, TicTacToe, Easy and more) and `atc Killer` plays one;
`atc -s` shows the scores.

## History

Ed James wrote ATC in 1986 and 1987 and contributed it to UC Berkeley,
where it became one of BSD's games. This edition is Mike Sharov's bsd-games, which compiled the
scenarios into the program and redrew the screen with curses.

bastet.title: Bastet
bastet.description: Falling blocks with a mean streak: instead of picking the next block at random, Bastet works out which one would hurt you most and sends that
bastet.provenance: Federico Poloni wrote Bastet in C++ and ncurses; it reached Slashdot in 2005, and he rewrote it for 0.43 in 2009.
bastet.page:
A falling-blocks game where the game is against you. Every other one
picks the next block at random; Bastet looks at your stack, tries every
block in every place it could go, and hands you the one that does you
the least good. Waiting for the long straight piece to fill a deep
gap is a plan that does not work here. Clearing even a few lines is an
achievement, and a long game is a real one.

Rows clear when they are full, as you would expect: 100 points for one
row, 300 for two, 500 for three and 800 for four at once. Every ten
rows the level goes up and the blocks fall faster.

There are two games. The normal one shows the next block, and Bastet
picks the block after that knowing you have seen it. The harder one
has no preview at all, and the chooser is tuned for that. Each has its
own top ten.

## Controls

- **Left**, **Right**: move the block
- **Down**: move it down one row
- **Space**: turn it clockwise, **Up**: turn it the other way
- **Enter**: drop it straight to the bottom
- **p**: pause
- **Ctrl+C**: quit at once (high scores already made are kept)

Every key can be changed in Customize keys.

## Files

Keys and high scores are kept in the player's data folder,
`~/.local/share/bastet` (`%APPDATA%\bastet` on Windows).

## History

Federico Poloni wrote Bastet; version 0.41 reached Slashdot in April
2005, and his 0.43 rewrite of 2009 split the chooser into the two games
above. It is packaged by Debian, Fedora and
others. This edition has Debian's fix for printing names, and fixes of
our own: Enter drops the
block as the documentation always said, scores and keys follow
`XDG_DATA_HOME` instead of needing a setgid binary, and it builds for Windows.

battlestar.title: Battlestar
battlestar.description: A tropical adventure in the classic style: escape a doomed starship, then explore an island of natives, wizards and a goddess
battlestar.provenance: David Riggle wrote Battlestar in 1979, and it became one of BSD's games; Mike Sharov modernised it in his bsd-games from 2016 to 2020.
battlestar.page:
You wake in a luxurious stateroom aboard the last battlestar, while
explosions shake the ship. Get off it, find your way down to a tropical
island, and explore its beaches, palm groves, caves and a village, until
you win the hand of a goddess.

It is an adventure in the classic style, typed in plain English, but
less of a puzzle box than most: the fun is in exploring its 275 rooms.
Along the way there is a fight in space, played in real time.

## Controls

Type a command and press Enter. The parser understands simple English,
several objects at once and the word you used last:

- **take**, **drop**, **wear**, **draw**, **put on**, **take off**,
  **throw**, **eat**, **open**, **use** and many more: `take knife and
  sword, drop all`
- **ahead**, **back**, **left** and **right** (or **a**, **b**, **l**,
  **r**), **up** and **down**: move. Directions are relative to where
  you face; find a compass to know where north is
- **look**, **inven**, **score**
- **save**: save the game; it is restored the next time you start
- **quit**: leave

## History

David Riggle wrote Battlestar in 1979 "to experiment with the niceties
of the C Language", and it became one of BSD's games.
This edition is Mike Sharov's bsd-games. Between 2016 and 2020 he made
the space fight winnable within its time limit, took out the original's
sexual violence (marrying the goddess now wins the game), renamed the
parts borrowed from Battlestar Galactica, and added saving and a score
table.

beneath-a-typographic-sky.title: Beneath a Typographic Sky
beneath-a-typographic-sky.description: Revolution's Beneath a Steel Sky in the terminal: Union City rebuilt out of Braille dots, its words set in type
beneath-a-typographic-sky.provenance: Revolution Software made Beneath a Steel Sky in 1994 and released it as freeware in 2003. This edition brings it to the terminal through a Rust port of ScummVM's engine.
beneath-a-typographic-sky.page:
Robert Foster grew up in the Gap, the wasteland outside Union City, until security men came for him and his helicopter came down in the city. Now he is on the run in a vast city of soaring tower blocks, with only Joey, a talking robot circuit board, for company, and he wants to know why they took him.

This is Revolution Software's Beneath a Steel Sky, the whole game, in your terminal. Every pixel of Dave Gibbons' art becomes a dot of a Braille character, so Union City is rebuilt out of type, and everything the game says is set in your terminal's own font. The speech, effects and AdLib music play as they did in 1994.

## Controls

- **Left click**: look at something
- **Right click**: use it, take it, talk, or walk through an exit
- **Pointer to the top edge**: the inventory; click an item to hold it, then right click it onto something
- **F5** or **q**: options, save, restore, subtitles and speech, language, restart, quit
- **Esc**: skip the intro or a cut scene; **.** skips a line of speech
- **p**: pause; **F2**: Braille, half blocks or quadrants; **Ctrl+F**: fast mode

The intro plays the first time; after that a start menu offers Continue, which picks up where you quit. Saves go to `~/.local/share/typographic-sky`.

## Options

- `--skip-intro`: start a new game at once
- `--mute`: no sound
- `--game-font`: the game's own pixel fonts instead of type, for very large terminals

The game starts in your system's language when it has it (English, German, French, Swedish, Italian, Portuguese or Spanish subtitles; the speech is English) and remembers the one you choose in F5.

## History

Revolution Software released Beneath a Steel Sky in 1994 for MS-DOS and the Amiga, and gave it away as freeware in 2003. ScummVM brought it to modern systems from Revolution's own source. This edition runs the unmodified CD version's data in a Rust port of ScummVM's engine and draws it in a terminal.

## Credits

- Beneath a Steel Sky: Revolution Software, 1994; directed by Charles Cecil; art and characters by Dave Gibbons; written and scored by Dave Cummins; programmed by David Sykes, Tony Warriner and James Long
- Game content (C) Revolution Software Ltd, freeware: free to share, never to be sold
- The sky engine: Robert Goeffringmann, Oliver Kiehl, Joost Peters and the ScummVM team (GPL-3.0-or-later)
- AdLib music: Nuked-OPL3 by Nuke.YKT, in Tony Gies' Rust port (LGPL-2.1-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse, GPL-3.0-or-later

blightmud.title: Blightmud
blightmud.description: Terminal MUD client in Rust with Lua scripting and screen-reader support
blightmud.provenance: Blightmud is Linus Probert's MUD client in Rust, developed with its contributors on GitHub.
blightmud.page:
Blightmud is a terminal MUD client built for scripting: everything from
triggers and aliases to its own plugins is written in Lua. It speaks GMCP
and MSDP for MUDs that send structured data, has a screen reader mode,
spellchecks what you type and can play a MUD's sounds.

## Getting started

- `blightmud --connect <host>:<port>`: connect straight away
- `/connect <host> <port>`: connect from inside Blightmud
- `/help`: the built-in manual
- `/quit`: quit

## Credits

- Blightmud: Linus Probert and contributors
- Asciiverse edition: builds and packaging, no code changes
- License: GPL-3.0

blue-chairs.title: Blue Chairs
blue-chairs.description: One strange drink at a party, and the night turns into a dream you have to walk through
blue-chairs.provenance: Chris Klimas wrote Blue Chairs in 2004. It came second in that year's Interactive Fiction Competition and won Best Game at the 2004 XYZZY Awards.
blue-chairs.page:
A party at a house you have never been to, an attic stacked with junk and folding chairs painted carnival blue, and a guy with a cough syrup bottle full of something green: twenty-three dollars for the best dream of your life. What follows is a strange, sad and funny night that goes a long way from that attic.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/blue-chairs`.

## Credits

- Blue Chairs: Chris Klimas, 2004
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

book-and-volume.title: Book and Volume
book-and-volume.description: A new sysadmin is paged all night across a strange tech-boom city
book-and-volume.provenance: Nick Montfort wrote Book and Volume, a satire of the dot-com office, in 2005.
book-and-volume.page:
Sunday, 9:05 pm. You wake in your new apartment in nTopia to a pager buzzing like a dental drill. You are the new system administrator, and the errands come one after another across the city of nTopia, each with its deadline.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/book-and-volume`.

## Credits

- Book and Volume: Nick Montfort, 2005
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 2.5
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

braincurses.title: BrainCurses
braincurses.description: Crack a hidden code of four colours in ten guesses, led only by red and white markers: a classic code-breaking game
braincurses.provenance: Brian Derr wrote braincurses in 2002 and rewrote it in C++ on ncurses in 2015 and 2016.
braincurses.page:
The computer picks a secret code of four colours, repeats allowed, from
red, green, yellow, blue, magenta and white. You have ten guesses to find
it. After each guess, markers tell you how close you came: a red X for
every colour in the right place, a white X for every right colour in the
wrong place. The markers are always listed reds first, so they never say
which of your colours earned them.

Work it out from the answers; the secret is shown when you crack it or
run out of guesses.

## Controls

- **r g y b m w**: type a colour (red, green, yellow, blue, magenta,
  white); the guess is scored once every place has a colour
- **Left**, **Right**, **Backspace**: move back and change a guess
- **y** or **Enter** after a game: play again; **n** stops
- **q**: quit

## Options

- `braincurses -c 5` or `-c 6`: a longer code
- `braincurses -g 12`: the number of guesses (1 to 15)

## Credits

- braincurses: [Brian Derr](https://github.com/bderrly/braincurses), under
  the GPL version 2
- Asciiverse edition: q to quit, the
  result kept on screen, fixes for 5 and 6 colour codes and incomplete
  guesses, and a Windows build

bsd-backgammon.title: BSD Backgammon
bsd-backgammon.description: The BSD backgammon of 1980: you against the computer or a friend, with the doubling cube, saved games and a tutorial that teaches the rules
bsd-backgammon.provenance: Alan Char wrote backgammon and its tutorial, teachgammon, at UC Berkeley by 1980, and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on.
bsd-backgammon.page:
Backgammon as it came with BSD Unix: you play White against the
computer, or two players share the keyboard. The board is redrawn in
place after every move, the computer offers and takes doubles, and a
game can be saved and picked up later.

New to the game? Answer yes when it asks whether you want the rules:
teachgammon explains backgammon section by section and then plays a
practice game with you, move by move.

## Controls

At your colour's prompt:

- **Space** or **Enter**: roll the dice
- **d**: double
- **r** or **Ctrl+L**: redraw the board
- **s**: save the game, **q**: quit

At the Move prompt, type your moves and press **Enter**:

- **8-5**: move a man from point 8 to point 5
- **13/4**: move a man on point 13 by a roll of 4
- separate moves with commas or spaces: `8-5,6-5`
- **b** is the bar and **h** is home: `b-20`, `3-h`

## Options

- `-w` or `-r`: play White or Red against the computer, skipping the
  questions; `-b`: two players
- `backgammon <name>`: pick up the game saved under that name

## History

Alan Char wrote backgammon and its tutorial at UC Berkeley (the
copyright is from 1980), and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on. This
edition keeps saved games in the player's own data folder. One fix changes
how the computer plays: when it judged whether a lone man of yours could
be hit, it looked at the wrong squares, past the end of the board. It is
part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

bsdtrek.title: BSD Trek
bsdtrek.description: Eric Allman's 1976 Star Trek for Unix: hunt Klingons by warp, phaser and torpedo, one typed command at a time
bsdtrek.provenance: Eric Allman wrote Trek at UC Berkeley in 1976 and it shipped with BSD's games; Kenji Rikitake's bsdtrek later made the FreeBSD and DragonFly BSD version build on Linux.
bsdtrek.page:
The original Star Trek game of BSD Unix. The Klingons are invading the
Federation, and the Enterprise has a limited number of stardates to
destroy them. Warp between the quadrants of the galaxy, scan for enemies,
fight with phasers and photon torpedoes, and dock at starbases to refuel
and repair, while damage, novas, black holes and distress calls get in
the way.

It plays like a 1970s terminal session: you type a command, the computer
prints the result. Nothing is on screen until you ask for it, so the
scans are your eyes.

## Controls

Type a command and press Enter. Each command can be shortened to its
first letters, and anything the game needs that you leave out, it asks
for. `?` lists what it accepts at any prompt.

- `srscan` and `lrscan`: short and long range scans
- `move`: travel under warp power, at the factor set with `warp`;
  `impulse` for short hops
- `phasers` and `torpedo`: fight
- `shield up` or `shield down`, `cloak`
- `dock` and `undock` at a starbase, `rest` to repair
- `status`, `damages`, `computer` for charts and course calculations
- `dump` saves the game; answer `restart` to "What length game" to
  continue it
- `terminate` ends the game

At the start you choose the length (`short`, `medium`, `long`) and the
skill (`novice` to `impossible`).

## History

Eric Allman wrote Trek at UC Berkeley in 1976, and it was part of BSD's
games from then on. This edition comes from Kenji Rikitake's bsdtrek,
the FreeBSD and DragonFly BSD version made to build on Linux. The
Asciiverse fixes the build for current compilers and Windows, keeps the
saved game safe from updates, and makes restoring work again: it had
been broken on every current system.

The same game, without the Star Trek names and with the whole map always
on screen, is in the catalog as Space Pirate Hunt, from BSD Games.

candybox2.title: Candy Box 2
candybox2.description: You have 1 candy. Eat it, throw some on the ground, ask for new features, and watch a candy counter grow into a whole ASCII world of quests, spells and lollipops
candybox2.provenance: aniwey made Candy Box in 2013 as a programming exercise; it went viral, and he promised its sequel would be free software. Candy Box 2 came out on 24 October 2013.
candybox2.page:
You have 1 candy.

That is all you get at first: a number, ticking up once a second, and a
button to eat them. Eat them, or throw ten on the ground and see what
happens. Before long you are requesting new features from the developer
with your hard-earned sweets, and every one of them opens the world a
little wider: a status bar, a health bar, a map.

Then the map turns out to be a whole country. A village with a candy
merchant who would do anything for candies, a forge, a lonely house, a
lighthouse with questions, a desert, a bridge, a cave, a castle full of
things that want to hit you. You go questing with whatever you can carry,
cast spells from a grimoire, brew potions in a cauldron by the book, farm
lollipops, boot up a computer that runs GNU/Candies, and find out what is
really inside your box. All of it drawn in ASCII art, all of it in your
terminal.

Candy Box 2 is aniwey's sequel to his 2013 browser hit, and it is full of
jokes, secrets and surprises that are much more fun found than read
about. So this page will stop here.

## Controls

- **Mouse**: click buttons and links, hover over items for their
  descriptions, wheel to scroll (Shift+wheel sideways)
- **Tab** / **Shift+Tab**: move between buttons, lists and fields;
  **Enter** presses the highlighted one, so the game plays without a mouse
  too
- **Typing**: click a field (or Tab to it) and type; Enter sends
- **Page Up** / **Page Down**: scroll a long page; **Shift+arrows**
  sideways; on the world map the **arrows** move the view
- In quests and minigames the game has its own keys; in
  terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol (kitty, Ghostty, foot,
  WezTerm) held keys work as in the browser
- **Ctrl+C** or **Ctrl+Q**: quit. Save first, on the game's **SAVE** tab
  (it can also save every ten minutes); `candybox2 --slot 1` starts with
  slot 1

The game's own **CFG** tab changes the language (seventeen translations besides English)
and has "Invert colors?" for a black page instead of the white one.

## Credits

- Candy Box 2: aniwey (2013), ideas, game design and code;
  [github.com/candybox2/candybox2.github.io](https://github.com/candybox2/candybox2.github.io),
  kept by Andrei Kvapil
- ASCII art: Tobias Nordqvist, dixsept, Dani "Deinol" Gómez, GodsTurf and
  aniwey (CC BY-SA 3.0)
- Translations by their translators, credited in the game's CFG tab
- Terminal edition: Asciiverse, on QuickJS-ng (Fabrice Bellard, Charlie
  Gordon and the QuickJS-ng authors, MIT)
- License: GNU GPL version 3 or later for the code, CC BY-SA 3.0 for the art

canfield.title: Canfield
canfield.description: The solitaire with a betting account: buy the deal, build down in alternate colours, and keep a running tally of what you won and lost
canfield.provenance: Steve Levine wrote Canfield at UC Berkeley by 1980; Steve Feldman moved it to curses, Kirk McKusick and Mikey Olson added card counting and McKusick the betting, with interface work by Eric Allman.
canfield.page:
Canfield is a solitaire played for money. Thirteen cards make
the stock; the first card of the foundation sets the base rank for all
four foundations, which build up by suit and wrap from king to ace. The
four tableau piles build down in alternate colours and move only as
whole piles, and an empty space is filled from the stock. Deal the
hand to the talon three at a time.

This version keeps the books. The deal costs $13, a look at
the game before buying it another $13, the rest of the game $26, and
every card on a foundation pays $5. Each run through the hand after the
first costs $5, card counting costs $1 a card, and time costs $1 a
minute. Your account carries over from game to game.

## Controls

Each move is two letters or digits, typed at the Move prompt:

- **s#** and **sf**: stock to tableau pile #, or to the foundation
- **t#** and **tf**: talon to a tableau pile, or to the foundation
- **##**: tableau pile to tableau pile
- **#f**: tableau pile to the foundation
- **ht**: deal the hand to the talon
- **c**: card counting on or off
- **b**: the betting account, **i**: the instructions, **x**: hide the box
- **q**: give up this game

## History

Steve Levine wrote Canfield at UC Berkeley (the copyright is from 1980).
Steve Feldman moved it to curses and debugged it, Kirk McKusick and
Mikey Olson added card counting, McKusick the betting, and Eric Allman
and McKusick cleaned up the interface. This edition keeps the betting account
in the player's own data folder rather than a system file. It is part
of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

cataclysm-dda.title: Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead
cataclysm-dda.description: Survive the end of the world in a huge open-world roguelike: scavenge, craft, build, drive and fight the dead and far stranger things
cataclysm-dda.provenance: Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead began as a fork of Whales' Cataclysm (on GitHub from 2010) by Kevin Granade, TheDarklingWolf and GlyphGryph, and has been built by CleverRaven and thousands of contributors since.
cataclysm-dda.page:
The world has ended, and you are one of the few left. Cataclysm: Dark Days
Ahead drops you into a huge, persistent, randomly made world overrun by
the dead, giant insects, killer robots and things far stranger. Scavenge
the ruins for food and gear, learn skills by using them, craft and build
almost anything, fix up a car and get out of town. Every turn counts and
death is final, but a new world is always waiting.

This is the terminal edition, drawn entirely in text, with all of the
game's translations.

## Controls

- `h` `j` `k` `l` `y` `u` `b` `n`, the arrow keys or the number pad: move
  (walk into a door to open it, into a monster to attack it)
- `.` or `5`: wait a turn; `<` and `>`: go up and down stairs
- `g`: pick up; `e`: examine; `o` and `c`: open and close; `s`: smash
- `i`: inventory; `w`: wield; `W`: wear; `E`: eat or drink; `a`: use an item
- `f`: fire; `t`: throw; `r`: reload
- `&`: craft; `*`: construct; `$`: sleep
- `m`: overmap; `x` or `;`: look around; `P`: messages
- `?`: all key bindings, which can be changed
- `S`: save and quit; `Esc`: game menu

## History

Whales wrote Cataclysm, a grab-bag apocalypse roguelike, around 2010. Kevin
Granade, TheDarklingWolf and GlyphGryph forked it into Dark Days Ahead, a
grittier and more realistic survival game, and the project has grown under
CleverRaven into one of the largest open-source games, with around two
thousand contributors. Asciiverse builds it as is, with every file a
player has, saves and
options alike, kept in the player's data folder.

## Credits

- Original game: Whales
- Dark Days Ahead: CleverRaven and contributors, project manager Kevin
  Granade
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: CC BY-SA 3.0; the bundled fonts and libraries under their own
  licences, listed in LICENSE.txt

cataclysm2.title: Cataclysm II
cataclysm2.description: Whales' unfinished alpha rewrite of the zombie survival roguelike Cataclysm: wash up on a beach, make your way to town and fight what is left of it
cataclysm2.provenance: Whales wrote Cataclysm II from 2013 to 2016 as a ground-up rewrite of Cataclysm, the roguelike Whales wrote from 2010 to 2013, and left it an early alpha. It is a separate project from Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead, the community fork of the first Cataclysm.
cataclysm2.page:
**An unfinished alpha.** Cataclysm II is the rewrite of Cataclysm that its
author, Whales, began in 2013 and stopped working on in 2016. It is
playable for a while, but much is missing, things are rough, and
characters cannot be saved yet: each game is one sitting.

Fifty years after the cataclysm that filled the world with monsters and
raised the dead, you wash up on the beach of a shipwreck with a few things
from your old life. Make a character from stats, traits and a profession,
pick through the wreck, read the world map and set out across fields,
forests, swamps and salt marsh. Towns are where the zombies are: fast
ones, brutes, spitters and smoke zombies. Every character starts with a
handful of small missions (eat this, read that) that pay experience, and
experience buys skills.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn** or the numpad: move, the last four diagonally; walk into a
  monster to attack it, into a door to open it
- **,**: pick up, **d**: drop, **i**: inventory
- **w**: wield, **W**: wear, **T**: take off, **e**: eat, **R**: read,
  **a**: apply
- **t**: throw, **f**: fire, **r**: reload
- **o** and **C**: open and close, **s**: smash, **x**: examine,
  **;**: look
- `<` and `>`: stairs up and down
- **:** or **M**: the world map (**q** leaves it)
- **@**: your character, **K**: skills
- **Q**: end the game

On the first screen, **H** opens the manual, with every key and how the
game works; **W** makes and chooses worlds.

## Saving

Worlds you make under **W: Manage Worlds** are kept in your data folder
and can be played again with a new character. Characters themselves are
not saved: **L: Load Character** was never finished.

## History

Whales wrote Cataclysm, a post-apocalyptic roguelike, from 2010 to 2013;
its players carried it on as Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead, the big
community fork that is still developed today. Cataclysm II
is a different project: Whales' own start over, with new code, its own
interface layer and data files, set fifty years after the first game. It
was never finished, and its last change, in 2016, did not even compile.
This edition adds two contributors' unmerged fixes
and crash fixes of our own, keeps the game data beside the program and
your worlds in your data folder, and leaves the game as Whales left it.

## Credits

Whales, with Aninimouse, Trevmillion, superninjakiwi, WeendVidente,
Drakasin and others. GNU General Public License, version 3.

cbirds.title: cbirds
cbirds.description: A flock of birds wheels across the terminal in braille: Reynolds' boids, with sliders, hawks and a mouse that scatters them
cbirds.provenance: cbirds is by Alessandro Palliccia (clainstone), in C99 with nothing but the C library, from 2025.
cbirds.page:
A flock of birds in your terminal, drawn in braille: eight hundred boids
that keep their distance, match their neighbours and stay together, the
rules Craig Reynolds published in 1987. It opens by writing BOIDS in birds,
lets go, and flocks. Move the pointer into the flock and it scatters; leave
it alone for a minute and it starts moving its own sliders.

## Controls

- **q**: the flock flies off the top, and cbirds quits
- **h**: the panel of sliders: **b**/**B** boundary, **s**/**S**
  separation, **a**/**A** alignment, **t**/**T** turning, **p**/**P**
  perception, **v**/**V** speed (lowercase lowers, uppercase raises)
- **Space**: pause, **.** one frame
- **+** and **-**: more birds, fewer; **k** and **K**: a hawk more, one fewer
- **e**: tails; **Tab**: next preset; **0**: back to the defaults
- **Mouse**: the pointer scatters the flock

## Options

From a terminal: `--preset murmuration` for the starling look, `--hawks 2
--color ice`, `--flocks 3 --color ember`, `--3d` for a murmuration in three
dimensions, `--clock` or `--say "back in five"` to have the flock write,
`--matrix` for raining birds, `--render kitty` for real sprites in Kitty
or Ghostty, and `--screensaver` to quit on any key. `cbirds --help` lists
them all.

## Credits

- cbirds: [Alessandro Palliccia](https://github.com/clainstone/cbirds), after
  Craig Reynolds' boids (SIGGRAPH 1987)
- Asciiverse edition: upstream's program unchanged, built static for
  Linux and for macOS
- License: MIT

cblocks.title: cblocks
cblocks.description: Twelve classic sliding-block puzzles, from Dudeney's Motor-Car Problem of 1903 to Conway's Century-and-a-Half, with undo and the fewest steps to beat
cblocks.provenance: Brian Raiter wrote cblocks in C for the Linux console and curses (2000, last updated 2020).
cblocks.page:
Slide the blocks around the tray until they stand where the puzzle
wants them. Blocks only slide into empty space; they cannot be lifted
or turned. Each puzzle has a known shortest solution, counted in steps
(a step is any number of slides of one block), and the game shows how
close you came.

Twelve classic puzzles are included, among them H. E. Dudeney's
Motor-Car Problem (1903), Sam Loyd's Moving Day Puzzle (1914) and John
Conway's Century-and-a-Half (1982), and more can be added as text files.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the selection square by square
- **h j k l**: select the next block in that direction
- **H J K L**: slide the selected block; or drag a block with the mouse
- **g**: show the goal
- **x** / **z**: undo / redo a slide; **X** / **Z**: undo / redo a step
- **R**: start again; **s** / **r**: save / restore a position
- **N** / **P**: next / previous puzzle
- **?**: help; **q**: quit

## Credits

- cblocks: Brian Raiter ([muppetlabs.com/~breadbox](https://www.muppetlabs.com/~breadbox/software/cgames.html)),
  2000 to 2020, written in C with curses; part of his cgames
- Puzzles: the classics of H. E. Dudeney, Sam Loyd, John Conway and
  others, as collected by Brian Raiter
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

cbonsai.title: cbonsai
cbonsai.description: A bonsai tree grows in its pot branch by branch, then another, and another: a calm terminal screensaver
cbonsai.provenance: cbonsai is by John Allbritten and contributors, in C on ncurses, since 2020.
cbonsai.page:
A bonsai tree grows in its pot, one branch at a time: the trunk climbs and
twists, shoots split off left and right, and leaves gather at the tips in
light and dark green. When the tree is done it stands for a few seconds,
then a new one starts from a fresh seed, never the same twice. Leave it
running as a quiet screensaver.

If you quit halfway through a tree, it is kept, and the next time you start
cbonsai that tree finishes growing before new ones follow.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit (the tree in progress is saved)

From a terminal, cbonsai has many more options: `cbonsai -l` grows one
tree and keeps it on screen, `cbonsai -p` prints a tree and exits,
`cbonsai -m "text"` puts a message beside the tree, and `-L`, `-M` and `-c`
change its life, branching and leaves. `cbonsai --help` lists them all.

## Credits

- cbonsai: [John Allbritten and contributors](https://gitlab.com/jallbrit/cbonsai)
- Asciiverse edition: saves in your data folder, Ctrl+C saves too, and a
  Windows build
- License: GPL-3.0-only

cgram.title: Cgram
cgram.description: Sunday-paper cryptograms: crack a substitution cipher hiding one of La Rochefoucauld's maxims, letter by letter
cgram.provenance: David A. Holland wrote cgram around 2004 and added it to NetBSD's games in 2013; Roland Illig reworked it in 2020 and 2021.
cgram.page:
A cryptogram, the puzzle from the Sunday paper. A saying is written in a
substitution cipher, every letter swapped for another, and you work out
the key. Put the cursor on a letter and type what you think it really
is: every copy of that letter changes at once, so one good guess lights
up the whole text. Short words and common letters are the way in.

Each game hides one of the maxims of François de La Rochefoucauld, the
17th century French moralist ("Self-love is the greatest of
flatterers"), in J. Hain Friswell's 1871 translation, 456 of them in
all, with a fresh key every time. When every letter is right, the game
says so.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, or **Ctrl-B**, **Ctrl-F**, **Ctrl-P**, **Ctrl-N**: move
  the cursor
- **A letter**: decode the letter under the cursor as that letter
- **\***: hint mode, which shows correctly decoded letters in bold
- **~**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `cgram file` makes a cryptogram of that file's
text instead of a maxim.

## History

David A. Holland wrote cgram around 2004 "for my own amusement", as he
put it when he added it to NetBSD in 2013; Roland Illig reworked it in
2020 and 2021. It takes its text from the fortune program, which the
Asciiverse does not ship, so this edition brings its own collection of
maxims from Project Gutenberg. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog, under the BSD licence.

changes.title: Changes
changes.description: Crash-landed on a strange forest world, wake up as something new and learn to survive
changes.provenance: David Given wrote Changes for the 2012 Interactive Fiction Competition.
changes.page:
You wake and see blood, and a dying face that turns out to be your own reflection in a cockpit canopy. Then you wake again, somewhere warm and soft, and something is different. On a forest world after a crash, you have to work out what you are now, and how the life of this forest fits together.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/changes`.

## Credits

- Changes: David Given, 2012
- License: Creative Commons BY-ND (the author's terms); shipped unchanged
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

checkers.title: Checkers
checkers.description: Checkers against the computer or a friend, with forced jumps, chains of jumps and kings
checkers.provenance: abakh wrote Checkers for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
checkers.page:
Each side starts with 12 men. Men move one square diagonally forward;
a man that reaches the far side becomes a king (**K**), which moves
diagonally both ways. You capture by jumping over an enemy piece, and
can capture several in one turn with a chain of jumps. If you can jump,
you must. A side wins when the other cannot move, and 50 turns without
any gain for either side is a draw.

At the start the game asks who plays each side: by default you play
black, shown in red, which moves first, and the computer plays white.
Two people can share one keyboard, and the computer can play itself.
Without `-p` the computer starts out weak, so a beginner can win the
first game, and after that it adjusts to how well you play.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: on your piece, pick it up; on a free square, move it there.
  In a chain of jumps, pick the same piece up again for each jump
- **Mouse**: click instead of Enter
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: resign

## Options

- `-1 h` or `-1 c`: a human or the computer plays black
- `-2 h` or `-2 c`: the same for white; either one skips the questions
- `-p 3`: a fixed strength for the computer, from 1 to 127
- `-n`: quit after one game instead of offering a rematch

## History

Checkers is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

chess-tui.title: chess-tui
chess-tui.description: Chess in the terminal: against Stockfish at five strengths, a friend on the same keyboard or over the network, or anyone on Lichess
chess-tui.provenance: chess-tui is Thomas Mauran's terminal chess game in Rust and Ratatui, from 2023 and still maintained with many contributors.
chess-tui.page:
Chess in the terminal, with a proper board: large pieces drawn in block
characters on a big enough terminal, chess symbols on a smaller one.
Play against Stockfish, which comes with the game, at full strength or at
one of four easier levels; play a friend on the same keyboard, or over
the network; or sign in to Lichess and play people online.

Choose a clock from bullet to classical, or none. Move with the cursor
keys or the mouse, or type a move in chess notation. The move history and
the captured pieces sit beside the board, and a game can be saved, loaded
from a PGN file and stepped through.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: pick up a
  piece, then put it down
- **m**: type a move in chess notation (`e4`, `Nf3`, `O-O`)
- **Esc**: put the piece back; **s**: change the board's look
- **?**: help with every key; **q**: quit
- In the menus: **Up** and **Down** to choose, **Enter** to go on

## Options

- `--difficulty easy`, `medium`, `hard` or `magnus`: the computer's
  strength for Play Bot
- `-e <path>`: use another UCI chess engine instead of the bundled
  Stockfish
- `-l <token>`: a Lichess API token, for playing on Lichess
- `--no-sound`: no move sounds (macOS and Windows; this build has none on
  Linux)

## Credits

- chess-tui: Thomas Mauran and contributors
  ([github.com/thomas-mauran/chess-tui](https://github.com/thomas-mauran/chess-tui)),
  2023 on, written in Rust with Ratatui
- Stockfish 11: the Stockfish developers
  ([stockfishchess.org](https://stockfishchess.org)), GPL-3.0-or-later,
  shipped beside chess-tui with its licence and source
- Asciiverse edition: Stockfish included and found without any setting
- License: MIT (chess-tui), GPL-3.0-or-later (Stockfish)

christbashtree.title: Christmas Tree
christbashtree.description: A tree of green stars with coloured lights twinkling on and off and a flashing greeting: ChristBASHTree as one small program
christbashtree.provenance: Sergio Lepore wrote ChristBASHTree in bash and tput in 2014, with later contributions to 2018.
christbashtree.page:
A Christmas tree of green stars stands on its trunk above a greeting.
Coloured lights come on all over the tree one after another and go out
again, and the word CODE in the greeting flashes in the colour of the
newest light: "MERRY CHRISTMAS, And lots of CODE in" next year.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `christbashtree es` shows the Spanish tree: "FELICES
FIESTAS, Y mucho CODIGO en" next year.

## History

Sergio Lepore wrote ChristBASHTree for Christmas 2014 as a short bash
script that drew with `tput`, run straight from the web with curl, and
others added to it until 2018. Asciiverse ported it to one small C
program with the same tree, lights and pace, so it runs on Windows too
and needs no bash; any key quits.

## Credits

- ChristBASHTree: [Sergio Lepore](https://github.com/sergiolepore/ChristBASHTree) and contributors
- Asciiverse edition: the C port, any key quits, Windows
- License: public domain (the Unlicense)

chroma.title: Chroma
chroma.description: An abstract puzzle game: steer two pieces through traps of falling arrows and bombs to collect every star, with unlimited undo
chroma.provenance: Amf wrote Chroma in C (2010 to 2025), with a graphical version and this terminal one, chroma-curses.
chroma.page:
Chroma is an abstract puzzle game. Each level is a maze of walls, dots,
arrows and bombs with stars scattered through it, and you have two
player pieces. Collect every star, then leave through the door. It
starts simple enough to pick up at once, and gets hard enough to tax
anyone.

The pieces are not explained. Arrows slide the way they point whenever
there is room, and a moving one can crush a player piece; bombs, circles
and dots have rules of their own, and part of the game is finding out
exactly how they behave and set each other off. The first
six levels of each set bring the pieces in one by one. Later levels
need both player pieces working together.

There are 21 levels in two sets, nine for beginners and twelve for
experts, and they can be played in any order. Mistakes cost nothing:
undo goes back as far as you like, and redo plays it forward again.
Positions can be saved and loaded, and a saved solution replays move by
move. A level editor lets you build and test your own, and Chroma can
also play levels from the similar games XOR and Enigma.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the active player piece
- **Space** or **Enter**: swap to the other player piece
- **Delete**, **Backspace** or **U**: undo a move
- **Insert** or **Y**: redo
- **F**: let everything moving come to rest at once
- **P**: pause
- **Escape**: the game menu (save, load, replay, revert, display
  options, leave the level)

Keys can be changed under Display Options. In the editor, Page Up and
Page Down choose a piece and Space places it.

## Files

Saved and solved positions, levels under construction and the display
options are kept in `~/.local/share/chroma` (`%APPDATA%\chroma` on
Windows). Exported levels and solutions go to your home folder.

## History

Amf released Chroma in 2010 with a graphical SDL version and this
terminal one, and kept it going until version 1.21 in November 2025;
there is also a browser version and a port to the BBC Micro. It is
packaged by Debian. The Asciiverse edition is the terminal version, with
the levels found beside the program and saved positions in the player's
data folder.

## Credits

Chroma is by Amf (level7.org.uk), under the GNU GPL version 2 or later.

clani.title: CLiAni
clani.description: Endless scrolling noise patterns in ASCII: Voronoi cells, Perlin clouds and cellular shapes, with rain, zig-zag and static effects
clani.provenance: Ryan Huth (hury) wrote CLiAni in C++ on ncurses (2020 to 2024), with resize handling by Sergeant-Salz.
clani.page:
Patterns made of plain characters scroll down the screen without end, a
new row every tenth of a second. Faint dots and colons rise into dense
blocks of D, # and @ wherever the noise is strongest. Each run starts from
a new random seed, so the landscape is never the same twice.

Started from a terminal, CLiAni picks its pattern from options; with none
it opens a menu to choose.

- **Flavours**: Voronoi (the default here), Perlin noise and cellular
  Voronoi
- **Effects**: scrolling, raining (the pattern shows only in falling
  streaks), zig-zag, and static
- **Characters**: any ten, from faint to dense

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

From a terminal: `clani -f cell -e raining` picks the flavour and effect,
`-s 42` a fixed seed, `-c " .oO@"` your own characters, and `clani` on its
own opens the menu (arrows, Enter, F1 to leave). `clani -h` lists the
options.

## Credits

- CLiAni: [Ryan Huth](https://github.com/hu-ry/CLiAni), resize handling by
  Sergeant-Salz
- Asciiverse edition: options that start an animation at once, any key to
  quit, current ncurses, and bug fixes
- License: GPL-3.0-only

clidle.title: clidle
clidle.description: A five-letter word-guessing game in the style of Wordle: six tries, letters that turn colour one by one, a keyboard that keeps track of your letters, and a running score
clidle.provenance: Ajeet D'Souza wrote clidle, a terminal word-guessing game, in Go in 2022 and still maintains it.
clidle.page:
Guess the hidden five-letter word in six tries. Type a word and press
Enter, and its letters turn colour one at a time: green for a letter in
the right place, yellow for a letter that is in the word somewhere else,
grey for a letter that is not in it at all. Only real words count.

Below the board, an on-screen keyboard colours each letter as you learn
about it, so you can see at a glance which letters are left. Every game
picks a new word at random, and a running score adds up how well you
do: 100 points for one guess, down to 50 for six.

clidle is a five-letter word-guessing game in the style of Wordle.

## Controls

- **a** to **z**: type a letter
- **Backspace**: clear the last letter
- **Enter**: check the guess; after a game, start the next one
- **Ctrl+R**: start a new word at any time
- **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

The on-screen keyboard needs a terminal of at least 58 columns by 30
rows.

## Options

- `-serve 0.0.0.0:1337`: run clidle as an SSH server, so others can play
  it with `ssh -p 1337 your-host`

## Credits

- clidle: Ajeet D'Souza
  ([github.com/ajeetdsouza/clidle](https://github.com/ajeetdsouza/clidle)),
  2022 on, written in Go with Charm's Bubble Tea and Lip Gloss
- Asciiverse edition: letters revealed one by one, Esc to quit, the
  score kept in view in a 30-row terminal, long messages fitted to narrow
  windows; written to be offered back upstream
- License: MIT

clines.title: Console Lines
clines.description: Color Lines in the terminal: slide coloured chips across a 9x9 board to line up five of a kind before the board fills, by keyboard or mouse
clines.provenance: Pawel S. Veselov wrote Console Lines in C on curses (2002 to 2006), after the classic Color Lines.
clines.page:
The Lines game in your terminal. Coloured chips appear on a 9x9 board
three at a time. Each turn you move one chip to any free cell it can
reach by sliding up, down, left and right around the others. Line up
five or more of the same colour, across, down or diagonally, and they
vanish, and you get another move before new chips arrive. When the board
is full, the game is over.

Every chip removed scores a point, and longer or crossing lines score
more: n chips removed at once score n + n x (n - 5). Clearing on several
turns in a row adds a growing bonus, b x b for the b-th such turn after
the first.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h**, **j**, **k**, **l**: move the cursor
- **Space**: pick up the chip under the cursor (it starts to jump), then
  put it down on a free cell
- **Mouse**: click a chip, then the cell to send it to
- **Ctrl+L**: redraw; **q**: quit (your score is saved)

## Options

- `-l`: list the high scores
- `-m b`: black and white, with letters for the colours
- `-w`, `-t`, `-c`, `-i`, `-n`, `-N`: board width and height, number of
  colours, line length, chips per turn and chips to start with (scores
  are only kept with the defaults)

## High scores

Your best score is kept in your own folder
(`~/.local/share/clines`), so it survives updates, and shows under the
board while you play.

## History

Pawel S. Veselov started Console Lines in 2002, after the classic Color
