Lines, added mouse support (both the terminal's and GPM on the Linux
console) and scoring, and released 1.0.4 in October 2006 with resizing,
smaller terminals, black and white mode and saved high scores. His site
has since gone; ALT Linux and OpenBSD kept packaging it.

The Asciiverse edition keeps scores in your own folder, animates the
jumping chip without curses calls inside signal handlers, and makes sure the mouse keeps
working in terminal emulators.

cmines.title: cmines
cmines.description: Minesweeper as it should be: Beginner, Intermediate and Expert fields, a timer and best times, flags and chording, keys or mouse
cmines.provenance: Brian Raiter wrote cmines in C for the Linux console and curses (2000, last updated 2020).
cmines.page:
Clear the minefield without stepping on a mine. Every square you open
tells you how many of its eight neighbours hide mines; flag the ones you
are sure of and open the rest. The first square you open is never a
mine.

Three fields come ready: Beginner (8x8, 10 mines), Intermediate (16x16,
40 mines) and Expert (16x30, 99 mines), each with its own best time. Add
your own to the setup file, or start with one by name: `cmines Expert`.

When a number already has all its mines flagged, Return (or both mouse
buttons) opens all its other neighbours at once, the quick way through a
field.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move; **H J K L**: move by three
- **Space** or **left click**: open a square
- **.** (dot) or **right click**: flag a mine
- **Return** or **middle click**: open the neighbours of a number
- **p**: peek at a square
- **?**: help and the best times
- **n**: new game; **b**, **i**, **e**: Beginner, Intermediate, Expert
  (between games); **q**: give up the game; **Q**: quit

## Options

- `-t`: keep the timer running on screen
- `-e`: show the game's mood as an emoticon
- `-s FILE`: use another setup file

## Credits

- cmines: Brian Raiter ([muppetlabs.com/~breadbox](https://www.muppetlabs.com/~breadbox/software/cgames.html)),
  2000 to 2020, written in C with curses; part of his cgames
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

colossal-cave.title: Colossal Cave Adventure
colossal-cave.description: The original text adventure: explore the cave, gather its treasures, and say the magic word
colossal-cave.provenance: Will Crowther wrote Adventure in 1976 and Don Woods expanded it in 1977. Eric S. Raymond ported their last version, Adventure 2.5 (1995, 430 points), to modern C as Open Adventure.

upstream.name: Eric S. Raymond, after Will Crowther (1976) and Don Woods (1977)

colossal-cave.page:
Somewhere nearby is Colossal Cave, where others have found fortunes in treasure and gold, though it is rumored that some who enter are never seen again. You start at the end of a road, before a small brick building. Take what you need, find the way in, and bring the treasures back. The cave is full of passages, mazes and puzzles, a pirate and some unfriendly dwarves, and words of magic scrawled on its walls.

This is the game that started the genre, in the 430-point version 2.5 that its authors finished in 1995.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in one or two words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **score**
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**), and **in**, **out**, **building**
- **take lamp**, **light lamp**, **unlock grate**, **drop bird**
- **help** and **info** explain more; the game offers hints when you seem stuck, at a cost in points
- **save** writes your game to a file you name, and quits; to continue, start a new game and say **resume**
- **quit** to stop

The up and down arrows recall earlier commands. Saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/colossal-cave` (on Windows, `%APPDATA%\colossal-cave`).

## History

Will Crowther wrote Adventure in 1976 in FORTRAN on a PDP-10 at Bolt, Beranek and Newman, modelled on the Colossal Cave complex in Kentucky. Don Woods expanded it at the Stanford AI Lab in 1977 into the 350-point game that spread across the world's computers. The two kept working on it until 1995 and Adventure 2.5, with more cave and 430 points. Eric S. Raymond ported that version to modern C as Open Adventure; it plays the same game, with a command line that remembers.

## Credits

- Adventure: Will Crowther, 1976; Don Woods, 1977; both, version 2.5, 1995
- Open Adventure: Eric S. Raymond and contributors, BSD-2-Clause
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

counterfeit-monkey.title: Counterfeit Monkey
counterfeit-monkey.description: A spy fused from two people slips through an island of wordplay, changing things by changing their names
counterfeit-monkey.provenance: Emily Short's Counterfeit Monkey (2012) won Best Game and four more categories at the 2012 XYZZY Awards; its community now maintains it in an open-source repository.
counterfeit-monkey.page:
Can you hear me? Two people have just been synthesised into one body to escape the island of Anglophone Atlantis, and you are both of them. In your pocket is a letter-remover: point it at a thing and take a letter out of its name, and the thing changes. A pear becomes a pea, a crate becomes a rate. A big, generous puzzle game built entirely on wordplay.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/counterfeit-monkey`.

## Credits

- Counterfeit Monkey: Emily Short, 2012; maintained by the Counterfeit Monkey contributors
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 (the feelies are not included)
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

crawl.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup
crawl.description: The open-source roguelike: go down through the Dungeon and its branches for the Orb of Zot, with gods to serve and runes to win
crawl.provenance: Linley Henzell wrote Linley's Dungeon Crawl in 1997, and the Stone Soup team has developed it as Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup since 2006, in the open on GitHub.

upstream.name: Linley Henzell (1997) and the Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup team (since 2006)

crawl.page:
The big open-source roguelike, still in active development. Pick one of
27 species and 26 backgrounds, go down through the Dungeon and its
branches, collect at least three runes and bring the Orb of Zot back to
the surface. Turn-based, one life per character, no grinding: autoexplore
and autotravel take you through the dull parts, and the game is about the
choices in the dangerous ones. This is the console edition, drawn in text.

## Controls

- **h j k l y u b n**, the arrow keys or the number pad: move, and attack
  by moving into a monster; with **Shift**, run
- **o**: explore the level automatically
- **Tab**: fight the nearest monster
- **5** or **s**: rest or wait
- **g** or **,**: pick up; **i**: inventory
- **w**: wield; **W**: wear armour; **P**: put on jewellery
- **q**: drink; **r**: read; **z**: cast a spell; **a**: abilities
- **f**: fire or throw; **V**: evoke
- **<** and **>**: take the stairs; **G**: travel to a level; **X**: map
- **?**: every command
- **Ctrl-S**: save and quit; your game continues the next time you start

## History

Linley Henzell wrote Linley's Dungeon Crawl in 1997; Brent Ross
maintained it later and released its final alpha, 4.1, in 2005. Since
2006 the Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup team has carried it on, with new
versions ever since, in the open on GitHub. The Asciiverse edition is
the console game, without tiles, with saves, morgue files and init.txt
in your data folder (`~/.local/share/crawl`).

## Credits

- Game: Linley Henzell; Brent Ross and the Crawl 4.0 team; the Dungeon
  Crawl Stone Soup team and contributors (see CREDITS.txt in the game's
  docs)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

cribbage.title: Cribbage
cribbage.description: Cribbage against the computer, to 61 points: discard to the crib, play to 31, count your hand, and peg round the board
cribbage.provenance: BSD's cribbage was written by Earl T. Cohen, with Ken Arnold's screen interface (UC Berkeley, 1980). Mike Sharov rewrote it from scratch for his bsd-games in 2016.

upstream.name: Mike Sharov, after Earl T. Cohen and Ken Arnold (1980)

cribbage.page:
Cribbage for one player against the computer. Each hand you are dealt
six cards and lay two away into the crib, which belongs to the dealer.
Then the two of you take turns laying cards and calling the count,
scoring for fifteens, pairs, runs and reaching 31, and finally each hand
is counted with the turned-up starter card. The pegs on the board keep
the score.

A game here is played to 61 points, once round the board, and a match
ends after seven games, with a skunk counting as two. The computer
counts both hands, and waits before the show so you can count yours
first.

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**, or **j** and **k**: choose a card
- **Space** or **Enter**: discard or play the chosen card, and go on
  after a pause
- **q** or **F10**: quit

Cards that would take the count past 31 are skipped, and when only one
card can be played it is played for you.

## History

Cribbage was one of the early BSD games: Earl T. Cohen wrote the game
logic and Ken Arnold added the screen interface (UC Berkeley, 1980).
Mike Sharov replaced it with a rewrite of his own in 2016 for his
bsd-games, and has since fixed its scoring of pairs, runs and flushes
and taught the computer to avoid easy fifteens for its opponent. Suits
show as card symbols in a UTF-8 terminal.

csokoban.title: csokoban
csokoban.description: Sokoban with 1,043 levels by David W. Skinner, from the gentle Microban sets to the very hard Sasquatch ones, with undo and saved solutions
csokoban.provenance: Brian Raiter wrote csokoban in C for the Linux console and curses (2000, last updated 2020).
csokoban.page:
Push every box onto a goal square. You can only push, never pull, and
only one box at a time, so a box in a corner is stuck there for good.
The rules take a minute to learn; the levels take much longer.

This csokoban comes with David W. Skinner's fifteen finished sets, 1,043
levels. Start with **Microban**: small puzzles, each showing one idea,
good for beginners and children. **Mas Microban**, **Microban III** and
**IV** carry on in the same spirit. The **Sasquatch** sets, I to XI, range
from medium to very hard, many of them built on symmetry.

The game remembers your best solution to every level, in moves and in
pushes, and starts where you left off. Undo and redo as far as you
like, save a position to come back to, or record a sequence of moves and
play it again. Some of the later levels are big; when one does not fit,
the game says how much room it needs and waits for a bigger window.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: walk and push; **H J K L**: walk as far
  as you can
- **x** / **z**: undo / redo a move; **X** / **Z**: undo / redo eight
- **R**: start the level again; **s** / **r**: save / restore a position
- **N** / **P**: next / previous level
- **m**, **p**: record moves, play them back
- **?**: help; **q**: quit

## Options

- `csokoban sasquatch-03`: start with a set by name; `csokoban -l` lists
  them
- `csokoban -12`: start at level 12

## Credits

- csokoban: Brian Raiter ([muppetlabs.com/~breadbox](https://www.muppetlabs.com/~breadbox/software/cgames.html)),
  2000 to 2020, written in C with curses; part of his cgames
- Levels: David W. Skinner <sasquatch@bentonrea.com>, Microban (2000),
  Mas Microban (2002), Microban III and IV, and Sasquatch I to XI (1999
  on), freely distributed with credit, as he asked
- Sokoban: Hiroyuki Imabayashi, Thinking Rabbit, 1982
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

curse-of-war.title: Curse of War
curse-of-war.description: Real-time strategy on a hex map where you never move a unit: plant flags, build cities and let your people march
curse-of-war.provenance: Alexey Nikolaev wrote Curse of War in C on ncurses in 2013.
curse-of-war.page:
A fast real-time strategy game on a map of hexagons, where you never
command a single soldier. Four countries start in the corners; you rule the
green one and win by conquering the whole map.

Your people are your army. They grow in villages, towns and fortresses and
spill out over the grassland around them. Plant flags and they gather
there; push a line of flags into enemy land and your crowds will fight
theirs tile by tile. Surround a gold mine to own it, and spend the gold on
new cities. The game plays out like a war of fronts and supply lines, and
the computer rulers each fight with their own personality.

Start gently with `curseofwar -i4 -q1 -dee`: the strongest starting
position against the easiest opponents.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the cursor
- **Space**: add or remove a flag
- **r** or **v**: build a village, then grow it into a town and a fortress (160, 240 and 320 gold)
- **x**: remove all your flags
- **c**: remove half of your flags
- **f** and **s**: speed up and slow down
- **p**: pause
- **q**: quit, after confirming with **y**

Keys are lowercase; with Caps Lock on only **q** works.

Your flags show as a white **P** on the right of a tile, computer flags as
an **x** on the left. Dots and colons on grassland show how many people live
there.

## Options

- `-W N`, `-H N`: map width and height (default 21)
- `-S rect`, `-S rhombus`, `-S hex`: map shape; hex maps hold six countries
- `-l N`: number of countries
- `-i 0` to `-i 4`: how unequal the starting positions are
- `-q N`: start in the best (1) or a worse position
- `-r`: completely random start
- `-d ee`, `e`, `n`, `h`, `hh`: computer difficulty, easiest to hardest
- `-s sss` to `-s fff`: game speed
- `-R N`: map seed, to replay the same map
- `-T`: show the population timeline
- `-E N`: host a game for N players over the network (UDP port 19140)
- `-C address`: join a hosted game

## History

Alexey Nikolaev released Curse of War in 2013 and developed it in the open
on GitHub, where others contributed fixes until 2021; Debian, Ubuntu and
other distributions have packaged it ever since. It also has an SDL
graphical version, which is not part of this edition.

## Credits

- Game: [Alexey Nikolaev](https://a-nikolaev.github.io/curseofwar/), with contributions from the [curseofwar](https://github.com/a-nikolaev/curseofwar) community
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

curses.title: Curses
curses.description: Hunting for a map in the family attic leads into myth, history and a house full of puzzles
curses.provenance: Graham Nelson's Curses (1993) is a landmark of the years after Infocom.
curses.page:
That tourist map of Paris must be up here somewhere in all this clutter. Your search through the attics of Meldrew Hall, an old family house full of junk, curiosities and ancestors, turns into something much larger. A long, witty and famously hard puzzle game.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/curses`.

## Credits

- Curses: Graham Nelson, 1993 to 1995
- License: The author's terms: free to distribute and use, provided no profit is involved and the file is unmodified
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

dab.title: Dots and Boxes
dab.description: Dots and boxes against the computer: draw one line a turn, close a box to claim it and move again, and the board grows each time you win
dab.provenance: Christos Zoulas wrote dab, in C++, for NetBSD's games in 2003. Mike Sharov rewrote it in C for his bsd-games in 2016.
dab.page:
The pencil and paper game, against the computer. Take turns drawing one
line between two neighbouring dots. Whoever draws the fourth side of a
box owns it and must draw again, so a single careless line can hand
over a whole chain of boxes. When the board is full, the player with
more boxes wins.

Win, and the next board is one box bigger in each direction, up to
level 9. Lose, and the game is over.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: move to a line
- **Space** or **Enter**: draw it
- **q** or **F10**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `dab 5` starts at level 5; levels go from 1 to 9.

## History

Christos Zoulas wrote dab for NetBSD's games in 2003, in C++. Mike
Sharov rewrote it in C for his bsd-games in 2016. For the strategy, its
manual points to Elwyn Berlekamp's book The Dots and Boxes Game.

darrt.title: Darrt
darrt.description: Twenty-six letters fly around a target: stop them with their keys and land them on the bullseye
darrt.provenance: abakh wrote Darrt for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
darrt.page:
Darts with the keyboard. The twenty-six letters of the alphabet fly
around the screen, bouncing off its edges, over a round target. Press a
letter's key and that letter keeps going for a moment, then stops where
it is and stays there. You have ten shots to land letters as near the
centre of the target as you can.

The nearer a letter lands, the more it scores, doubling with every step
toward the middle; a letter outside the target costs points, and one
exactly in the middle scores a million. Since the letters keep
moving for a while after you press, the skill is in judging where each
one is going. When the ten shots are used up, your score goes on a list
of the best eleven.

The game needs an 80 by 24 terminal.

## Controls

- **A** to **Z**: stop that letter
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **Esc**: end the round; at the end of a round, **n** quits and **y**
  plays again (pressing **Q** a second time in a round also ends it)
- **Ctrl-C**: quit at once

## History

Darrt is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

doctor-m.title: The Life (and Deaths) of Doctor M
doctor-m.description: A doctor wakes in a windswept land between life and death, and walks back through his life
doctor-m.provenance: Michael D. Hilborn entered The Life (and Deaths) of Doctor M in the 2011 Interactive Fiction Competition, under the name Edmund Wells.
doctor-m.page:
You land in an endless meadow of shale and scrub under a funnel of storm clouds, beside a signpost that will not keep still. In the sky, paramedics are working on someone. As Doctor M, you go back through the scenes of a life, talking to the people in it, to find out what you did and what it was worth. Type ABOUT and CONVERSATION first.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/doctor-m`.

## Credits

- The Life (and Deaths) of Doctor M: Michael D. Hilborn, 2011
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

dopewars.title: dopewars
dopewars.description: Thirty days to pay off the loan shark: buy low, sell high and dodge the cops across New York, alone or online
dopewars.provenance: Ben Webb has written and maintained dopewars since 1998, after John E. Dell's MS-DOS game Drug Wars.
dopewars.page:
You start in the Bronx with $2,000, a $5,500 debt to the loan shark that
grows every day, and a coat with room for 100 units. You have a month. Buy
drugs where they are cheap, jet to another part of New York, sell where
they are dear, and stay ahead of Officer Hardass and his deputies. Prices
crash and spike with the news on the street; guns, the bank and a bigger
coat are there if you can pay for them.

Play alone, or connect to a dopewars server and deal against other people,
who can trade with you, page you and tip off the cops about you.

## Controls

Each screen tells you which keys it takes. In the market:

- **b**: buy, **s**: sell
- **j**: jet to another part of town
- **l**: list players or high scores
- **g**: give money or drugs to another player (online)
- **q**: quit

When the cops catch up with you, **r** runs and **f** fights, if you have a
gun.

## Options

- `-n`: single player, without the server menu
- `-o host`: connect to a dopewars server, `-p port` (default 7902)
- `-s`: run a public server, `-S` a private one
- `-c`: add a computer player to a server
- `-a`: "antique" mode, as close to the original Drug Wars as possible
- `-P name`: your dealer's name
- `-b`: no colours

High scores are kept in `~/.local/state/dopewars.sco`.

## History

John E. Dell's Drug Wars was an MS-DOS game; Ben Webb rewrote it as
dopewars for Unix and Windows from 1998, adding networked multiplayer, a
metaserver listing public servers, and a configurable everything.

The Asciiverse edition is the text-mode client and server only, with two
small changes: high scores
go in your own state folder, and the static build finds your system's
certificates to reach the metaserver.

## Credits

- Original game: John E. Dell (Drug Wars)
- dopewars: [Ben Webb](https://dopewars.sourceforge.io/) and contributors
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

drop4.title: Drop4
drop4.description: Fit the falling four-square shapes into complete rows before the stack reaches the top
drop4.provenance: Drop4 is BSD's tetris, which Chris Torek and Darren F. Provine adapted from a 1989 International Obfuscated C Code Contest winner (UC Berkeley, 1992). Mike Sharov renamed it and changed its look in 2016 for his bsd-games.

upstream.name: Chris Torek and Darren F. Provine (1992), Mike Sharov

drop4.page:
Shapes of four squares fall into a well one at a time. Move and turn
each one as it falls so they pack together: every row you complete
vanishes and the rows above drop down. When the stack reaches the top,
the game is over. The game speeds up as you go, and dropping a shape
early scores more.

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**, or **j** and **l**: move
- **Up** or **k**: turn a quarter counterclockwise
- **Space** or **Down**: drop
- **>**: go faster
- **p**: pause
- **q**, **F10** or **End**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `drop4 5` starts at level 5. Levels go from 1 to
9; at level n the shapes fall n times a second.

## History

This is BSD's tetris, which Chris Torek and Darren F. Provine adapted
from a winning 1989 entry to the International Obfuscated C Code
Contest (UC Berkeley, 1992); Hubert Feyrer added the preview of the next shape in 1999. In
2016 Mike Sharov renamed it Drop4 for his bsd-games and changed its
look: a wider well, no animation when rows clear, and the score and
next shape on the right. The high score table is kept per player.

durthang.title: Durthang
durthang.description: Terminal MUD client in Rust and Ratatui, with passwords kept in the system keyring
durthang.provenance: Durthang is Raimo Geisel's MUD client in Rust.
durthang.page:
A terminal MUD client: keep your servers and characters in one list, pick
one, and you are in. Durthang keeps
passwords in your system's keyring (never in its config file), and has
aliases, triggers, an automap panel and notes per character.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move through servers and characters
- **Space**: expand or collapse a server
- **N**: add a server; **n**: add a character
- **Enter**: connect with the selected character
- **Ctrl+Q**: disconnect, back to the list
- **q**: quit

## Credits

- Durthang: [Raimo Geisel](https://github.com/Pommersche92/durthang)
- Asciiverse edition: packaging, and keyring stores for macOS and Windows
- License: GPL-3.0-only

fate.title: Fate
fate.description: A pregnant queen sees her child's future in a crystal ball and sets out to change it
fate.provenance: Victor Gijsbers entered Fate in Spring Thing 2007.
fate.page:
You are nine months pregnant and the contractions have begun. Trapped in a castle with more enemies than friends, Queen in name but not in influence, you look into your crystal ball to see what waits for your son. You can wait in your den for his fate to arrive, or act, quickly and ruthlessly, before the waters break.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/fate`.

## Credits

- Fate: Victor Gijsbers, 2007
- License: GNU GPL version 2 or later; the source (Fate-source.zip) is in the archive
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

fifteen.title: Fifteen
fifteen.description: The fifteen puzzle: slide the shuffled tiles back into order, with the keys or the mouse
fifteen.provenance: abakh wrote Fifteen for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
fifteen.page:
The classic sliding puzzle. Fifteen numbered tiles sit in a four by four
frame with one gap, shuffled. Slide tiles into the gap until they are in
order again, 1 to 9 and then a to f, with the gap in the bottom right
corner. A tile turns green when it is in its right place.

Put the cursor on a tile in the same row or column as the gap and press
Enter: that tile moves toward the gap, and so do all the tiles between
them, so a whole line can move in one go.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: slide
- **Mouse**: click a tile to slide it
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, Fifteen takes the size of the board, from 3 to 7:

- `fifteen -s 5`: a five by five board; past 9 the tiles carry letters,
  lower case and then upper case
- `-n`: do not ask to play again after a solved board

## History

Fifteen is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

firework-rs.title: Fireworks
firework-rs.description: An endless fireworks show in ASCII: rockets burst in showers of colour all over the window
firework-rs.provenance: Fireworks is the demo of firework-rs, a Rust crate for ASCII-art fireworks by Wayoung7, from 2024.
firework-rs.page:
A fireworks show that never ends: rockets burst all over the window in
showers of coloured ASCII, sparks trailing and falling as they fade, a few
at a time in a small window and many in a big one. Every burst picks its
own place, moment and palette, from embers and golds to ice blue and
neon pink.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `firework -d 0` to `firework -d 4` play five designed
shows (add `-l` to loop one), `-g` fades the sparks through a colour
gradient (best on a black background), `--fps` sets the frame rate from 5
to 30, and `--cjk` suits fonts with wide characters.

## Credits

- firework-rs: [Wayoung7](https://github.com/Wayoung7/firework-rs), the
  crate and its `firework` demo
- Asciiverse edition: any key quits
- License: MIT

fisher.title: Fisher
fisher.description: Drop a hook through ten rows of sea life and reel in the deep catches, without letting a fish cross your line
fisher.provenance: abakh wrote Fisher for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018, as a port of Deep Sea Fisher, a MikeOS game.
fisher.page:
A fishing game. Your line hangs from a boat into ten rows of water, and
something swims along each row, half of them one way and half the other.
Lower the hook to a row and wait: when that row's swimmer reaches the
line it bites, and you reel it up to the boat for points.

The deeper the catch, the more it is worth: one point for a plastic bag
near the surface, then PVC bottles, face masks, shrimp, algae, jellyfish,
molluscs, actual fish and salmon, up to 100 points for a tuna at the
bottom. But anything that swims into the line above your hook takes the
hook with it. You have ten hooks, and when they are gone the game is
over and your score goes on the high score list.

## Controls

- **Down arrow** or **s**: lower the hook
- **Up arrow** or **w**: raise the hook, and reel in a catch
- **F1** or **?**: help
- **q** or **Esc**: end the game; it shows the high scores and asks whether to play again

## History

Fisher is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
It is a port of "Deep Sea Fisher", a MikeOS game. The collection is
packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and
pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

fortress-earth.title: Fortress Earth
fortress-earth.description: The sky opens over a great city, then another, then another. Ten armies, twelve cities, one world slowly turning red. Your move, Commander.
fortress-earth.provenance: Filip Hracek wrote Fortress Earth in Dart between 2019 and 2025 as a keyboard-only strategy tech demo for the browser: armies that spread over a map of the Earth like a cellular automaton.
fortress-earth.page:
The first one comes down twenty days in. Nobody knows what they are. HQ
calls them the Arrivals, which is the polite word for it.

They land near the great cities and spill out across the land, red and
hungry, tile by tile. You have ten armies (Marines, Infantry, a couple of
Squads, the Air Force and HQ itself) and a map of the whole planet that
breathes. Throw them at Cairo. Hold Paris tight. Turn the Air Force loose
and let it hunt.

Every patch of ground is fought over. Your units pour into the gaps like
water, the enemy shoves back wherever it is strong, and the world goes
white or red one tile at a time. Your armies can fly; the war on the
ground stops at the shoreline.

Ten landings are coming, each one sooner than the last. Smash a landing
site outright, or ring it in once it runs dry and let it starve. Lose six
cities at once, or every last army, and that's it: Earth has fallen.

Your generals will keep you posted. Mostly with bad news.

## Controls

- **0** to **9**: pick an army, then:
  - **G** and a city's letter: go there
  - **T**: hold tight around the city
  - **E**: spread out further
  - **D**: go after the enemy anywhere
- **Space**: pause
- **F1**, **?** or **H**: how to play
- **Q** or **Esc**: leave (it asks first), **Ctrl+C**: leave at once

Fortress Earth shows the whole world at once and needs a terminal of at
least 186 columns by 55 rows: a big window, or a smaller font.

## Options

- `--demo`: watch the computer fight the war

## Credits

- Fortress Earth: Filip Hracek
  ([github.com/filiph/fortress-earth](https://github.com/filiph/fortress-earth)),
  2019 to 2025, written in Dart with Bob Nystrom's malison and piecemeal;
  the armies' simulation is his
- Map: Natural Earth (public domain)
- Asciiverse edition: the war around his simulation (landings, cities,
  sieges, reports, victory and defeat), the help screen, the map redrawn
  for terminal cells, and the terminal build
- License: MIT

frobtads.title: FrobTADS
frobtads.description: The terminal player for TADS 2 and TADS 3 stories, I Am Prey among them
frobtads.provenance: FrobTADS is Nikos Chantziaras' terminal player for TADS, the adventure system by Michael J. Roberts.
frobtads.page:
FrobTADS plays text adventures written with TADS, Michael J. Roberts'
Text Adventure Development System. TADS 2 games
(.gam) and TADS 3 games (.t3) both run, from the 1990s classics to
modern stories such as I Am Prey, with a status line, colours and
scroll-back. Give it a story file and play.

## Use

- `frob <story file>`: play a story (.gam and .t3 files)
- `frob -d <story file>`: the same, keeping saved games in the current
  folder instead of the story's
- `save` and `restore` inside a story keep your place
- At `[More]`, Space shows the next page and Enter the next line

In Asciiverse, story titles such as I Am Prey come with FrobTADS built in,
so you only need this to play story files of your own.

## Credits

- FrobTADS: Nikos Chantziaras; TADS: Michael J. Roberts
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, two small fixes
  (builds without libcurl; `-d` keeps TADS 3 saves in the current folder)
- License: TADS Freeware Source Code License; free to share, never sold

frotz.title: Frotz
frotz.description: The standard player for Z-machine stories: Infocom's games, Zork among them
frotz.provenance: Stefan Jokisch wrote Frotz, a player for Infocom's Z-machine games; David Griffith and contributors maintain it.
frotz.page:
Frotz plays text adventures written for the Z-machine, the virtual
computer Infocom created in 1979 so its games could run anywhere. That
covers Infocom's own catalogue, Zork among them, and most interactive
fiction written since in Inform. Give it a story file and play.

## Use

- `frotz <story file>`: play a story (.z3, .z5, .z8 and Blorb files)
- `save` and `restore` inside a story keep your place

In Asciiverse, story titles such as Zork come with Frotz built in, so you
only need this to play story files of your own.

## Credits

- Frotz: David Griffith and contributors, after Stefan Jokisch's original
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, no code changes
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

galaxis.title: Galaxis
galaxis.description: Find four lifeboats adrift in a starfield with probes that tell how many they can see, in as few tries as you can
galaxis.provenance: Eric S. Raymond began Galaxis in 1994 as a curses clone of Christian Franz's Macintosh freeware game, and still maintains it.
galaxis.page:
Four lifeboats from a crippled interstellar liner are adrift in a
starfield of 20 by 9 squares. To find them, drop probes: a probe looks in
all eight compass directions and tells you in how many of them it sees a
lifeboat (only the nearest boat in each direction counts). Drop a probe
right on a lifeboat and it is found. Find all four in as few tries as
you can, before the passengers run out of oxygen.

The rays from the cursor are highlighted, so you can see what a probe
would look along. Mark the squares you have ruled out; the game marks
the obvious ones for you as the boats turn up.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **h j k l y u b n** or the **number pad**: move (the
  field wraps round)
- **p**: drop a probe, or ask an old probe again
- **Space**: mark a square as empty, or unmark it
- **o**: turn the ray highlighting off or on
- **Mouse**: click to mark, double-click to drop a probe
- **?**: the rules; **q**: give up and see where the boats were

## Credits

- Galaxis: Eric S. Raymond ([gitlab.com/esr/galaxis](https://gitlab.com/esr/galaxis)),
  1994 on, written in C with curses
- After Christian Franz's freeware Galaxis for the Macintosh
- License: BSD-2-Clause

glider.title: Glider
glider.description: John Calhoun's Glider 4.0 in the terminal: fly a paper glider through a house, riding the air from the floor vents past candles, toasters, darts and sparking outlets
glider.provenance: John Calhoun wrote Glider 4.0 for the Macintosh in THINK Pascal, published by Casady & Greene in 1991, and released its source, art, sounds and houses in 2016.
glider.page:
You are at the controls of a paper glider loose in a big old house, and
the way out is through every room of it. A glider only falls; what keeps
it up is the air from the floor vents, so you drift from vent to vent,
steering left and right and climbing to the ceiling, while the room does
its best to bring you down. "Foresight and daring are rewarded," as John
Calhoun put it in 1991.

He also confessed he had no intention of telling you what everything in
the rooms does: the floor, tables, shelves and books are most certainly
bad, the clocks most certainly good, and you'll enjoy figuring out the
rest. A few freebies: candles lift you too, but not from too close; toast
leaps from the toaster, fish from their bowls; outlets spark, grease
spills, shredders wait; and through the air come slow balloons, paper
'copters of mysterious origin and fast, unforgiving darts. Folded paper
is an extra glider, a battery a burst of speed, rubber bands your only
defense. Ducts and stairs lead on, switches bring back the lights, the
air or a fan, and the faster you cross a room, the bigger its time bonus.

Twelve houses come with it, from The House and Calhoun's own Mad House to
the fans' houses of the day: the 120 rooms of the House of the Rising
Sun, the Glass House with a window in every room, and Hands-off House,
which plays itself. Any Glider 4 house file plays too.

It is Calhoun's game, translated from his Pascal, with his art, sounds
and houses read from his own files. The silhouette view is made for the
terminal: the room softened behind box-drawn furniture, and everything
that moves or hurts drawn sharp in solid colour. Or press **V** for his
art itself, in half blocks.

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **,** and **.**): fly; let go and the glider
  just falls
- **Up** or **Enter**: burn the battery; **Space** or **Down**: fire a
  rubber band
- Mouse: point left or right of the room's middle to fly that way, as on
  the Mac; the button burns the battery
- Gamepad: d-pad or stick to fly, **A** fires, **B** or the right
  trigger boosts, **Start** pauses
- **Tab**: pause; **V**: the other view; **M**: sound; **B**: music;
  **Q**: end the game
- Type **Ozma** on the title screen for fifty gliders, as in the original

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm,
Ghostty and others). Elsewhere a tap sets the glider going that way, as
Glider's own tap control did; the mouse and a gamepad don't depend on it.

## Options

- `glider "Mad House"`: start in a built-in house; `--houses` lists them
- `glider path/to/house`: play a Glider 4 house file from disk
- `--watch`: no controls, for Hands-off House
- `--silhouette`, `--original`: which view to start in
- `--mute`: no sound

## History

Calhoun wrote Glider 4.0 for the Macintosh in THINK Pascal, and Casady &
Greene published it in 1991, "a wistful flight of fancy for those rainy
days". It came with a Room Editor, and players built houses of their own
and passed them around on America Online. Steve Sullivan offered $10 to
the first player to send him a screenshot of his House of the Rising Sun
finished, and soon after, Calhoun wrote asking to include it in a
collection of houses to be sold. Calhoun followed Glider 4 with Glider
PRO in 1994, and released Glider 4's source, art, sounds and houses
under the MIT licence in 2016.

This edition keeps his rules and his house files as they were. Three
timers in Hands-off House are moved, as it was tuned on a slower Mac, so
it still plays itself to the end.

## Credits

- **Glider 4.0**: John Calhoun, 1991, published by Casady & Greene;
  sound code by Patrick Buckland, electric bass by John Gnaegy
- **Houses**: John Calhoun (The House, Mad House), Ward Hartenstein
  (Hands-off House, Glass House), Steve Sullivan (House of the Rising
  Sun), JeffrC (House Full of Stuff and the one Next Door, House of
  Doom), Tony Korlath (Lumpy's Home), Brian Eaton (Usher House); Combo
  House joins The House to Mad House
- **Terminal edition**: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

glulxe.title: Glulxe
glulxe.description: The standard player for Glulx stories: most Inform 7 games, Counterfeit Monkey among them
glulxe.provenance: Glulxe is Andrew Plotkin's player for Glulx, the virtual machine he designed in 1999 when Inform games outgrew the Z-machine.
glulxe.page:
Glulxe plays stories written for Glulx, the virtual machine Andrew Plotkin
designed in 1999 when Inform games outgrew the Z-machine. Most Inform 7
games are Glulx stories: Counterfeit Monkey, Kerkerkruip, Rover's Day
Out and many more. Here they run in the terminal with GlkTerm, so status
lines, side panels and Unicode text all work. Give it a story file and
play.

## Use

- `glulxe <story file>`: play a story (.ulx and .gblorb files)
- `save` and `restore` inside a story keep your place; saves go in the
  current folder
- Page Up and Page Down scroll back through the story

In Asciiverse, Glulx story titles come with Glulxe built in, so you only
need this to play story files of your own.

## Credits

- Glulxe and GlkTerm: Andrew Plotkin
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, four GlkTerm fixes
- License: MIT

gofish.title: Go Fish
gofish.description: The children's card game against the computer: ask for ranks, go fish, and collect the most books of four
gofish.provenance: Muffy Barkocy wrote fish for BSD Unix. Mike Sharov gave it a curses display and one-key play in 2016 and renamed it Go Fish in 2020.
gofish.page:
The traditional children's card game, against the computer. Each of you
gets seven cards and the rest of the deck waits face down. Take turns
asking each other for a rank you already hold: if the other player has
any, they hand them all over and you ask again. If not, you are told to
go fish and draw from the deck; draw the rank you asked for and you keep
going, otherwise it is the other player's turn.

Four cards of one rank make a book, which is set aside. The game ends
when either of you runs out of cards, and the one with the most books
wins. Your hand, the cards left in the deck and the books are always on
show in the panel at the bottom.

## Controls

- **a**, **2** to **9**, **1** (for 10), **j**, **q**, **k**: ask for that rank
- **?** or **F1**: the rules
- **x** or **F10**: quit

## History

Fish was written by Muffy Barkocy for BSD Unix (copyright 1990, with the
University of California). In Mike Sharov's bsd-games, the modern Linux
port of the BSD games, it got a curses display and one-key play in 2016,
and in 2020 its name became Go Fish, so the program no longer collides
with the fish shell. Go Fish is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog, under the BSD licence.

gomoku.title: Gomoku
gomoku.description: Five in a row on a 19 by 19 board against Ralph Campbell's computer player, moved with the cursor
gomoku.provenance: Ralph Campbell wrote Gomoku for BSD in 1994, with a board display based on Peter Langston's goref. Mike Sharov reworked it in 2016 for modern curses, with cursor keys for moves.
gomoku.page:
Gomoku is five in a row, the game played with stones on a Go board, here
against the computer on a 19 by 19 grid. Take turns placing
stones; the first to get five in an unbroken line, across, down or
diagonally, wins.

The computer picks at random who starts, and X always moves first. It
weighs every line of five on the board for both sides, building threats
of its own and blocking yours, so an open three left alone soon becomes
a line that cannot be stopped. Your stones and its stones
are in different colours, and the last move of each side is highlighted
so you can see what just happened.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: move the cursor
- **Space** or **Enter**: place your stone
- **q** or **F10**: end the game

## History

Ralph Campbell wrote Gomoku for BSD Unix in 1994, building the board
display on goref, a program by Peter Langston. Its computer player looks
for combinations of threats in every direction.

Mike Sharov reworked Gomoku in 2016 for his bsd-games, the modern Linux
port of the BSD games: a boxed board centred in
the terminal, moves chosen with the cursor instead of typed coordinates,
and colour for each side. Gomoku is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog, under the BSD licence.

gorched.title: Gorched
gorched.description: Two tanks, one cannon each, a fresh range of hills every round: Scorched Earth for the terminal
gorched.provenance: Ján Čabala (zladovan) wrote Gorched in Go on termloop in 2020, as a homage to Wendell Hicken's 1991 DOS game Scorched Earth.
gorched.page:
Two tanks face each other across a range of procedurally generated hills,
trees and clouds. Take turns setting your cannon's angle and charging up
your shot, watch the shell's arc, and blow craters in the landscape until
one of you lands a hit. The winner scores, the hills are swept away and the
next round starts on new terrain.

Two players share one keyboard. Between rounds each player spends the
points they earned on Attack (bigger explosions, more shooting power) or
Defense (more armour).

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: turn the cannon
- **Space**: start charging; press again to fire at the power shown
- **s**: score board
- **a**: player attributes
- **h**: help
- **Ctrl+R**: restart the round
- **Ctrl+N**: skip to the next round
- **Ctrl+C**: quit

In the score and attributes windows, **Tab** moves between buttons and
**Enter** presses one.

## Options

- `--seed N`: replay the same sequence of rounds
- `--width N`, `--height N`: set the world size instead of filling the terminal
- `--ascii-only`: draw the tanks with plain ASCII, if you see question marks
- `--low-color`: use only the 8 basic colors, if the colors look wrong
- `--fps N`: lower the frame rate to save CPU

## History

Ján Čabala wrote Gorched in Go in 2020 as a homage to Scorched Earth,
Wendell Hicken's 1991 DOS artillery game, and has kept releasing it since.

## Credits

- Game: [Ján Čabala (zladovan)](https://github.com/zladovan/gorched)
- Engine: [termloop](https://github.com/JoelOtter/termloop) by Joel Auterson, terrain from [opensimplex-go](https://github.com/ojrac/opensimplex-go)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

greed.title: Greed
greed.description: Munch as much of a grid of numbers as you can; each number decides how far you move
greed.provenance: Matt Day wrote Greed in C (to 3.0a, 1990); Eric S. Raymond has maintained it since and ported it to Rust in 2026.

upstream.name: Eric S. Raymond, after Matt Day

greed.page:
## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **h j k l y u b n** or the **numeric keypad**: move in any of eight directions
- **p**: show or hide the moves you can make
- **Ctrl+L**: redraw the screen
- **q**: quit

Moving eats as many squares in that direction as the first number you
meet. You cannot leave the board or cross a square you have already eaten;
when no move is left, the game ends. Your score is the number of squares
eaten.

## Options

- `-f`: fit the board to the terminal (av starts Greed this way)
- `-w N`, `-h N`: set the board's width and height
- `-p`: start with possible moves highlighted
- `-r N`: fixed random seed, for replaying the same board
- `-s`: show the high scores

## History

Matt Day wrote the C version and released it up to 3.0a in 1990; it
probably goes back to a DOS game of the 1980s. Eric S. Raymond took over
maintenance and has kept it going since, porting it to Rust in 2026.

## Credits

- C version: Matt Day
- Maintainer and Rust port: [Eric S. Raymond](https://gitlab.com/esr/greed)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: BSD-2-Clause

hack.title: Hack
hack.description: The 1985 dungeon crawl that NetHack grew from: down through the Mazes of Menace for the Amulet of Yendor, with your dog at your side
hack.provenance: Jay Fenlason wrote Hack in 1982 with Kenny Woodland, Mike Thome and Jon Payne, after Rogue, and Andries Brouwer reworked it at the CWI in Amsterdam into the 1985 game, version 1.0.3, that NetHack grew from.
hack.page:
Hack is the dungeon crawl that NetHack grew from. You go down through the
Mazes of Menace, level by level, fighting what you meet, finding armour,
weapons, potions, scrolls, rings and wands, and learning what they do by
trying them. Somewhere far below lies the Amulet of Yendor. You choose to
be a Tourist, Speleologist, Fighter, Knight, Cave-man or Wizard, and your
little dog comes along.

Everything is a letter on the map: you are the `@`, monsters are letters
of their own, `#` is a corridor and `>` the stairs down. Death is final,
and the dead you leave behind may haunt the next player on that level.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the vi way (diagonals on yubn); with **Shift**,
  run
- **s**: search, **.**: rest, **>** and **<**: stairs
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **w**: wield, **W**: wear, **q**: quaff, **r**: read, **e**: eat,
  **z**: zap a wand, **t**: throw
- **?**: help, **/**: what is that symbol
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit, **^R**: redraw

## History

Jay Fenlason wrote Hack in 1982, his first-semester programming
project, with Kenny Woodland, Mike Thome and Jon Payne, after the game
Rogue. Andries Brouwer then reworked it at the CWI in Amsterdam ("in fact an entirely
different game", says its manual), and that 1985 version, 1.0.3, was
shipped with BSD and became the base of NetHack.

NetBSD keeps the original game; Mike Sharov's bsd-games trimmed it in
2018 and later dropped it. The Asciiverse edition ports it to Linux and
macOS and keeps its record, saved games and bones in the player's own
data folder.
Hack is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD
licence.

hangman.title: Hangman
hangman.description: Guess the computer's word a letter at a time before the gallows is finished
hangman.provenance: Ken Arnold wrote Hangman for BSD in 1983, and Mike Sharov cleaned it up for modern curses in 2016.
hangman.page:
The computer thinks of a word and shows a dash for each letter. Guess
the letters one at a time: a right guess fills in every place that
letter appears, a wrong one adds a piece to the gallows. Seven wrong
guesses and the figure is hanged and the word revealed.

Words are at least six letters long. The game keeps playing word after
word, with your average number of wrong guesses for the current game
shown beside the gallows, so you can try to bring it down.

## Controls

- **a** to **z**: guess a letter
- **Space**: give up on this word and go to the next
- **Enter**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `-d` takes a different word list, one word per
line, and `-m` sets the shortest word length, as in `hangman -m 8`.

## History

Ken Arnold wrote Hangman for BSD Unix in 1983, and Mike Sharov cleaned
it up for modern curses in 2016 for his bsd-games, the modern Linux port
of the BSD games. Hangman is part of BSD Games in
the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

The original reads the system's dictionary, which many computers no
longer have, so this edition comes with its own: 61,494 everyday English
and American words from SCOWL 2020.12.07, Kevin Atkinson's Spell Checker
Oriented Word Lists, used under SCOWL's permissive licence.

hauberk.title: Hauberk
hauberk.description: A hundred floors of dungeon, rebuilt every time you take the stairs. Light a candle, grip your stick, and go find out what happened to the last adventurer.
hauberk.provenance: Bob Nystrom has written Hauberk in Dart since 2012 as a roguelike for the web browser, and still works on it.
hauberk.page:
There's a little town at the top of a very long staircase. It has a home
for your loot, six shops with names like Dirk's Death Emporium and
Skullduggery and Bamboozelry, and not much else. Everything interesting is
downstairs.

A hundred levels down, to be exact, and none of them hold still: every
time you take the stairs, the dungeon builds itself anew. Rooms and halls,
dark water and narrow bridges, pools of candlelight and long stretches of
nothing at all. Bring a light. Seriously, bring a light.

Down there: sewer rats, giant cockroaches, scurrilous imps, frosty slimes,
a murderous eye or two and, if you make it that far, The Rat King. Also
the odd hapless adventurer, who got here before you and is not doing well.

Make yourself a dwarf, an elf, a gnome, a human or one of the fae, then an
adventurer, a barbarian or a sorceror. Then decide how much death should
hurt. Gentle: you lose what you found since the last stairs or shop.
Honest: you lose the hero, for good.

Fight, loot, haul it home, sell it, buy something sharper, go deeper.
Repeat until legendary, or dead.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, the **number keys**, or **i o p k ; , . /**: move;
  walk into a monster to attack it
- **Shift** with a direction: run
- **L**: rest, **g**: pick up, **e**: equip, **u**: use, **d**: drop,
  **t**: throw, **x**: swap weapons, **c**: operate doors and chests
- **a**: use an ability, **Shift+E**: spend experience, **Shift+A**: about
  your hero
- In item lists, a **capital letter** shows the item's details
- **h**: help, with every key
- **q** or **Esc** on the main menu, or **Ctrl+C**: quit

Hauberk needs a terminal of at least 80 columns by 40 rows.

## Saving

Heroes are saved in your data folder (`~/.local/share/hauberk`, or
`%APPDATA%\hauberk` on Windows) whenever you take the stairs or leave a
shop.

## Options

- `--hero NAME`: start in the town with your hero NAME
- `--demo`: watch the computer play a new hero

## Credits

- Hauberk: Bob Nystrom
  ([github.com/munificent/hauberk](https://github.com/munificent/hauberk)),
  2012 on, written in Dart with his malison and piecemeal libraries
- Asciiverse edition: Hauberk's own code, unchanged, with a terminal
  screen and keyboard layer in place of the browser, and a demo mode
- License: MIT

hoosegow.title: Hoosegow
hoosegow.description: Thrown in a frontier jail with Muddy Charlie, plan a jailbreak
hoosegow.provenance: Ben Collins-Sussman and Jack Welch's comic Western Hoosegow (2010) won the Casual Gameplay Design Competition #7.
hoosegow.page:
You blew up a railroad tunnel, the sheriff got word ahead of time, and now you and Muddy Charlie are in the jail cell of a frontier town. There is a broken stool, a barred window, a stranger snoring on the bench and a deputy watching through the bars. Muddy has his harmonica; you have a pocketwatch and a scrap of paper. Time to plan a jailbreak.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/hoosegow`.

## Credits

- Hoosegow: Ben Collins-Sussman and Jack Welch, 2010
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-Share Alike 3.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

huarongdao.title: HuaRongDao
huarongdao.description: The Chinese sliding-block puzzle: slide the pieces around the box until the big square escapes through the gap at the bottom
huarongdao.provenance: Qingning Huo wrote hrd, a curses HuaRongDao in C++, in 2004 and packaged it for Debian.
huarongdao.page:
HuaRongDao is an old Chinese sliding-block puzzle. Ten pieces fill a box
four cells wide and five high, leaving two cells empty: a big square,
four tall rectangles, one wide one and four small squares. Slide
them, one at a time and never over each other, until the big square
reaches the gap in the middle of the bottom edge. The rules take a
minute to learn; the solution takes a good deal longer.

Moving one piece, even round a corner, counts as one step, and the step
counter shows how few you can manage. Undo and redo let you back out of
dead ends, and bookmarks keep a position to come back to.

This game ships one layout, the classic one. Other layouts can be
played by giving them as a pattern on the command line.

## Controls

- **0** to **9**: select the piece with that number, then
  **arrow keys** (or **l r u d**) to move it one or two cells
- **u**: undo a step, **r**: redo it
- **b**: save a bookmark in a slot (a letter or digit), **l**: load one
- **Enter**: clear the prompt, **Ctrl-L**: redraw
- **q**: quit (asks first)

## Options

- `hrd <pattern>`: play another layout, one letter a cell and a dot
  after each row: Q the big square, T and B the top and bottom of a tall
  piece, L and R the left and right of the wide one, P a small square,
  `_` empty. The classic layout is `TQQT.BQQB.TLRT.BPPB.P__P.`

## Files

Bookmarks are kept in `~/.local/share/hrd`.

## History

Qingning Huo wrote hrd in 2004 and maintained it in Debian until 2005.
The Asciiverse edition has his Debian build fix, bookmarks in the
player's data folder, and fixes for a crash without a home folder and
for unchecked memory mapping.

## Credits

hrd is by Qingning Huo, under the GNU GPL version 2 or later.

hunt.title: Hunt
hunt.description: Multiplayer deathmatch in a maze over your local network: find the other hunters, shoot, throw grenades and bombs, and be the last one standing
hunt.provenance: Conrad Huang, Ken Arnold and Greg Couch wrote Hunt at the University of California, San Francisco's Computer Graphics Lab, and Berkeley shipped it with 4BSD.

upstream.name: Conrad Huang, Ken Arnold and Greg Couch, UCSF Computer Graphics Lab

hunt.page:
A deathmatch in a maze for everyone on your network. There are no rooms,
treasures or monsters, only walls, doors, mines and the other players.
Wander the maze, find the others, and shoot them, throw grenades and
bombs, trip mines, and shoot down walls. The more players you kill before you
die, the better your score; when you die you can come straight back in.

Start Hunt and it looks for a game on your local network. If it finds
one, you join it (if it finds several, you pick); if there is none, it
starts a game on your machine for the others to find. Everyone who
starts Hunt on the same network ends up in the same maze.

## Controls

- **hjkl**: move left, down, up, right; **HJKL**: turn to face that way
- **f** or **1**: fire a bullet; **g** or **2**: throw a grenade; **F**,
  **G** and **3** to **0** and **@**: ever bigger bombs, each costing more
  ammunition
- **o**, **O**, **p**, **P**: throw slime
- **s**: scan for the other players, **c**: cloak against their scans
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw, **q**: quit

You can only fire the way you are facing.

## Options

Started from a shell: `hunt host` joins the game on that machine, `hunt
-q` lists the games on the network, `-m` joins as a spectator who
watches the whole maze, `-n name` sets your name and `-t digit` puts you
on a team.

## Network

Hunt finds games with a broadcast on UDP port 26740, and the game itself
runs over two TCP ports the server picks when it starts. If your
firewall asks, allow Hunt and its server, huntd, rather than a single
port.

## History

Conrad Huang, Ken Arnold and Greg Couch wrote Hunt at the University of
California, San Francisco's Computer Graphics Lab, and Berkeley
distributed it with 4BSD. The Asciiverse edition ports it to Linux and
macOS with its network play intact. It is part of BSD Games in the
Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

i-am-prey.title: I Am Prey
i-am-prey.description: Born in a sealed facility, outrun the Predator and collect a suit to escape the gas
i-am-prey.provenance: Joey Cramsey wrote I Am Prey, a TADS 3 game, in 2023.
i-am-prey.page:
You wake in the delivery room of a sealed facility, and a voice over the speakers tells you your name is Prey. The Predator is hungry and coming for you. Seven pieces of an environment suit are scattered around the place: collect them all and you can survive the poison gas and escape. A tense game of hiding, listening and running, a little different every time. Its characters swear.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/i-am-prey`.

## Credits

- I Am Prey: Joey Cramsey, 2023
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0
- Played with FrobTADS by Nikos Chantziaras, on Michael J. Roberts' TADS (TADS Freeware License)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

ioccc-chaos.title: Chaos
ioccc-chaos.description: A cube, a pyramid, a desk, an X-wing and the IOCCC's own name tumble in 3D wireframe: Alan De Smet's obfuscated object viewer
ioccc-chaos.provenance: Alan De Smet wrote chaos, a curses 3D wireframe viewer, for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest in 1998, where it won "Best object orientation".
ioccc-chaos.page:
Five objects turn in 3D, drawn as wireframes in dots, colons and
backticks that pack two lines of the picture into every row of text: a
cube, a pyramid, a desk, an X-wing fighter and the letters IOCCC, which
sway back and forth so they can be read. Each object tumbles about one
axis after another for a while, then the next takes its place.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `ioccc-chaos -t 20` gives every object 20 seconds, `-l`
lists them, and naming objects shows only those (`ioccc-chaos xwing`). A
data file of your own in the entry's format works too.

## History

Alan De Smet wrote chaos for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest
in 1998, his first entry, and won "Best object orientation". Left alone,
the original turns its object about one axis; its keys turn and zoom it
by hand. Asciiverse runs the entry as the IOCCC publishes it, inside a
small launcher that sends it those keys to tumble each object, shows the
five in turn and quits on any key.

## Credits

- 1998/chaos by [Alan De Smet](http://www.highprogrammer.com/alan/), from the [IOCCC](https://www.ioccc.org/1998/chaos/index.html)
- Copyright Landon Curt Noll, licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) ([the IOCCC's summary](https://www.ioccc.org/license.html))
- Asciiverse edition: the launcher, objects in turn, tumbling, any key quits; changes listed in PATCHES.md

jewels.title: Jewels
jewels.description: Falling pairs of jewels: line up four of a kind to blow them away before the pile reaches the top
jewels.provenance: abakh wrote Jewels for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
jewels.page:
Pairs of jewels drop into the well, and you move and turn each pair as
it falls. Line up four or more of the same jewel in a row or a column
and they explode for points; whatever was resting on them falls, and if
that sets off another explosion it scores more. The game is over when
the jewels pile up to the middle of the top row.

When one jewel of a pair lands, the other keeps falling on its own. The
next pair is shown at the top left. When the game ends, your score goes
on a top-ten list printed in the terminal.

## Controls

- **j** and **l**, **a** and **d**, or the **left** and **right arrows**: move the pair
- **k**, **w** or the **up arrow**: turn the pair
- **Space**: drop it
- **p**: pause
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Jewels is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

kerkerkruip.title: Kerkerkruip
kerkerkruip.description: A short roguelike told in words: fight your way down a random dungeon to the wizard Malygris
kerkerkruip.provenance: Victor Gijsbers and contributors first entered Kerkerkruip in the 2011 Interactive Fiction Competition and worked on it until 2014.
kerkerkruip.page:
You boasted, after too much to drink, that you could take on Malygris single-handed, and the prince's mage shoved you through a portal to prove it. Now you are in the dungeon of Kerkerkruip, a new one every game, with a few powers, a few items and a tension meter that keeps rising. A roguelike played by typing commands, with tactical fights and permanent death.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/kerkerkruip`.

## Credits

- Kerkerkruip: Victor Gijsbers and contributors, 2011 to 2014
- License: GNU GPL version 3 or later; the source is kept in theasciiverse/stories
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

klondike.title: Klondike
klondike.description: Solitaire in a box: build the four suit piles from Ace to King, played entirely from the keyboard
klondike.provenance: Mike Sharov wrote this Klondike in 2016 for his bsd-games, the modern Linux port of the BSD games, to replace canfield.
klondike.page:
The best known patience. Seven sorting stacks are dealt, from one card
in the first to seven in the last, with only the top card of each face
up. Move cards between the stacks, each one on a card one rank higher
and of the other colour, and build four final piles, one per suit, from
Ace up to King. The rest of the deck is dealt one card at a time, and
when it runs out the dealt cards turn over and become the deck again.
You win when all four suits are complete.

The table is laid on its side: the sorting stacks run across the screen,
one per row, with the deck and the final piles down the right. Instead
of picking cards up with a cursor, you step through the cards that can
move, and the game marks with a letter each place the selected card can
go.

## Controls

- **j** and **k**: select the next or previous card that can move
- **s**, **a**: move the selected card (and the cards on it) to the stack
  marked with that letter
- **f**: move the selected card to the final pile marked **f**
- **d**: deal a card from the deck
- **R**: start a new deal
- **q** or **F10**: quit

In a terminal with UTF-8 the suits are shown as symbols, otherwise as
the letters S, H, D and C.

## History

BSD Unix shipped Canfield as its solitaire. When Mike Sharov modernised
the BSD games for Linux in 2016, he replaced it with this Klondike,
written new, judging Canfield too rarely winnable to be fun. Klondike is
part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

larn.title: Larn
larn.description: Find the potion that cures your daughter in the caverns of Larn and the volcano below them, against the clock, in Noah Morgan's 1986 roguelike
larn.provenance: Noah Morgan wrote Larn in 1986 and posted it to the net, and it was soon part of the BSD games.
larn.page:
Your daughter has caught a strange disease and none of your remedies
help. The only hope is the potion of cure dianthroritis, somewhere in
the caverns of Larn, the old haunt of the magician Polinneaus, or in the
volcano beneath them. Larn is a roguelike with a deadline: time is
counted in mobuls and runs out, and the deeper you go, the more gold, magic and
danger you find.

It starts in a town with a bank, a school, a trading post and the
dungeon's entrance, so you can buy gear, learn, and come back up to
spend what you found. You cast spells, quaff potions and read scrolls,
and the map stays as you left it when you return to a level.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move (diagonals on yubn); with **Shift**, run
- **.**: stay, **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **g**: pack weight
- **c**: cast a spell, **r**: read, **q**: quaff, **e**: eat
- **w**: wield, **W**: wear, **T**: take off armour
- **^**: identify a trap, **D**: list everything found so far
- **?**: help, **S**: save, **Q**: quit, **^L**: redraw

## History

Noah Morgan wrote Larn in 1986 and posted it to the net "for the
enjoyment of all"; it was soon part of the BSD games. With Larn 12.0 he
let anyone use, modify and port the sources as long as no profit is
made from them.

The Asciiverse edition ports it to Linux and macOS and keeps its
scoreboard and saved games in the player's own data folder.
Larn is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

lexter.title: Lexter
lexter.description: Letters fall into a pit: steer them into words across or up and down, forwards or backwards, before the pit fills up
lexter.provenance: Mark Pulford wrote Lexter in C on curses from 1998 to 2001.
lexter.page:
Letters drop one at a time into a pit ten columns wide. Steer each one
left or right and let it land so that it spells words with the letters
around it: across or up and down, forwards or backwards, never
diagonally. A word of four letters or more scores and vanishes, and the
letters above fall into the gap. Palindromes count twice. The letters
fall faster as you find more words, and the game ends when the pit is
full.

Letter scores and how often each letter turns up come from the
dictionary itself, so rare letters are worth more. Now and then a blank
falls: press the letter you want it to be before it lands. Clearing the
whole pit earns a bonus.

Lexter picks its dictionary from your language: French if your system
is set to French, English otherwise. `lexter -d fr` or `lexter -d en`
chooses for yourself.

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: move the letter
- **Down**: lower it a row; **Space**: drop it
- a letter key: what a falling blank should be
- **P**: pause; **H**: help; **L**: letter scores and chances;
  **W**: the words found so far
- **S**: save a screenshot as text; **Q**: quit

The keys are capital letters: **P**, **H**, **L**, **W**, **S** and **Q**
with Shift, so lowercase letters stay free for blanks.

## High scores

The table keeps the best 20 games, with each dictionary getting an equal
share. It lives in your own folder (`~/.local/share/lexter/scores`), so it
survives updates; `lexter -s` prints it.

## History

Mark Pulford started Lexter in 1998 and released it in February 2001, with
1.0.3 that March as the last version. It came with an English and a
French dictionary and was built to take others: any plain list of words
makes a new game.

The Asciiverse edition keeps scores and screenshots in your own folder,
stops a spurious
dictionary error at start, and shows the French dictionary's accented
letters properly on today's UTF-8 terminals.

lost-pig.title: Lost Pig
lost-pig.description: Grunk the orc has lost the farm's pig and must find it in the dark woods and below
lost-pig.provenance: Admiral Jota's Lost Pig won the 2007 Interactive Fiction Competition and Best Game at the 2007 XYZZY Awards.
lost-pig.page:
Pig lost! Boss say it Grunk fault. Grunk go find pig, bring it back, or not bring back Grunk either. Grunk the orc follows the pig into the woods and under the ground, where a gnome and a lot of old things are waiting. Told entirely in Grunk's own words, and very funny.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/lost-pig`.

## Credits

- Lost Pig: Admiral Jota, 2007
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

mahjongg.title: Mahjongg
mahjongg.description: Mahjong solitaire in the terminal: GNOME Mahjongg's ten layouts, always solvable, mouse or keys
mahjongg.provenance: radha wrote this terminal Mahjongg in Rust in 2026, with layouts and game logic from GNOME Mahjongg.
mahjongg.page:
Mahjong solitaire, the tile-matching kind: clear the board by removing
matching pairs of free tiles. A tile is free when nothing lies on top of
it and its left or right side is open. Seasons match any season and
flowers match any flower. A faithful terminal clone of GNOME Mahjongg,
with all ten of its layouts, from the Turtle to the Red Dragon, and the
same deal generator, so every board can be cleared.

The board is drawn at the largest size that fits your window. Your game
is saved after every move and waits, paused, the next time you start.

## Controls

The whole game plays with the mouse: click two matching tiles, or the
buttons along the top. Double-click the background to finish once every
tile is free.

- **Arrow keys** or **H J K L**: move the tile cursor
- **Tab** and **Shift+Tab**: jump between free tiles
- **Enter** or **Space**: select or match
- **U** or **Ctrl+Z**: undo; **Shift+U** or **Ctrl+Y**: redo
- **Ctrl+H**: hint (adds 30 seconds; reshuffling adds 60)
- **P** or **Esc**: pause
- **Ctrl+N**: new game; **Ctrl+R**: restart
- **S**: best times; **M** or **F10**: menu, with layouts and tile themes
- **F1**: rules; **?**: all keys
- **Q**: quit (the game is saved)

## Credits

- Mahjongg for the terminal: [radha](https://github.com/radha/mahjongg)
- Layouts and game logic: [GNOME Mahjongg](https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-mahjongg), Mahjongg Contributors
- Asciiverse edition: settings, scores and saves work on Windows
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

mandelbrot.title: Mandelbrot
mandelbrot.description: Explore the Mandelbrot set in coloured characters: pan with the arrows, zoom a hundred levels into its spirals and seahorses
mandelbrot.provenance: David Ulrich wrote mandelbrot viewer in C on ncurses (2015 to 2016), built on Ken Perlin's one-line Mandelbrot.
mandelbrot.page:
The Mandelbrot set, drawn in characters and colour bands. It opens on the
whole set, fitted to your terminal; steer anywhere along its edge and zoom
in, and the spirals, seahorses and tiny copies of the set keep coming, a
hundred levels deep. Every point is worked out live as you move, from Ken
Perlin's famous one-line Mandelbrot.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the view
- **+** or **=**: zoom in
- **-**: zoom out
- **q** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

The most detail lives along the boundary of the black shape: try the
valley between the two big bulbs, or the tips of the small buds around them.

## Credits

- mandelbrot viewer: [David Ulrich](https://github.com/dulrich/mandelbrot-viewer),
  after Ken Perlin's one-line Mandelbrot
- Asciiverse edition: a view that fits your terminal, colour
  that works, more detail as you zoom, and a zoom limit instead of a hang
- License: AGPL-3.0-only

memoblocks.title: Memoblocks
memoblocks.description: Memory on a board of 128 hidden tiles: turn them one at a time and find all 64 pairs
memoblocks.provenance: abakh wrote Memoblocks for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
memoblocks.page:
A memory game. The board is 16 tiles wide and 8 high, and every tile
hides a glyph: a digit, a letter or a punctuation mark, in one of six
colours. Each glyph is on exactly two tiles. Turn a tile to see its
glyph, then try to find its twin.

Only the tile you turned last stays visible. A pair is made when you turn
a tile directly after its match, and then both stay face up; turn any
other tile and the first one hides again. The game is over when all 64
pairs are found, and it tells you how long that took.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: turn the tile
- **Mouse**: click a tile to turn it
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Memoblocks is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

miketron.title: Miketron
miketron.description: Drive a vehicle that leaves a trail it cannot cross, and grab pick-ups for flight, immunity and bombs
miketron.provenance: abakh wrote Miketron for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C; its manual page says it was copied from MikeOS.
miketron.page:
You drive a strange vehicle, the **+**, that never stops and leaves a
trail behind it. It can cross the edges of the board to come out on the
other side, and it survives explosions, but it cannot cross its own
trail: run into it and the game is over. Keep it running as long as you
can; the score counts up as it goes.

Pick-ups lie around the board:

- **?**: flight for a few moves, over the trail
- **&**: no trail for a while
- **%**: immunity for a while; trail you run over is wiped away
- **8**: a bomb that clears the board around it and sets off any bombs nearby
- **B**: five more pick-ups
- **S**: a stop; the vehicle waits until you press a key

Every hundred points, five more pick-ups and twenty pieces of loose trail
appear. The vehicle moves at half speed up and down. The board fits the
terminal, from 40 by 10 up to 80 by 24. When the game ends, your score
goes on a top-ten list.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: change direction
- **e**: turn off the colors (for the flashing effects)
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Miketron is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. Its manual page says it was copied from MikeOS. The collection is
packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and
pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

miscom.title: Miscom
miscom.description: Defend six cities from falling missiles: aim, fire, and catch the warheads in your explosions before they land
miscom.provenance: Graham Richards wrote Miscom in C on curses (1995 to 1996), a terminal take on Missile Command; Russell Marks, who wrote Ztrack, added colour and sound and released it in 1998.
miscom.page:
Missiles are falling on your six cities. Move the sight and fire: the
nearest of your three bases launches a missile, which bursts into a
fireball where you aimed, and any warhead that flies into it is gone.
Catch several in one blast, or let one explosion set off the next, to
make your ammunition last.

Some warheads split into several on the way down. Smart ones swerve
round your explosions. A bomber crosses now and then, low over the
cities, dropping missiles of its own; it shows as the terminal's cursor.
Your bases can be hit too, but they are rebuilt for the next level;
lost cities are not. Lose the last city and the game is over once the
level ends.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the sight
- **Space**: fire
- **p**: pause
- **Ctrl+C**: quit

On the title screen, **Return** starts a game and **Esc** quits.

## Credits

- Miscom: Graham Richards, 1995 to 1996, written in C with curses
- Colour, sound, the manual and the 1998 release: Russell Marks
- After Atari's Missile Command (1980)
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

moon-buggy.title: Moon-Buggy
