moon-buggy.description: Drive a buggy across the moon, jumping craters and shooting meteors out of your way, faster with every level
moon-buggy.provenance: Jochen Voss wrote Moon-Buggy in C on curses in 1998 and still maintains it.
moon-buggy.page:
Drive some kind of car across the moon's surface. Unfortunately there are
dangerous craters there. Fortunately your car can jump over them!

The ground scrolls towards your buggy and you time the jumps: too early
or too late and a wheel drops into the crater. Some craters are wider
than others, and they come faster with each level. Further on, meteors
roll along the ground; your laser breaks them up, three hits each, and
every shot costs a point. Crossing a crater and breaking a meteor score.
You have three buggies.

The high score table has a hundred places. The top three stay; the rest
expire after two weeks to six months, depending on the rank, and Thorin's
company of dwarves takes their places.

## Controls

- **Space** or **j**: jump
- **a** or **l**: fire the laser
- **q** or **n**: abort the game
- **r** or **Ctrl+L**: redraw the screen

On the title screen, **Space**, **Return** or **y** starts a game,
**s** shows the scores and **q** quits.

## Options

- `-r`: drive to the right instead of the left (the whole surface is
  drawn mirrored)
- `-n`: skip the title screen
- `-s`: print the high score table and exit

## Credits

- Moon-Buggy: Jochen Voss ([github.com/seehuhn/moon-buggy](https://github.com/seehuhn/moon-buggy)),
  1998 to 2025, written in C with curses; animations for version 1.0 by
  Piotr Grzybowski
- License: GNU GPL (no version named, so any version applies)

muncher.title: Muncher
muncher.description: Steer the muncher to the food and keep clear of the traps that pile up as your score grows
muncher.provenance: abakh wrote Muncher for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
muncher.page:
You steer the muncher, the **r**, around a walled board. It keeps moving
in the direction you last gave it, so every turn counts. Eat the food,
the **%**, and keep clear of the traps, the **^**: running into a trap or
a wall ends the game.

Each time you eat, new food appears somewhere else, often with new
traps, and more of them the higher your score. Past 2000 points a
flashing food sometimes shows up that makes you immune for a while:
traps you run into then just vanish. The muncher moves at
half speed up and down. The board fits the terminal, from 40 by 10 up to
80 by 24, and a smaller board scores more for each food. When the game
ends, your score goes on a top-ten list.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: change direction
- **p**: pause
- **e**: stop the flashing effects
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Muncher is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

myman.title: MyMan
myman.description: Pac-Man-like maze chase in curses: eat every dot, dodge four ghosts, turn the tables with a power pellet
myman.provenance: Benjamin C. Wiley Sittler wrote MyMan from 1998 to 2017.
myman.page:
Those scary ghosts are back, and they have mistaken you for their old
rival. Steer MyMan round the maze and eat every dot to clear it, while
four ghosts hunt you, each in its own way. Eat one of the big power
pellets in the corners and for a few seconds the ghosts turn and run,
and you can eat them for points. Fruit appears now and then for a bonus;
clear the maze and the next one is faster.

The maze scrolls to follow you, so it plays on any size of terminal.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or the number pad (**4 2 8 6**): move; a turn
  pressed early is taken at the next opening
- **P** or **Esc**: pause
- **S**: sound on or off
- **C**: colour on or off
- **T**: save a screenshot, as HTML and text, in the myman folder of your
  data folder
- **?**: help, with the credits for every maze
- **Q**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, MyMan takes options; `myman -h` lists them all.

- `-v VARIANT`: one of several hundred mazes, every one built in, among
  them `pacman`, `quackman`, and ones after old home-computer versions
  such as `paczx` (ZX Spectrum) and `pac64` (Commodore 64)
- `-z SIZE`: tile size, `small` (the default) or `big`, `huge` and more
- `-l NUM`: start with NUM lives

## History

Benjamin C. Wiley Sittler wrote MyMan on a dare on 28 June 1998, as 742
lines of C; colour and the small tiles came that December, and it grew
over the next twenty years into a game with hundreds of mazes that runs
on almost anything with a screen. Toru Iwatani's Pac-Man was the
inspiration.

This edition has the Termux and Fedora build fixes. Screenshots go to
your data folder rather than the game's own folder, and the attract
screen no longer leaves the ghosts' names behind on wide terminals.

## Credits

- Game: Benjamin C. Wiley Sittler
- Build fixes: Henrik Grimler (Termux), Jiri Vymazal (Fedora)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

nbsd-sos.title: SOS
nbsd-sos.description: Write S or O on the board and score for every S-O-S line you complete, against the computer or a friend
nbsd-sos.provenance: abakh wrote SOS for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
nbsd-sos.page:
Two sides take turns writing an S or an O in an empty square of a 5x6
board. Every S-O-S your letter completes in a straight line, across,
down or diagonally, scores you a point, and its letters take your
colour (green when both sides used them). Turns alternate whether you
scored or not. When the board is full, the higher score wins.

At the start the game asks who plays each side: by default you play
blue, which moves first, and the computer plays yellow. Two people can
share one keyboard, and the computer can play itself. Without `-p` the
computer starts out playing at random and adjusts after every game,
playing better after you win and worse after it wins.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: move
- **S** or **O**: write that letter
- **Mouse**: left click writes S, right click writes O
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

The command is `sos`.

- `-1 h` or `-1 c`: a human or the computer plays blue
- `-2 h` or `-2 c`: the same for yellow; either one skips the questions
- `-p 3`: a fixed strength for the computer, from 1 to 127
- `-n`: quit after one game instead of offering another

## History

SOS is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

ncmatrix.title: NCMatrix
ncmatrix.description: The Matrix's falling code, with your computer's network traffic falling in it: packets sent in red, received in magenta
ncmatrix.provenance: CMatrix is by Chris Allegretta from 1999 and Abishek V Ashok from 2017, with many contributors. In 2005 Thomas Bloedorn made NCMatrix from it, painting the packets the computer sends and receives into the rain.

developer.name: Chris Allegretta, Abishek V Ashok, Thomas Bloedorn and contributors

upstream.name: Chris Allegretta, Abishek V Ashok and contributors (CMatrix); Thomas Bloedorn (NCMatrix)

ncmatrix.page:
The falling green code of The Matrix, as CMatrix has drawn it in
terminals since 1999, with one thing more: your computer's network
traffic falls in it too. Every packet sent and received since the last
moment is painted into the rain as a bold run, red for what goes out and
magenta for what comes in, so a download pours magenta down the screen
and a quiet machine rains plain green.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit (Asciiverse starts it in screensaver mode)

## Options

From a terminal, `ncmatrix` without `-s` takes keys while it runs: `N`
turns the network display off and on, `a` asynchronous scroll, `b` and
`B` bold, `0` to `9` the speed, `! @ # $ % ^ &` the colour, `p` pause,
`q` quit. `-I wlan0` (or `en0` on a Mac, `Wi-Fi` on Windows) shows one
interface only, `-T` and `-R` change the traffic colours, `-c` uses
Japanese characters. `ncmatrix -h` lists them all.

## Credits

- CMatrix: [Chris Allegretta, Abishek V Ashok and contributors](https://github.com/abishekvashok/cmatrix)
- Network display: Thomas Bloedorn, NCMatrix 1.0 (2005)
- Asciiverse edition: the network display carried over to CMatrix
  and fixed, traffic read on macOS and Windows too, quits cleanly
  on SIGTERM and SIGHUP
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

neon-rain.title: Neon Rain
neon-rain.description: A rainy city street at night seen from above: buzzing neon signs mirrored on the wet road, cars with headlight beams, people under umbrellas and the odd flash of lightning
neon-rain.provenance: Asciiverse made Neon Rain in Rust in 2026, after a GIF of Terminal Rain, a cyberpunk roguelike shown on the TIGSource forums from 2015 that was never released.
neon-rain.page:
A city street at night in the rain, seen from straight above. Neon signs
hum over the shopfronts, buzz off now and then or lose a letter, and their
colours run down the wet road in shimmering streaks. Cars, trucks and
scooters swish past with their headlight beams sweeping the tarmac, and
now and then a police car flashes red and blue. People under umbrellas
walk the pavements, wait at the crossing while the traffic stops, or mill
about in a lit lobby. Steam drifts from the manholes, rain streaks pick up
the colour of whatever light they fall through, puddles ripple, and once
in a while lightning flashes over the rooftops.

Every start lays out a new street to fit the window.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `neon-rain -s 7` lays out the same street every time.
It draws in full RGB colour, and in 256 colours on terminals that do not
report truecolor.

## Credits

- Neon Rain: Asciiverse, after a GIF of Terminal Rain, an unreleased
  cyberpunk roguelike shown on the TIGSource forums
- License: MIT

netgame.title: Net
netgame.description: Turn the tiles until every pipe joins the network at the centre: the classic net (netwalk) rotation puzzle
netgame.provenance: Ben Falconer wrote Netgame in 2010, the net puzzle in a single C++ file that draws with ANSI escape codes.
netgame.page:
A grid of pipe pieces, scrambled: straights, corners, T junctions and
dead ends. The tile at the centre is the source, and everything joined to
it lights up green. Turn the tiles one by one until every piece is part
of a single network, with no loose ends and no loops. The count under the
board shows how many tiles are connected so far.

Lock a tile once you are sure of it, so a stray key cannot turn it again.
When the whole board lights up, press n for a fresh puzzle.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the cursor
- **Space** or **.**: turn the tile clockwise
- **,**: turn it anticlockwise
- **l** or **s**: lock or unlock the tile
- **n**: new puzzle
- **q** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

From a terminal, `netgame 15 20` plays on another size (2 to 99), and
`--wrapping` lets pipes run off one edge and back in at the other.

## Credits

- Netgame: [Ben Falconer](https://github.com/zed0/Netgame), under the MIT
  licence
- Asciiverse edition: wider tiles, n for a new puzzle, a clean exit on Ctrl+C, and a Windows build

nethack.title: NetHack
nethack.description: The great dungeon crawl: down through the Mazes of Menace and Gehennom for the Amulet of Yendor, with your pet at your side
nethack.provenance: Mike Stephenson merged the descendants of Andries Brouwer's Hack into NetHack 1.4 in 1987, and the NetHack DevTeam has developed it ever since.
nethack.page:
The dungeon crawl that has been in development for almost forty years.
You go down through the Mazes of Menace, past the Gnomish Mines,
Sokoban's puzzles and the Oracle, into Gehennom, to bring back the
Amulet of Yendor for your god. You choose to be one of thirteen roles,
from Archeologist and Valkyrie to Wizard and Tourist, with a kitten,
little dog or pony at your side.

Everything is a character on the map, and almost anything you think of
trying works: dip, engrave, pray, polymorph, kick, bargain with
shopkeepers. Death is final. New players can say yes to the tutorial
at the start.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift**, run
- **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T**
  take off, **P** put on, **R** remove, **a** apply
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors; **s**: search; **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **#**: extended commands, such as `#pray`
- **?**: help, **;**: what is that symbol, **Ctrl-P**: earlier messages
- **S**: save and quit

## Saving and options

**S** saves the game to your data folder (`~/.local/share/nethack`), and
starting NetHack again carries on from there. Your options go in
`~/.nethackrc`, or in `nethackrc` in that folder. At the end of each game
a full account of it is written to its `dumplog` folder.
`OPTIONS=windowtype:curses` switches to the curses interface.

## History

NetHack grew from Hack, which Jay Fenlason wrote with Kenny Woodland,
Mike Thome and Jon Payne after Rogue and Andries Brouwer reworked at the
Mathematisch Centrum in Amsterdam (Hack 1.0.3, 1985, is also in the
catalog). Mike Stephenson merged its descendants into NetHack 1.4 in 1987,
and the NetHack DevTeam took it on from there. NetHack 3.6 came out in
2015; the next release, long known as 3.7, became 5.0.0 on 2 May 2026,
with over 3100 fixes and changes and its levels written in Lua.

This edition is built for Linux and macOS, keeping everything it writes
in your own data folder.

## Credits

- Game: the NetHack DevTeam and contributors, after Hack by Jay
  Fenlason, Kenny Woodland, Mike Thome, Jon Payne and Andries Brouwer
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: NetHack General Public License

nettoe.title: netToe
nettoe.description: Tic-tac-toe against the computer at three levels, a friend at the same keyboard, or a friend across the network
nettoe.provenance: Gabriele Giorgetti wrote netToe in C in 2000 and 2001, and Mats Erik Andersson maintained it until 2014.

upstream.name: Gabriele Giorgetti and Mats Erik Andersson

nettoe.page:
Noughts and crosses in the terminal: get three in a row before your
opponent does. Play the computer at one of three levels, a friend sharing
your keyboard, or a friend on another machine over the network. A running
score is kept as long as you keep saying yes to another game.

The computer's levels play by rules rather than looking ahead. Weak is
easily fooled, Normal goes for its own wins first, and Better checks every
winning and blocking move, but traps are still possible if you find them.

## Controls

Moves and menus are typed and confirmed with **Enter**:

- **a1** to **c3**: your move, row (a, b, c) then column (1, 2, 3), as the
  coordinate grid beside the board shows
- the number of a menu item, or **q** to go back or quit
- **y** or **n** after a game: play again or not

## Playing over the network

One of you hosts: choose Two players over network, then Host the game,
and type a name. The screen lists this machine's addresses; tell your
friend one of them. Your friend chooses Connect to host and types that
address or the host's name. The game uses TCP port 7501, so the host's
firewall has to let it in; on a home network that usually means nothing
at all. Play is direct between the two machines, there is no server in
between.

## Options

- `-4`, `-6`: IPv4 or IPv6 only (both by default)
- `-nb`: no beeps; `-nc`: no colours

## History

Gabriele Giorgetti wrote netToe in 2000 and 2001, adding colours in 1.1.0
(July 2001); Debian has carried it since June 2001 (1.0.5). Mats Erik Andersson took it over in 2009 and added the
harder computer level, IPv6 and terminfo support, releasing 1.5.1 in March
2014, the last version.

The Asciiverse edition adds three fixes: the host screen now lists the
addresses a friend can actually connect to (it used to suggest 127.0.1.1
on many systems), colours no longer turn the screen bright red on
256-colour terminals when they reset, and prompts appear in the static
Linux build.

nflood.title: nFlood
nflood.description: Flood the whole board with one colour in as few moves as you can, spreading out from the top left corner
nflood.provenance: Alexandre Dantas wrote nFlood, a Flood-It puzzle in C and ncurses, between 2011 and 2014, with help from Yu-Jie Lin.
nflood.page:
A board of 14 by 14 cells in six colours, and one simple move: pick a
colour, and the patch in the top left corner turns that colour, swallowing
every neighbouring cell that already had it. Keep picking until the whole
board is one colour. The fewer moves it takes, the better.

It sounds like there is nothing to it, but which colour to pick next is
a real choice: grab the colour with the most cells along your edge, or
the one that opens a path into the far corner. The panel shows your
moves, how much of the board is flooded, and your best game.

## Controls

- **1** to **6**: flood with that colour (the panel shows which is which)
- **Mouse**: click a colour in the panel, or any cell of the board, to
  flood with its colour
- **r**: a new board (or click "r: New Game")
- **c**: centre the board, or move it back to the corner
- **q**: quit

After "Congrats!", **r** plays another board and any other key quits.

## Options

- `-W <width>`, `-H <height>`: a board of another size (only the
  standard 14x14 counts for the best score)

## Files

The best score is kept in `~/.local/share/nflood` (`%APPDATA%\nflood` on
Windows). It starts at 25 before any game is won.

## History

Alexandre Dantas wrote nFlood, his terminal version of the Flood-It
puzzle, between 2011 and 2014, with Yu-Jie Lin adding mouse support,
custom board sizes and the best score. This edition has fixes so it
builds with current compilers and deals a different board each time it
starts, the best score in the player's data folder and shown as soon as
it is set, a working New Game click and a Windows build.

## Credits

nFlood is by Alexandre Dantas and Yu-Jie Lin, under the GNU GPL version
3 or later. Its option parser is TJ Holowaychuk's Commander (MIT).

nhfourk.title: NetHack Fourk
nhfourk.description: NetHack rebalanced, with NetHack 4's friendlier interface: autoexplore, travel, status bars, an inventory sidebar and levels you can look back on
nhfourk.provenance: Nathan Eady began NetHack Fourk in 2014 as a variant of NetHack 4, Alex Smith's reworking of NetHack 3.4.3 from AceHack and Daniel Thaler's NitroHack, and still maintains it for the Hardfought servers.

upstream.name: Nathan Eady, after NetHack 4 by Alex Smith and others

nhfourk.page:
NetHack, rebalanced and given a friendlier interface. NetHack Fourk is
Nathan Eady's variant of NetHack 4: the same descent through the
Mazes of Menace, the Gnomish Mines, Sokoban and Gehennom for the
Amulet of Yendor, with careful changes to the balance (races matter
for your limits and skills, Barbarians are the strongest fighters,
ranged weapons and multishot reworked, amnesia gone, scrolls of
wishing), a new race, the sylph, and new levels and monster tricks.

From NetHack 4 it has the interface: status bars for health and
power, a sidebar with your inventory on a wide terminal, the game
remembering every level you have seen, autoexplore and travel, and
fewer ways to kill yourself with a typo. It is the version played on
the Hardfought public servers. Your first characters are human
Barbarians and Wizards; the other roles and races unlock as you
achieve things in play, and stay unlocked.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**, the cursor keys or the number pad: move, the last
  four letters diagonally; walking into a door opens it
- **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **f**: fire, **z**: zap
- **v**: explore automatically until something turns up
- **_**: travel to a spot (`<` or `>` there picks the stairs)
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **a** apply, **A** change your
  equipment (wield, wear, put on, take off, all in one)
- **s**: search, **.**: rest; a number first repeats, as in `20s`
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up; **Ctrl-O**: the levels you remember
- **#**: extended commands, such as `#pray`; **Ctrl-E**: write Elbereth
- **?**: help, **;**: what is that, **Ctrl-P**: earlier messages,
  **!**: the game menu
- **S**: save and quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder (`~/.local/share/nhfourk`);
pick it with **load game** in the main menu to carry on. Your options
(set from the main menu or with **O** in a game), the score list and a
full account of every finished game are kept there too.

## History

NetHack 4 began when Alex Smith merged his AceHack with Daniel Thaler's
NitroHack, two forks of NetHack 3.4.3, and rewrote much of the game's
insides and all of its interface while keeping the gameplay
conservative. Nathan Eady started NetHack Fourk from it in 2014 to try
out the balance changes NetHack 4 would not take, and still maintains
it; this edition is built for the terminal only, with its files in your
own data folder. NetHack itself is in the catalog too.

## Credits

- NetHack Fourk: Nathan Eady
- NetHack 4: Alex Smith and contributors, from AceHack and Daniel
  Thaler's NitroHack
- NetHack: the NetHack DevTeam, Stichting Mathematisch Centrum and
  M. Stephenson
- License: NetHack General Public License

ninvaders.title: nInvaders
ninvaders.description: Space Invaders in ncurses: hold back the descending alien block from behind four crumbling bunkers, and pick off the UFO for 500 points
ninvaders.provenance: Thomas Dettbarn wrote nInvaders in C on ncurses in 2002 and 2003 with Alexander Hollinger, Sebastian Gutsfeld and Matthias Thar, with code by Mike Saarna.
ninvaders.page:
Space Invaders in the terminal. Rows of aliens march side to side and drop
a step each time they reach the edge, bombing you as they come. Slide your
gun along the bottom, shoot them down before they land, and shelter behind
four bunkers that crumble with every hit. Now and then a UFO crosses the top
of the screen, worth 500 points if you can lead your shot.

Each alien row is worth more the higher it sits: 100, 150 and 200 points,
500 for the UFO. You start with three lives, and the block speeds up as it
thins out and as the levels go by.

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**, or **h** and **l**: move; hold the key down to
  move faster
- **Space** or **k**: fire
- **p**: pause, and again to go on
- **q**: quit
- **Space** on the title screen: start a game

## High scores

A score that makes the TOP 10 asks for your name after the game over
banner: type up to 8 letters and press **Enter**. The title screen shows
the table between its alien parades. Each skill level plays for its own
table: `-l 0` for the expert one, the default for the normal one, and
`-l 2` to `-l 9` for the beginner one. The table is kept in your own
folder (`~/.local/share/ninvaders/highscore`, or `%APPDATA%\ninvaders` on
Windows), so it survives updates.

## Options

- `-l 0` to `-l 9`: the skill level, from 0 (the game calls it "NIGHTMARE")
  to 9 ("May I play daddy?!"); 1 is the default
- `-gpl`: show the licence

## History

Thomas Dettbarn ("dettus") wrote nInvaders in 2002 with Alexander
Hollinger, Sebastian Gutsfeld and Matthias Thar, and code by Mike
Saarna; 0.1.1 (May 2003) added the title screen and a timer that made it
playable on more systems, and was the last release. Alexander Hollinger
and Sebastian Gutsfeld went on to add a high score table that summer,
which was never released; this edition has Debian's patches and brings
that table in, finished.

The Asciiverse runs the game in a loop instead of from a timer signal,
which makes it steadier and lets it run on Windows, and sends only what changes
to the terminal instead of repainting it 50 times a second. Each game now
plays out differently: the original never seeded its random numbers, so
every game was the same.

nsnake.title: nSnake
nsnake.description: The classic snake game in the terminal: eat the fruit, grow, and do not bite yourself; 31 levels and lots of game modes
nsnake.provenance: Alexandre Dantas wrote nSnake in C++ and ncurses from 2012 to 2014.
nsnake.page:
The snake game everyone played on their phone, in the terminal. Steer
the snake to the fruit; every fruit makes it longer and adds to the
score, and running into a wall or your own tail ends the game.

Arcade Mode is the classic game on an open board. Level Select has 31
mazes to play instead, from simple arenas to spirals, hearts and
letters, and each keeps its own high score. In Game Settings you set the
starting speed (1 to 10), how many fruits are on the board at once, the
board size, teleporting through the edges, random walls, and a board
that scrolls under you; scores are kept for each combination.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: steer the snake
- **p**: pause, **h**: help during a game
- **q**: quit at any time
- **Enter**: choose in the menus

Every key can be changed in the Controls menu, and colours and borders
in GUI Options.

## Levels

Levels are plain text files ending in `.nsnake`. Besides the 31 that
come with the game, nSnake reads your own from the `levels` folder in
its data folder (`~/.local/share/nsnake/levels`), where its settings
and scores are kept too.

## History

Alexandre Dantas wrote nSnake in C++ and ncurses from 2012 to 2014; it
is packaged by Debian, Fedora and others. This edition has a few fixes:
the bundled levels are found without copying them by hand, settings
follow `XDG_DATA_HOME`, and it builds for Windows.

nstars.title: nstars
nstars.description: Fly through a starfield: stars stream out from the centre and brighten as they rush past
nstars.provenance: nstars is the ncurses version of Philip J Freeman's stars, in C, from 2016 to 2020.
nstars.page:
The classic starfield: you are flying forward through space, and stars
stream out from the centre of the screen, faint and grey far away,
brightening to white as they rush past the edges. Below the sky sits a
small console with a frame counter and a command line, in the style of an
IRC client.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit (while the command line is empty)
- **/**: start a command, then **Enter** to run it
- **Up** and **Down**: earlier commands
- **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: quit at any time

## Commands

- `/sleep 10000`: the pause between frames in microseconds; higher is slower
- `/char *`: draw the stars with another character
- `/colormode mono` or `/colormode 256`: plain or shaded stars
- `/quit`: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `nstars -s '*'` sets the star character and `-c 256` (how
Asciiverse starts it) shades the stars; `-c mono` draws them plain.

## Credits

- stars and nstars: [Philip J Freeman](https://github.com/ph1l/stars)
- Asciiverse edition: any key quits, a memory fix and a Windows
  build
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

nudoku.title: nudoku
nudoku.description: Classic 9x9 sudoku in ncurses, with three difficulty levels, hints, number highlighting, undo and a saved game
nudoku.provenance: Michael Vetter (jubalh) has written nudoku in C and ncurses since 2014, with contributors adding translations.
nudoku.page:
Sudoku on the classic 9x9 board: fill every row, column and 3x3 box
with the numbers 1 to 9, each once. nudoku makes a new puzzle each
time, easy, normal or hard, and keeps out of the way: move around the
board, type numbers into the empty cells, and ask it to check your work
whenever you like.

When you are stuck, a hint fills in one cell for you, and the count of
hints used is shown when you finish. Marks light up every copy of the
number under the cursor, which makes it easy to see where a number can
still go. Mistakes can be deleted or undone, and a game in progress can
be saved and picked up again later.

## Controls

- **h j k l** or the **arrow keys**: move
- **1** to **9**: put a number in the cell, **x**, **Delete** or
  **Backspace** to clear it
- **u**: undo
- **c**: check the board so far
- **H**: a hint
- **m**: marks on or off
- **N**: a new puzzle
- **S**: show the solution
- **G**: save the game
- **r**: redraw
- **Q** or **Escape**: quit

## Options

- `-d easy`, `-d normal`, `-d hard`: the difficulty (easy unless given)
- `-r`: resume the saved game
- `-c`: no colours
- `-s <81 characters>`: play a puzzle of your own, given as one line of
  digits with `.` for the empty cells; `-o` prints a new one that way

The help text is translated into German, Spanish, French, Japanese,
Georgian, Russian, Turkish, Ukrainian and Vietnamese, chosen from your
language settings (Linux builds).

## Files

The saved game is kept in `~/.local/state/nudoku` (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\nudoku`
on Windows).

## History

Michael Vetter started nudoku in 2014 and has kept it going since, with
translations from contributors; it is packaged by Debian and many
others. This edition has the translations found beside the program,
saving that works in a fresh home folder, and a Windows build. The
optional export of puzzles to PDF and PNG is not included.

## Credits

nudoku is by Michael Vetter and contributors, under the GNU GPL version
3 or later.

nuzzle.title: Nuzzle
nuzzle.description: Three block-placing puzzles: drop shapes on the grid, fill rows, columns, squares or colour groups to clear them, and keep going as long as anything fits
nuzzle.provenance: Dead End wrote nuzzle in C on ncurses (2019 to 2023), a collection of three block-placing puzzles.
nuzzle.page:
Three puzzles about fitting blocks onto a board. Pieces wait beside the
grid, three at a time; pick one up, move it into place and drop it. Fill
a row or a column completely and it clears, one point for every block
removed. When all three are placed you get three new ones, and the game
ends when none of them fits anywhere.

- **Lines**: one colour on a 10x11 board; full rows and columns clear.
- **Squares-and-Lines**: a 9x9 board split into nine 3x3 squares; a full
  square clears as well as a full row or column.
- **Four-Colors**: one piece at a time, its blocks in four colours; four
  or more touching blocks of the same colour clear.

Each game keeps its own high score.

## Controls

- **Tab**: pick up a piece, or switch to the next one
- **Arrow keys**: move the piece onto the board, then around it
- **Enter**: drop the piece
- **Mouse**: click a piece to pick it up, move it without holding the
  button, click again to drop it; right click puts it back
- **Esc** or **m**: menu (continue, or start another game)
- **q** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

## Credits

- nuzzle: [Dead End](https://github.com/dead-end/nuzzle), under the MIT
  licence
- Asciiverse edition: scores in your data folder, colours for any
  256-colour terminal, and crash fixes

particles.title: Particle Fountain
particles.description: An emitter sprays particles that glow green, yellow and red as they age: steer it, add gravity and wind, and play
particles.provenance: Particle Fountain is particles.cpp by flarn2006, in C++ on curses, from 2013 to 2017, one of the programs in his MiscPrograms collection.
particles.page:
An emitter on the left of the screen sprays a fountain of particles that
fly out, glow green, turn yellow, then red, and vanish. The keys change
everything about them: how fast they leave, how long they live, which way
gravity pulls and how hard the wind blows. Move the emitter around with the
arrows and paint with it.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the emitter
- **-** and **+**: slower, faster
- **w** and **s**: pull up, pull down (gravity)
- **a** and **d**: wind to the left, to the right
- **[** and **]**: shorter life, longer life
- **x**: clear all particles
- **Backtick** (`` ` ``): change the display: help, emitter, both or neither
- **q**, **Q** or **Esc**: quit

## Credits

- particles.cpp: [flarn2006](https://github.com/flarn2006/MiscPrograms),
  2013 to 2017
- Asciiverse edition: just this program from his collection, Q and Esc
  quit too, and a Windows build
- License: MIT

pipes.title: Pipes
pipes.description: Lay pipes from the queue ahead of the sewage, which starts flowing when the countdown ends
pipes.provenance: abakh wrote Pipes for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
pipes.page:
Sewage is about to flow out of a source somewhere on the board, and you
have to keep a pipeline ahead of it. Pipes come from a queue: the next
five are shown on the left, and Enter lays the first of them under the
cursor. There are corners, straights and crossovers, and you get no say
in which comes next, so the ones that do not fit have to go somewhere
out of the way.

You have 70 seconds before the flow starts; after that it moves on by one
pipe every five seconds. Every pipe the sewage passes through scores a
point. Fast flow (**f**) moves it on much quicker for three extra points
per pipe, and running it through a crossover a second time scores six
more. Replacing a pipe that is already down costs a point, and pipes the
sewage has reached cannot be replaced. The game is over when the sewage
leaks out of the pipeline, and the score goes on a top-ten list.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: lay the next pipe, or replace the one under the cursor
- **Mouse**: click a cell to lay a pipe there
- **g**: start the flow now, without waiting for the countdown
- **f**: fast flow on or off
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit, after offering the high scores

## History

Pipes is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

pokertui.title: pokertui
pokertui.description: Texas Hold'em at a six-seat table: read the bots, watch the odds rail, and take their chips one pot at a time
pokertui.provenance: pokertui is Aleksandr Babarika's terminal Texas Hold'em in Rust and Ratatui, from 2026.
pokertui.page:
Five bots, ten thousand chips each, and one seat with your name on it.
Every hand you get two cards, a felt full of pods, and a rail that does
the arithmetic for you: your chance to win right now, the pot odds on the
call, and a blunt verdict on whether calling is worth it.

The bots are not all alike. One is tight and aggressive, one calls
anything, one bluffs more than it should, and one is a rock that only
moves with a monster. They remember how often you fold, and they lean on
you when you do. The game ends when one player has every chip on the
table. Make it you.

Tired of bots? `pokertui-server` comes in the box: start a room and your
friends join it over the network.

## Controls

- **F**: fold; **C**: check or call; **R**: raise; **A**: all-in
- **Up** and **Down**: change the bet size; **Enter**: confirm
- Any key after a hand: deal the next one
- **S**: settings (table size, blinds, bot speed, the odds rail);
  **Q**: quit

## Options

- `--join <host:port> --name <name>`: sit down at a network table
- `pokertui-server --seats 4`: host a table (port 4000; `--buy-in`,
  `--small-blind`, `--big-blind`, `--turn-secs` set the game)

## Credits

- pokertui: Aleksandr Babarika
  ([github.com/AlexAlexBabarika/pokertui](https://github.com/AlexAlexBabarika/pokertui)),
  2026, written in Rust with Ratatui
- Asciiverse edition: fits 100x30, smarter bots, no freeze on a short
  stack, Windows settings saved
- License: MIT or Apache-2.0

pq2.title: pq2
pq2.description: Nick Bollom's remake of Progress Quest, Eric Fredricksen's 2002 RPG parody that plays itself: roll up a hero, then watch the bars fill
pq2.provenance: Nick Bollom's remake in C++ and ncurses (2016 to 2025) of Progress Quest, the idle RPG parody Eric Fredricksen released in 2002.

upstream.name: Nick Bollom, after Eric Fredricksen's Progress Quest

pq2.page:
A role-playing game that plays itself. You roll up a hero, pick a race
and a class from lists of splendidly silly ones (Half Halfling, Land
Squid, Battle-Felon, Fighter/Organist), and from then on there is
nothing to do but watch: your hero kills monsters, loots their parts,
sells them in town, buys better gear, learns spells, gains levels and
works through quests and the acts of an epic plot, all as progress bars
filling on their own.

pq2 is Nick Bollom's remake of Progress Quest, the parody of
level-grinding RPGs that Eric Fredricksen released in 2002, rebuilt in
C++ with the same races, classes, monsters, spells and items. It is not
the original, which you can still play at
[progressquest.com](http://progressquest.com). Leave it running in a
spare terminal and check in on your hero now and then; it only advances
while it is open.

## Controls

- **Up**, **Down** and **Enter**: the main menu; **Esc** quits
- On the character sheet: **Tab** or the arrow keys move between the
  fields, **Enter** picks one (a random name, the race and class lists,
  Roll, Unroll), letters and digits type a name, **Backspace** deletes,
  and **Sold!** starts the game; **Esc** goes back
- **F1** equipment, **F2** spells, **F3** inventory, **F4** plot, **F5**
  quests; **Up** and **Down** scroll a list, **Esc** closes it
- **p**: show or hide the percentages on the bars
- **-** and **+**: redraw faster or slower
- **Esc** on the game screen: save and quit

## Saving

The game saves to your data folder when the character is created, at
every new level, act and finished quest, and when you quit. To carry
on, choose Load Game, which lists your saved heroes, or start it from a
shell as `pq2 <name>`.

## History

Eric Fredricksen wrote Progress Quest for Windows in 2002 as a send-up
of the online role-playing games of the day, and has kept it going for
over twenty years, with a web version and online realms (Windows
version 6.4.4 came out in 2022). He
released it under the MIT licence. Nick Bollom began his cross-platform
remake in 2016, with Qt, GTK and ncurses editions; this is the ncurses
edition, with saved games in your data folder
and a few bugs fixed.

## Credits

- Progress Quest: [Eric Fredricksen](http://progressquest.com), MIT
- pq2: [Nick Bollom](https://github.com/nbollom/pq2), GPL-3.0
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

pwmangband.title: PWMAngband
pwmangband.description: Multiplayer Angband: go down a hundred levels to face Morgoth, alone on your own server or with others on someone else's
pwmangband.provenance: PWMAngband is a multiplayer Angband, based on Angband 4.2 and MAngband 1.5 and maintained by the MAngband and PWMAngband developers on GitHub.

upstream.name: MAngband and PWMAngband developers (draconisPW and others)

pwmangband.page:
Angband for many players. You create a character, set out from the town,
and go down into the dungeon below, level after level, towards Morgoth,
Lord of Darkness, a hundred levels deep. Everything is a letter on the map:
you are the `@`, monsters are letters of their own, and the numbers in town
are the shops' doors. Races run from Hobbits and Ents to Dragons and
Hydras, classes from Warriors and Mages to Necromancers and Shapechangers.

PWMAngband is always a server and a client. Started from Asciiverse, it runs
a private server on your machine and connects you to it: the world and your
characters are kept for the next time, and friends on your network can join
the same world. The first time, you choose an account name and password;
they protect your characters on that server.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **1** to **9**: walk (diagonals on 1, 3, 7 and 9);
  walking into a shop's number goes inside, **Escape** leaves
- **<** and **>**: stairs, **R**: rest, **,**: stay still
- **i**: inventory, **e**: equipment, **g**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **w**: wear or wield, **q**: quaff, **r**: read, **E**: eat,
  **f**: fire, **m**: cast a spell
- **l**: look, **M**: map of the level
- **:**: chat with other players
- **?**: help, **Ctrl-X**: save and quit (**Q** and **Ctrl-C** retire the
  character for good)

## Playing online

`pwmangband-play <host> [port]` joins a server elsewhere (the default port
is 18346), and `pwmangband-play --list` shows the servers listed on the
mangband.org metaserver. A server must run the same version.
On 17 October 2026 none on the list did: it showed MAngband servers and one
older PWMAngband 1.4.0 server, which did not answer, and the servers named in
PWMAngband's own manual no longer exist.

## History

Angband goes back to 1990, to Umoria and to VMS Moria (1985). MAngband
made it a game for many players, and PWMAngband carries that on: it is
based on Angband 4.2 and MAngband 1.5, and the MAngband and PWMAngband
developers maintain it on GitHub. This edition has only its curses
client, with your files kept in your own data folder.

## Credits

- Game: the MAngband and PWMAngband developers (draconisPW and others), after
  Angband by Ben Harrison, Robert Alan Koeneke and James E. Wilson
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0 (or the Angband licence)

rabbithole.title: Rabbithole
rabbithole.description: A rabbit in a hidden maze: find every carrot before the time runs out
rabbithole.provenance: abakh wrote Rabbithole for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
rabbithole.page:
You are a rabbit in a maze, and carrots are scattered through it. Gather
them all before the clock runs out. The walls are hidden: the maze shows
only the passages you have already walked, so finding the carrots is a
matter of choosing your paths well and moving fast.

The maze is made to fit the terminal when the game starts, and a bigger
maze has more carrots and more time: one carrot for every 50 cells and
one second for every 5. In a 100x30 terminal that is 47 by 11 cells, 10
carrots and 103 seconds. When the time is up, the game tells you what
share of the carrots you gathered.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
  (the timer keeps running while you read them)
- **q** or **Esc**: quit
- **y** or **n** at the end: play again, or stop

## History

Rabbithole is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

rain.title: Rain
rain.description: Raindrops land on a still pond and spread out in widening rings, one after another: the BSD screen piece from 1980
rain.provenance: Eric P. Scott wrote rain at Caltech High Energy Physics in November 1980, after the VAX/VMS program of the same name, and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on.
rain.page:
Drops of rain fall on a still pond. Each one lands as a dot, swells to a
small o and then a big O, and spreads out in two widening rings before
it fades and another drop lands somewhere else. Five ripples are on the
water at any time, all in plain characters, and it never repeats the
same pattern twice.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `rain -d 50` sets the pause between drops in
milliseconds (the default is 120).

## History

Eric P. Scott wrote rain at Caltech High Energy Physics in November
1980, modelled on the VAX/VMS program of the same name, and it has
shipped with BSD Unix ever since. This edition quits on any key and
makes a new pattern every run. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog.

## Credits

- rain: Eric P. Scott, from [NetBSD's source tree](https://github.com/NetBSD/src/tree/trunk/games/rain)
- License: BSD-3-Clause, copyright The Regents of the University of California

rantaiwarna.title: rantaiwarna
rantaiwarna.description: SameGame in the terminal: clear groups of same-coloured elements from the board, and the bigger the group, the bigger the score
rantaiwarna.provenance: Guido Berhoerster wrote rantaiwarna, a SameGame (Chain Shot!) for curses terminals, in C in 2014 and kept it in Mercurial until 2016.
rantaiwarna.page:
The board starts full of elements in four colours. Pick any group of
two or more touching elements of the same colour and they vanish; the
elements above fall into the gap, and when a whole column empties, the
columns to its right slide over. The game is over when no group of two
is left.

A group of n elements scores (n - 1) squared, so two at a time earns
almost nothing and twenty at once earns 361. Clearing the board
completely adds a bonus of 1000. The trick is to leave the small groups
alone until the colours around them have run together into big ones.
The best ten scores are kept for each board size and number of colours.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the cursor
- **Space** or **Enter**: remove the group under the cursor
- **Left mouse button**: remove the group you click
- **n**: a new game
- **i**: the high score table, **H**: help, **a**: back to the game
- **Ctrl+L**: redraw
- **q**: quit

## Options

- `-c <colours>`: two to five colours (four unless given)
- `-w <width>`, `-h <height>`: the board's size, at least 5 by 5 (20 by
  10 unless given)

## Files

High scores are kept in `~/.local/share/rantaiwarna`.

## History

SameGame goes back to Chain Shot!, a 1985 game by Kuniaki Moribe. Guido
Berhoerster wrote rantaiwarna in 2014 for any curses that follows the
X/Open standard, from ncurses to the native curses of Solaris and
NetBSD, and kept it in a Mercurial repository until 2016. This edition
has its history rebuilt in git, the high scores moved to the player's
data folder, and a terminal that starts too small now waiting to grow
instead of quitting.

## Credits

rantaiwarna is by Guido Berhoerster, under the MIT licence.

redsquare.title: Redsquare
redsquare.description: Move a red square through Conway's Game of Life: catch the X, or crowd out the white cells with red ones
redsquare.provenance: abakh wrote Redsquare for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
redsquare.page:
A puzzle played in Conway's Game of Life. The board is full of white
cells, **#**, that live, die and are born by Life's rules, and you move
a red square of four cells through them. Life moves on a generation
every time you press a key, or by itself after a short wait.

Red cells live by the same rules, and a cell that is born or survives
takes the colour of most of its neighbours, so when your square touches
other cells it starts reactions that can spread red, **O**, or wipe it
out. Once the square has come apart you cannot move it, until a new red
square with nothing around it forms somewhere and you take control of
that one.

You clear a level by catching the X, which wanders around the board, in
your square for two turns in a row, or by having red cells outnumber
the white ones until no white cell is left. You lose when no red cell is
left. A few set levels come first, then random ones. When the board
settles down for long, the game scatters new red and white cells over
it.

The board is 50 by 35 and wraps around at every edge; on a terminal
shorter than 42 rows it scrolls to follow your square.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the square
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Redsquare is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

revenge.title: Revenge
revenge.description: Push rows of blocks to box in the cats before they catch you, and trapped cats turn to cheese
revenge.provenance: abakh wrote Revenge for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
revenge.page:
You are the rat (**r**), starting in the middle of a big square of
blocks (**#**), and a cat (**f**) is coming for you. Moving into a block
pushes it, together with every block in line behind it, as long as
there is a free cell at the end of the row. Use the blocks to wall the
cats in: once every cat is boxed in and cannot move, they all turn to
cheese (**%**), worth 75 points each, and a new wave of two to eight
cats comes in. Eating a piece of cheese, or pushing a block onto it, is
worth 100 more. More cats also turn up every five minutes. If a cat
reaches you, the game is over.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move and push
- **y**, **u**, **b**, **n**: move and push diagonally
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit; after a lost game, **y** plays again and **n**
  or **q** quits

## Options

Started from a shell, `revenge -n` does not ask whether to play again
after a lost game.

## History

Revenge is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games.

reversi.title: Reversi
reversi.description: Reversi against the computer or a friend: outflank the other side's discs and turn them
reversi.provenance: abakh wrote Reversi for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
reversi.page:
Black (X) and white (O) take turns putting a disc on the 8x8 board. A
disc has to trap at least one line of the other side's discs between
itself and another disc of yours, across, down or diagonally, and every
trapped disc turns over to your side. A side that cannot move is skipped;
when neither can, the side with more discs wins.

At the start the game asks who plays each side: by default the computer
plays white and you play black, which moves first. Two people can share
one keyboard, and the computer can play itself. Without `-p` the
computer starts out playing at random and adjusts after every game,
playing better after you win and worse after it wins.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: put your disc
- **Mouse**: click to put your disc
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: resign

## Options

- `-1 h` or `-1 c`: a human or the computer plays white
- `-2 h` or `-2 c`: the same for black; either one skips the questions
- `-p 3`: a fixed strength for the computer, from 1 to 127
- `-n`: quit after one game instead of offering another

## History

Reversi is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

risorgimento-represso.title: Risorgimento Represso
risorgimento-represso.description: Escape a dull lecture and stumble into a magical mess you have to clean up
risorgimento-represso.provenance: Michael J. Coyne wrote Risorgimento Represso in 2003 and revised it in 2006 and 2017.
risorgimento-represso.page:
Celtic Elements in Early Teutonic Settlements: a class so dull it might never end. You slip out of the lecture looking for something better to do, and find a world of magic that has gone badly wrong. A long, good-humoured puzzle adventure.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/risorgimento-represso`.

## Credits

- Risorgimento Represso: Michael J. Coyne, 2003, 2006 and 2017
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivs-NonCommercial 1.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

robotfindskitten.title: robotfindskitten
robotfindskitten.description: Yet another zen simulation: you are robot, and your job is to find kitten
robotfindskitten.provenance: Leonard Richardson wrote robotfindskitten in 1997 for the Nerth Pork magazine's contest of the same name, and contributors have kept it going since.
robotfindskitten.page:
You are robot. Your job is to find kitten. This task is complicated by
the existence of various things which are not kitten, scattered across
the screen, and every one of them looks like a random character, just
as kitten does. Robot must touch each thing to find out what it is:
perhaps a stack of 7 inch floppies wobbling precariously, perhaps some
coconut crabs milling about. There are 726 of them to meet. The game
ends when robotfindskitten.

There is no score, no timer and no way to lose. It is a zen simulation.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or the number pad: move robot; **yubn** (or
  **Home**, **PgUp**, **End**, **PgDn**) move diagonally
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw the screen
- **q** or **Ctrl-C**: give up

## Options

Started from a shell in its folder: `-n NUM` puts NUM things on the
screen (20 by default), `-s SEED` sets the layout, and `-f FILE` reads
the things from another list. Your own `.nki` files in
`~/.robotfindskitten` join the 726.

## History

In 1997 Peter A. Peterson II held a contest in his magazine Nerth Pork
for the best piece of art entitled "robotfindskitten". Leonard
Richardson submitted the winning (read: only) entry. This is the
canonical C version for terminals: Alexey Toptygin's 2004 to 2005 code,
merged by Eric S. Raymond in 2012 when he recovered the project's
history, and maintained since by Ryan Finnie, who moved it to Codeberg
in 2026. The game is upstream's, unchanged.

## Credits

- Game: Leonard Richardson and contributors
- C version: Alexey Toptygin, Eric S. Raymond, Ryan Finnie and contributors
- Windows console support: [PDCurses](https://pdcurses.org)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

robots.title: Robots
robots.description: Lure the dim but deadly robots into crashing into each other, with nothing but a teleporter to save you
robots.provenance: Robots was first written at the University of California in 1980, and Christos Zoulas contributed a new version to NetBSD in 1999. Mike Sharov rewrote it from scratch in 2016 for his bsd-games, keeping the play and the look of the field.

upstream.name: UC Berkeley (1980), Christos Zoulas (1999), Mike Sharov (2016)

robots.page:
Evil robots fill the field, and every time you move, each of them takes
one step straight toward you. They are not very bright: when two robots
run into each other they crash into a junk heap, and any robot that
walks into a heap is destroyed too. You have no weapons, so the only way
to win is to move so that they wreck each other.

Each robot destroyed scores a point. Clear the field and a new one
starts with more robots, up to 64, and a bonus for the level. When you
are cornered, teleport to a random empty spot: it can save you, or drop
you right next to a robot. When a robot finally reaches you the game is
over, and your score goes on the table of the top 16.

## Controls

- **h**, **j**, **k**, **l**: move left, down, up, right
- **y**, **u**, **b**, **n**: move diagonally up left, up right, down
  left, down right
- **.** or **Space**: stay where you are for a turn
- **t**: teleport
- **q** or **F10**: quit

The keys are also shown beside the field while you play. Robots are
`+`, junk heaps `*` and you are `@`.

## History

Robots is one of the oldest BSD games, first written at the University
of California in 1980. Mike Sharov rewrote it from scratch in 2016 for
his bsd-games, the modern Linux port of the BSD games, keeping the play
and the look of the field from Christos Zoulas's 1999 NetBSD version.
Robots is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD
licence.

rogue.title: Rogue
rogue.description: The game that named the roguelikes: go down through the Dungeons of Doom, fight what you meet, and bring back the Amulet of Yendor
rogue.provenance: Timothy Stoehr's rewrite of Rogue 5.3, the game by Michael C. Toy, Kenneth C. R. C. Arnold and Glenn Wichman; he mailed Kirk McKusick at Berkeley about it in 1987, and it has been part of BSD since.

upstream.name: Timothy Stoehr, after Michael C. Toy, Kenneth C. R. C. Arnold and Glenn Wichman

rogue.page:
The game every roguelike is named after. You are an adventurer at the
top of the Dungeons of Doom, and somewhere below the 20th level lies the
Amulet of Yendor. Each level is a new map of rooms and corridors, drawn
as you explore it, full of monsters, gold, potions, scrolls, wands,
rings, weapons and armour, most of which you will not recognise until
you try them. Death is final; your score is the gold you bring back,
with a tenth off for getting killed.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way, with **Ctrl** run until something is next to you
- **f** or **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest a turn
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start Rogue from
a shell as `rogue rogue.save`; a saved game is deleted once it is
restored, as in the original.

## History

Rogue's manual credits Michael C. Toy, Kenneth C. R. C. Arnold and Glenn
Wichman, the authors of the original, together with Timothy Stoehr,
whose rewrite of Rogue 5.3 this is: his November 1987 mail to Kirk
McKusick at Berkeley about this "public domain rogue" is still among its
sources, and it has been part of BSD's games since. Its notice lets
anyone change and share it but not sell it. This edition keeps saves and scores in
your own data folder. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

rogue36.title: Rogue 3.6
rogue36.description: Rogue as Berkeley shipped it in 1981: the Dungeons of Doom, 26 monsters from A to Z, and the Amulet of Yendor below the 20th level
rogue36.provenance: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold's Rogue 3.6 of 1981, restored by Nicholas J. Kisseberth in the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold (1981); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

rogue36.page:
Rogue as it was in 1981, the version that reached BSD Unix. You go down
through the Dungeons of Doom, a new map of rooms and corridors on every
level, to find the Amulet of Yendor somewhere below the 20th and bring
it back. Twenty-six monsters, one for each letter, wait on the way;
potions, scrolls, rings and wands are unknown until you try them. Death
is final, and your score is the gold you carry out.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **p**: zap a wand in a direction, **z**: zap
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **space**: rest
- `>`: stairs down
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `rogue36 -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Michael Toy and Glenn Wichman prototyped Rogue at UC Santa Cruz in
1980, and with Ken Arnold made the 1981 version 3.6, which reached BSD
Unix (it is in the reconstructed 4.1BSD release). Nicholas J. Kisseberth (Yendor) restored it for modern systems
in the Roguelike Restoration Project, releases 3.6.1 to 3.6.5, and keeps
it at rogueforge. This edition keeps its files in your data folder and
fixes a table overflow at
the start of every game and saved games that never restored. It is part
of the Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse catalog, next to
NetBSD's Rogue, a later clone of 5.3.

## Credits

Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by Nicholas J.
Kisseberth. BSD licence.

rogue52.title: Rogue 5.2
rogue52.description: Rogue as Berkeley had it in 1982: the Dungeons of Doom, now with stairs back up, traps you can name and a list of what you have found
rogue52.provenance: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold's Rogue 5.2 of 1982, restored by Nicholas J. Kisseberth in the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold (1982); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

rogue52.page:
Rogue as it was in 1982, a year after 3.6. You still go down through
the Dungeons of Doom for the Amulet of Yendor, a new map on every level,
monsters from A to Z, magic you learn by trying it, death for good and
gold for a score; but the stairs now lead up as well as down, you can
ask what a trap is, and **D** lists everything you have identified.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **z**: zap a wand in a direction, **^** and a direction: name a trap
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **D**: what you have discovered
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `rogue52 -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Rogue 5.2 is Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold's Berkeley
version of 1982, between the 3.6 of BSD and the 5.4 that most later
ports grew from. Nicholas J. Kisseberth (Yendor) restored it in the
Roguelike Restoration Project, releases 5.2.1 to 5.2.3, and keeps it at
rogueforge. This edition keeps its files in your data folder and fixes an overflow in the top
ten. It is part of the Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse
catalog.

## Credits

Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by Nicholas J.
Kisseberth. BSD licence.

rovers-day-out.title: Rover's Day Out
rovers-day-out.description: A spaceship's computer dreams through a morning routine that is not what it seems
rovers-day-out.provenance: Jack Welch and Ben Collins-Sussman's Rover's Day Out won the 2009 Interactive Fiction Competition.
rovers-day-out.page:
Janet and David are testing a new program on the MARSpace mission. Beep, beep, beep: an alarm clock by the futon, and an ordinary morning to get through, with a dog called Rover who needs his walk. Something underneath that morning is badly wrong, and the way the story is told is part of the puzzle.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/rovers-day-out`.

## Credits

- Rover's Day Out: Jack Welch and Ben Collins-Sussman, 2009
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-Share Alike 3.0
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

sail.title: Sail
sail.description: Command a man-of-war in the age of sail: work the wind, choose your shot and fight 31 historical sea battles against the computer
sail.provenance: Dave Riggle wrote Sail at UC Berkeley from 1980, after Avalon Hill's Wooden Ships and Iron Men, with Ed Wang as co-author and Craig Leres making it portable; it shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov rewrote it in 2016 as a single-player game with its own computer captains.

upstream.name: Dave Riggle and Ed Wang, UC Berkeley (1980)

sail.page:
Naval combat in the days of wooden ships, from the 1770s to the end of
Napoleonic France. You command one man-of-war in a historical battle,
from single-ship duels such as Ranger against Drake to John Paul Jones
boarding the Serapis at Flamborough Head and full fleet actions: 31
scenarios in all. The computer captains the other ships.

Every turn you give your orders: how far to sail and when to turn, which
sails to set, when to fire your broadsides and with what shot, when to
grapple and board. The wind decides what is possible. Full sails make
you fast but get shredded by round shot, a ship that stops moving starts
to drift, and the captain who holds the weather gage usually wins.

Ships are shown as two characters for bow and stern, such as `a0` for
the first American ship. A capital letter means full sail is set, `!`
means the ship has struck its colours, `~` that it is sinking and `#`
that it is on fire.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **j** and **k**: choose a scenario, ship and loads at the start; **Tab** or **Space** moves between the lists, **Enter** starts
- **m**: move, then a string of turns and moves such as `l3` (turn left, three ahead)
- **f**: fire broadsides, **l**: reload, **L**: unload to change shot
- **c**: change sails, **r**: repair
- **g**: grapple or let go, **u**: try to unfoul
- **b**: board an enemy ship, **B**: recall boarding parties
- **i**: the closest ship, **I**: all ships, **F**: find ships
- **C**: centre the view on your ship, **U**, **D**, **H**, **J**: move the view, **S**: follow your ship or not
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw, **q**: quit

The game's manual (`man sail`, also in the archive as `sail.6`) explains
movement, wind, shot types, boarding and every scenario in detail.

## History

Dave Riggle wrote the first Sail on a PDP-11/70 at Berkeley in the fall
of 1980, after Avalon Hill's board game Wooden Ships and Iron Men. Ed
Wang rewrote it almost from scratch in 1983, and Craig Leres made it
portable. It shipped with BSD Unix as a multi-player game for everyone
logged in to the same machine, with a separate driver program moving the
computer's ships.

In 2016 Mike Sharov rebuilt it for his bsd-games as a single-player
game: one program with its own computer captains, a new curses display
and the 31 scenarios built in. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog.

salvo.title: Salvo
salvo.description: Hide five ships on a 10x10 sea, then fire blind into the enemy's until one fleet is on the bottom: against the computer or a friend on the same keyboard.
salvo.provenance: abakh wrote it as Battleship for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018. It plays here as Salvo, the name the pencil-and-paper game was sold under in the 1930s.
salvo.page:
**HIDE YOUR FLEET. FIND THEIRS. SINK THE LOT.**

A carrier, a battleship, a destroyer, a submarine and a patrol boat, on a
10x10 sea. Lay them out where nobody would think to look. Then take turns
firing blind into the other side's waters, one shot at a time: `*` is a
hit, `~` is a splash. Sink a ship and you hear about it ("You have destroyed
my destroyer!!"), and the first fleet on the bottom loses.

Take on the computer, which will crow "Hahaha! I won!" if it gets there
first, or a friend on the same keyboard. For two players there's even an
anti-cheater screen between turns: type the given letter three times before
you may look.

- **Single player or two on one keyboard**
- **Keys or mouse**: click to place and fire, right click to turn a ship
- **Help built in**: F1 for the controls, F2 for how to play

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: place a ship, or fire
- **R**: turn the ship while setting up
- **Mouse**: left click to place or fire, right click to turn
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Salvo is one of the games abakh wrote, as Battleship, for New BSD Games, a
collection of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic
BSD games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR. Here it plays under the
pencil-and-paper game's old name: Salvo was what the paper game was sold as in
the 1930s, decades before plastic pegs and trays.

savoir-faire.title: Savoir-Faire
savoir-faire.description: A broke aristocrat returns to an empty chateau, with a talent for linking things
savoir-faire.provenance: Emily Short's Savoir-Faire (2002) is set in an alternate France where magic links like things to like.
savoir-faire.page:
Fifteen years of champagne and carriage rides, and you are in debt. You come back to the Count's chateau hoping for an advance, and find it empty: no Count, no Marie, not even the cook. Somewhere in the house is what you need, and you have a magic for getting it, linking two similar things so that what happens to one happens to the other.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/savoir-faire`.

## Credits

- Savoir-Faire: Emily Short, 2002 to 2004
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivs-NonCommercial 1.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

scissor.title: Scissor
scissor.description: Rock, paper, scissors as a live action game: steer your scissor into papers and away from rocks
scissor.provenance: abakh wrote Scissor for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
scissor.page:
Rock, paper and scissors bounce around the screen: rocks (**O**), papers
(**#**), scissors (**>**) and one magic piece (**?**). When two meet, the
winner turns the loser into its own kind: rock blunts scissors, scissors
cut paper, paper wraps rock. The magic piece turns scissors into paper,
paper into rock and rock into scissors.

You steer the highlighted scissor. Every time it hits a piece of another
kind you score 47 points, so the game is to hunt papers, dodge rocks
and manage the populations. If your scissor is turned into
something else, another scissor on the screen becomes yours; you have
extra lives as long as there are scissors left. When the last one is
gone, the game is over. Some of the other scissors follow your keys
too, now and then.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: steer up, down, left and right
- **y**, **u**, **b**, **n**: steer diagonally, which is faster
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: end the game; at the end, **y** plays again and **n**
  or **q** quits

## History

Scissor is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games.

scrap.title: Scrap
scrap.description: A robot roguelike written in ten days: shoot enemy robots to wrecks and build your own from the systems you salvage, twenty levels down
scrap.provenance: Thijs van Ommen wrote Scrap in ten days for the Ten-Day Roguelike in 2005, extended it in 2006 and published it on GitHub in 2017.
scrap.page:
You are a robot, the **@**, in a world full of hostile robots, and the
only way out is down through twenty levels: open grass and woods, rough
ground, enemy buildings, caves, chasms, flooded ruins and a metal fortress
at the bottom. Every robot, yours included, is built from up to eight
systems: power cells, weapons, propulsion, sensors and armour. Shots damage
systems rather than hit points; a system at 50% or less stops working until
your power cell repairs it, and one at 0% is gone for good. If a power
cell is destroyed, it explodes and takes the robot with it.

Destroy an enemy's power source and it becomes a wreck (**%**). Drive into
the wreck to salvage what is left of it: a buggy's minigun, a tank's
caterpillar tracks for crossing rough ground, a sentry's X-ray scope for
seeing through walls. Your robot grows into whatever you take from the
robots you beat.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**, the cursor keys or the numeric keypad: move, the last
  four diagonally; drive into a wreck to salvage it
- **1** to **8**: use a system; for a weapon, the nearest target is picked,
  **+** and **-** cycle through targets, **x** cancels and any other key
  fires; a power cell chooses which system it repairs, a sensor looks
  around
- **d**: details of your systems, or of the robot being looked at
- **r**: reorder your systems, **s**: switch a system on or off
- **.**: wait, `>`: take the exit to the next level
- **@**: which level you are on, **?**: the controls
- **S**: save and quit, **R**: restore the saved game, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder and quits. Start Scrap again
and press **R** to carry on; a saved game can be restored once, then it
is deleted, as in the original.

## History

Thijs van Ommen wrote Scrap in ten days, a Ten-Day Roguelike released
in March 2005. In October and November 2006 he released the Extended 10DRL
and its 1.1, which added saving and the other features the ten days had
left out while keeping the game itself as it was, and in 2017 he put it
on GitHub under the GPL. This edition keeps the savefile in your data
folder.

shade.title: Shade
shade.description: Waiting for dawn in your small apartment before a trip, the place starts to change
shade.provenance: Andrew Plotkin wrote Shade for the 2000 Interactive Fiction Competition.
shade.page:
Odd, how the light just makes your apartment gloomier. Your luggage is packed for the desert, the hyacinth by the window needs water, and morning will not come. Something about this small, familiar room is wrong, and the longer you look, the more it shows. A short game, best played without knowing more.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/shade`.

## Credits

- Shade: Andrew Plotkin, 2000
- License: The author's terms: may be distributed for free, but not sold
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

sil-q.title: Sil-Q
sil-q.description: Steal a Silmaril from Morgoth's iron crown and escape alive, in the Tolkien roguelike of the First Age that grew out of Angband
sil-q.provenance: half and Scatha made Sil, a Tolkien roguelike grown from NPPAngband and Angband, from 2012 to 2016; Quirk continued it as Sil-Q from 2017 to version 1.5.0 (2022), and Michael G. Noll carries it on today.

upstream.name: Michael G. Noll and Quirk (Sil-Q), after Sil by half and Scatha

sil-q.page:
Steal a Silmaril from Morgoth's iron crown and escape alive. You are an
elf, a dwarf or a man of the First Age who has found a way into
Angband, the Dark Lord's fortress, unarmed and with little food, and
you must go down a thousand feet to his throne room. Sil-Q is the
continuation of Sil, a roguelike that stays close to Tolkien: no
classes, no wizards or priests, no magical scrolls and no town, but
eight skills to train, songs of power, smithing at the forges, stealth,
and careful, tactical combat with few easy escapes.

Experience comes from meeting new creatures, going deeper and
identifying things as much as from killing, so sneaking past a sleeping
troll is a real choice; the game can be won without ever attacking.
Every level is made afresh, and as time passes you can no longer go back
up past a minimum depth, so you must keep going down. Death is final.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or the **number keys** (1 to 9): move; walk into a
  monster to attack it
- **Z**: rest, **z**: stay in place, **.** and a direction: run
- **<** and **>**: take stairs up and down
- **g**: pick up, **i**: inventory, **e**: equipment, **w**: wear or
  wield, **r**: take off, **d**: drop
- **E** eat, **q** quaff a potion, **u** use an item, **a** use a staff,
  **f** and **F** fire from the first or second quiver, **t** throw
- **s**: sing a song, **S**: stealth mode, **Tab**: abilities,
  **0**: smithing at a forge
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors, **T**: tunnel, **D**: disarm
- **x**: examine an item, **l**: look around, **M**: map of the level,
  **@**: character sheet
- **?**: help, **Esc** or **m**: the menu, with options (a keyset with
  hjkl movement is there too)
- **Ctrl-S**: save, **Ctrl-X**: save and quit

## Saving

**Ctrl-X** saves your character and goes back to the title menu; choose
"Open saved character" and give the character's name to carry on.
Saved characters, the high scores, character dumps and options are kept
in your data folder (`~/.local/share/sil-q`).

## History

Sil was made by half and Scatha and released in 2012; its last version,
1.3, came out in 2016. It grew from NPPAngband, a variant of Angband,
but kept little of it. Quirk took up the Sil 1.3 code in 2017 as Sil-Q,
rebalancing abilities, smithing and the enemies with Scatha's feedback,
and released 1.5.0 in 2022 with tiles and a new manual by MicroChasm.
Michael G. Noll has carried it on since 2026, fixing the bugs reported
against 1.5.0 without changing the play.

This edition keeps your files in your own data folder and saves a new
character under its own name. Sil-Q is under the GNU GPL, version 2.

silent-night.title: Silent Night
silent-night.description: A snowy forest at night: wind and gusts blow the snow into drifts around a lit cabin, under the stars and a faint aurora, with the sound of the wind and the forest
silent-night.provenance: Asciiverse made Silent Night in Rust in 2026 for Christmas, after finding no terminal snow with wind, drifting snow or depth.
silent-night.page:
Night in a snowy forest. Snow drifts down at three depths, near flakes
fast and large, far ones faint. The wind comes and goes: a gust sweeps in
from one side, bends the spruces, shakes the snow off their branches in
clumps and lifts the snow off the open field in a low blizzard, laying it
down again behind the cabin and the trees, so the drifts grow and creep
downwind. Snow settles on the roof until it slides off.

A log cabin glows at its windows with smoke drifting from the chimney, a
spruce beside it is lit for Christmas, and above the mountains the stars
twinkle, the moon shines and a faint aurora moves. Every now and then a
sleigh crosses the sky.

The sound is made as it plays, nothing recorded: the wind in the trees
rises and falls with the gusts you see, whistles in the strongest, snow
thumps off the branches and the roof, an owl calls far off, and sleigh
bells ring while the sleigh is up.

## Controls

- **m**: sound off and on
- **Any other key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal: `silent-night --mute` starts quiet, `--no-sound` has no
