sound at all, and `-s N` builds the same forest every time.

## Sound

On Linux the sound goes to PipeWire, PulseAudio or ALSA (through
`pw-cat`, `paplay` or `aplay`), or to `ffplay`, whichever is there; on
macOS and Windows to the default output. Without any of them it is a
silent night.

## Credits

- Silent Night: made by Asciiverse, 2026
- License: MIT

sjump.title: Square Jump
sjump.description: Time your jump: send the O flying from square to square and build up a combo
sjump.provenance: abakh wrote Square Jump for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
sjump.page:
An O runs round the border of a square. Press **Enter** and it flies
off in the direction it sits from the middle of the square: from the
middle of the right-hand side it goes straight across, from higher or
lower it climbs or falls on the way. It has to land in the next square; if it flies off
the screen or past the square, the game is over.

Every landing scores the combo and raises it by one. Landing on the top
or bottom edge of the square scores the combo times 101. The combo drops
back to 1 each time the O passes the bottom right corner of its square,
so it pays not to wait a whole round.

## Controls

- **Enter**: jump
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **q**: end the game; at the end, **y** plays again and **n** or **q** quits

## History

Square Jump is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a
collection of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the
classic BSD games.

snake.title: Snake
snake.description: Grab the money and reach the exit before the snake eats you: the 1980 BSD chase game, where the snake gets hungrier as you get richer
snake.provenance: Snake is a 1980 chase game from UC Berkeley that shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov gave it a new chase algorithm and a longer, deadlier snake in 2016 for his bsd-games.
snake.page:
You are the red `@`. Somewhere on the field is a `$`, and somewhere an
exit, `#`. A green snake, `@` for its head and `s` for its body, hunts
you all the while. Grab the money, and a new `$` appears; the richer you
get, the hungrier the snake. Leave by the exit whenever you like to bank
your winnings, but getting eaten is worth nothing.

You keep moving in the direction you last chose, so plan your path
around the snake. When it has you cornered, a space warp throws you to a
random spot, at a price. If the snake does catch you, a lucky roll on
the last digit of your winnings can still warp you free.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: change direction
- **w**: space warp, at a cost
- **q** or **F10**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `snake 40 20` plays on a field 40 wide and 20 high
instead of the whole terminal, and `snake -s` prints the high scores.

## History

Snake was written at UC Berkeley in 1980 and shipped with BSD Unix as one
of its "crt hack" games, made for the video terminals of the day. Mike Sharov
gave it a new chase algorithm and a longer, deadlier snake in 2016 for
his bsd-games, the modern Linux port. Only players who escape by the
exit make the high-score table.

snakeduel.title: Snakeduel
snakeduel.description: A light-cycle duel against the computer: both snakes leave walls behind, and the first to crash loses the round
snakeduel.provenance: abakh wrote Snakeduel for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
snakeduel.page:
Your snake against the computer's. Both start side by side in the middle
of the board, yours on the right, and both leave a wall behind them
wherever they go. Run into a wall, the other snake or yourself and you
lose the round; make the computer crash first and you win it.

The computer plays to block your way and keep room for itself. The first
to five wins takes the match, and from four all it goes on until one
side is two ahead. The colours of the snakes change from round to round.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: change direction (not straight back)
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, Snakeduel fits the board to the terminal, or takes
its size:

- `-w`: the width, from 40 to 127
- `-l`: the length (height), from 10 to 127
- `-h`: help on the options

## History

Snakeduel is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

so-far.title: So Far
so-far.description: Walk off a stifling theatre stage into a chain of strange, linked worlds
so-far.provenance: Andrew Plotkin's So Far (1996) was nominated in the 1996 XYZZY Awards.
so-far.page:
Hot, foul and dark: an indoor theatre in high summer, a play you love, and Aessa, who was supposed to meet you, nowhere to be seen. From there the way leads out of the theatre and into worlds joined by doors and choices, each with its own logic and its own price. A long, demanding puzzle game about distance and resolution.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/so-far`.

## Credits

- So Far: Andrew Plotkin, 1996
- License: The author's terms: it may be copied, distributed and played freely
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

solitty.title: Solitty
solitty.description: Ncurses-based Klondike solitaire, packaged for the Asciiverse catalog
solitty.provenance: Murilo Pereira wrote solitty, an ncurses Klondike, between 2010 and 2018.
solitty.page:
Klondike solitaire in your terminal: the classic seven-column patience
game, drawn with Unicode card frames and colored suits, played with the
keyboard or the mouse.

Turn cards from the stock, build down the seven columns in alternating
colors, and move every card up to the four foundations, ace to king.
solitty notices when you have won.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the cursor
- **Space**: turn a card from the stock, flip a face-down card, or pick
  up a card and put it down where the cursor is
- **Space** twice on the same card: send it to a foundation if it fits
- **m** / **n**: while holding a column, take one more or one fewer card
- **M** / **N**: take every face-up card in the column, or only the top one
- **Esc**: put the held cards back
- **Left click**: pick up or put down; **right click**: cancel
- **q**: quit

## Options

- `--passes N`: how many times you may go through the stock (default 3)
- `--four-color-deck`: give each suit its own color
- `--no-background-color`: keep your terminal's own background

## History

solitty was written by Murilo Pereira, first released in 2017, and
developed through 2025. The Asciiverse edition adds a fairer
Fisher-Yates shuffle, a terminal that is restored properly when the
game is interrupted, and further fixes and tests.

## Credits

- Original game: [Murilo Pereira](http://murilopereira.com)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

spider-and-web.title: Spider and Web
spider-and-web.description: A spy caught breaking in is made to tell the story, and not all of it is true
spider-and-web.provenance: Andrew Plotkin wrote Spider and Web in 1998.
spider-and-web.page:
A dead-end alley in a foreign capital, and a plain metal door with no handle. You are a tourist, or so you say. Your interrogator has other ideas, and the story of how you got past that door is told, and retold, under questioning. Pay attention to what you say, and to what you do not.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/spider-and-web`.

## Credits

- Spider and Web: Andrew Plotkin, 1997 to 1998
- License: The author's terms: it may be copied, distributed and played freely
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

spirhunt.title: Space Pirate Hunt
spirhunt.description: Clear the galaxy of space pirates before time runs out: warp between quadrants, fire plasers and torpedoes, dock at starbases, with the whole map always on screen
spirhunt.provenance: Eric Allman wrote trek at UC Berkeley in 1976, and it shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov removed its Star Trek content and brought it back in 2020 as Space Pirate Hunt, then gave it a full-screen curses display and grid navigation.

upstream.name: Eric Allman, UC Berkeley (1976); Mike Sharov (2020)

spirhunt.page:
The galaxy is overrun with space pirates, and you have limited time to
destroy them all. You command a warship with energy,
shields, plaser banks and ten torpedoes, and starbases where docking
restores your energy, shields and torpedoes. The pirates fight back, and so do
supernovas and black holes.

The screen always shows the sector you are in, your ship `Y` among
stars `*`, starbases `#`, pirates `P` and inhabited planets `@`, beside a
chart of the whole galaxy and a panel with your condition, energy,
torpedoes, the pirates left and the time remaining. You move by giving a
grid position: two digits for a spot in this sector, four to warp to
another.

## Controls

Each command is one key; the game then asks for what it needs.

- **m**: move, to a position such as `44` here or `3544` in another sector
- **I**: move under impulse, **w**: set the warp factor
- **p**: fire plasers, **t**: fire torpedoes, **R**: ram something
- **s**: shields up or down, **c**: cloak on or off
- **d**: dock or undock at a starbase, **H**: call a starbase for help
- **r**: rest, **i**: damage report
- **C**: ask a pirate to surrender
- **D**: self-destruct
- **?**: list the commands
- **S**: save and quit (the next start carries on), **Q**: quit at once

## History

Eric Allman wrote trek at UC Berkeley in 1976, and it shipped with BSD
Unix. Mike Sharov dropped it
from his bsd-games for its Star Trek content, then brought it back in
2020 as Space Pirate Hunt, with the same game and no Trek references.
Later that year he replaced its typed scan commands with a full-screen
curses display, moved navigation to a grid and simplified aiming.

The original teletype game, Klingons and all, is also in the catalog as
BSD Trek.

srogue.title: Super-Rogue
srogue.description: Bell Labs' bigger Rogue of 1982 to 1984: 52 monsters, magic pools, mazes, a Flea Market and four stats to watch, down to the Amulet of Yendor
srogue.provenance: Robert D. Kindelberger and co-workers at AT&T Bell Labs made Super-Rogue from Rogue 3.6 between 1982 and 1984; Kindelberger gave the 9.0 source to Nicholas J. Kisseberth in 2004, who restored it for the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Robert D. Kindelberger (1984); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

srogue.page:
The Rogue that Bell Labs built up. You are sent into the Dungeons of
Doom by your fighters' guild to bring back the Amulet of Yendor, as in
Rogue, but there are 52 monsters in both cases of the alphabet, magic
pools that do strange things to what you dip in them, mazes, a Flea
Market, and strength, dexterity, wisdom and constitution to keep up. Two
status lines show them all, with how much you carry.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **p** and a direction: zap a wand that way, **z**: zap
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **a**: your best stats so far
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring, **D**: dip something
  in a pool
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>`: stairs down
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `srogue -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Super-Rogue was made at AT&T Bell Labs between 1982 and 1984 from Rogue
3.6, with Robert D. Kindelberger as the public face of the group; 9.0 is
its last version. Kindelberger gave its source to Nicholas J. Kisseberth
(Yendor) in 2004, and the Roguelike Restoration Project released 9.0-1
in 2005. This edition keeps your files in your data folder and fixes
it for 64-bit machines. It is part of the Roguelike Restoration Project
in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Robert D. Kindelberger and his co-workers at Bell Labs, after Rogue by
Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by Nicholas J.
Kisseberth. BSD licence with clauses on the name Super-Rogue.

sshtron.title: SSHTron
sshtron.description: Lightcycles over SSH: leave a wall of light behind you, cut across the others, and be the last trail still moving
sshtron.provenance: Zach Latta and Max Wofford built SSHTron in about twenty hours at BrickHack 2 in March 2016, a Tron game anyone could join with nothing but ssh, and its public server is still running.
sshtron.page:
The grid is black. Your cycle is moving, and it is not going to stop.
Behind you it leaves a wall of light, and every other rider leaves one
too. Touch a wall, any wall, yours included, and you are gone: back at
once somewhere else on the grid with a score of zero and a fresh trail,
leaving a spot of your colour in the one you hit.

Your score climbs for every second you stay alive, and faster the more
riders there are. Box the others in, cut across their path, leave them
nowhere to turn. Seven colours fit in one arena: red, green, yellow,
blue, magenta, cyan and white.

SSHTron was made to be played with nothing but `ssh`, and it still can
be. Pick **Play** and you race computer riders on a grid hosted on your
own machine; anyone on your network can ride in with `ssh -p 2022` and
your address, or with SSHTron's own **Join a friend**. **Play online**
takes you to the original public server at sshtron.zachlatta.com, where
whoever else is online that day shares the grid.

## Controls

- **W A S D**, the **arrow keys** or **h j k l**: steer (also **z q s d**
  and **, a o e**)
- **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: leave the game

In the menu, **Colour** asks for the colour you ride in; a computer rider
in it makes way for you.

## Options

- `-play`, `-online`, `-join host[:port]`: skip the menu
- `-color red`: ask for a colour
- `-bots N`: computer riders in each game (3, up to 6)
- `-demo`: watch the computer ride for you; any key ends it
- `-server`: run only the server, for others to join with `ssh -p 2022`

## Credits

- SSHTron: Zach Latta and Max Wofford, with Ali Yousuf and others
  ([github.com/zachlatta/sshtron](https://github.com/zachlatta/sshtron)),
  2016, written in Go at BrickHack 2
- Arrow keys and trail fixes: Yerlotic
  ([github.com/yerlotic/sshtron](https://github.com/yerlotic/sshtron))
- Asciiverse edition: the menu, the built-in SSH client, computer riders,
  games on the local network, and fixes for a server
  that could crash under load
- License: MIT

starlanes.title: Star Lanes
starlanes.description: Found shipping companies between the stars, buy their stock and merge your way to the biggest fortune: the classic trading game for one to four players at one keyboard
starlanes.provenance: Brian "Beej" Hall wrote this curses Star Lanes in C (1995 to 1997, 1.2.2), after the Osborne version of Steven Faber's game, and modernised it himself in 2026 (1.4.0).
starlanes.page:
The classic game of interstellar commerce for one to four players, taking
turns at one keyboard. Each turn you pick one of five sectors on the star
map. Land next to a star or an infant company and you found a shipping
company, with five free shares for the founder; land next to a company and
it grows. Then you trade: buy stock in the companies you think will
prosper, sell what looks doomed.

A company is worth $100 a share for every sector it holds, plus $500 for
every sector next to a star and minus $500 for every sector next to a black
hole. Push a rival's company into a black hole and its stock is gone. When
two companies touch, the bigger swallows the smaller: shares in the loser
turn into half as many in the winner, and its shareholders get a cash bonus.
Prices over $3,000 split two for one. Every turn pays you 5% of your
holdings in cash. The game ends when companies fill 54% of the map, and the
richest player wins.

## Controls

- **1** to **5**: take one of the five sectors numbered on the map
- **Up** and **Down** (or **k** and **j**): choose a company while trading
- **Enter**: trade in that company; type a number of shares (negative to
  sell), **m** for as many as you can afford, **n** to sell them all
- **Esc**: end your trading and pass to the next player
- **s**: the standings; **c**: company details (size and total worth)
- **q** or **Ctrl+C**: quit, after showing the final standings
- **Ctrl+L**: redraw the screen

## Options

- `-c`: force colour; `-m`: force black and white

## History

Steven Faber's Star Lanes was printed as a BASIC listing in Interface Age
in June 1977 and went round many home computers from there (Brian "Beej"
Hall traced it in his starlanes-info notes). Beej played it from a
First Osborne Group disk in about 1982 and wrote this curses version in C
in 1995 to 1997, releasing 1.2.2 in 1997. His version has black holes,
which the original did not, "to give players who have fallen behind a
chance to shaft the leaders". In 2026 he took it up again, broke the one big source file
into modules and released 1.4.0.

sudoku.title: Sudoku
sudoku.description: Sudoku in the terminal, from 4x4 up to 49x49, with hints and the mouse
sudoku.provenance: abakh wrote Sudoku for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
sudoku.page:
Fill the grid so that every row, every column and every smaller box
holds each symbol once. About half the cells start filled in, shown in
bold; a number that clashes with another is shown in red. The game ends
when every cell is filled by the rules, and asks whether to start a new
board.

Boards are not guaranteed to have only one solution: any filling that
follows the rules wins.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move
- **1** to **9**: write a number; on boards bigger than 9x9 the letters
  from **a** on are symbols too
- **Enter**: step the number in the cell up by one
- **Space**: clear the cell
- **Mouse**: left click to step the number up, right click to clear
- **?**: hint, fills in the cell under the cursor (after showing the help)
- **r**: clear everything you wrote, **n**: a new board
- **F1**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **PgUp**, **PgDn**, **<** and **>**: scroll a board that does not fit
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

On the biggest boards some of these letters are symbols: **n** stops
working from 25x25, **q**, **r** and **Esc** from 36x36. **Q** always quits.

## Options

Started from a shell, Sudoku takes the size of the boxes:

- `-s 4` plays a 16x16 board; anything from `-s 2` (4x4) to `-s 7`
  (49x49) works, and the default is 3 (9x9)
- `-f` makes boards with a faster, cruder generator, which is always
  used from 25x25 up

## History

Sudoku is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

swarm.title: Swarm
swarm.description: Stranded on an alien planet, you build and program robots in a small functional language to explore, gather and craft
swarm.provenance: Swarm is by Brent Yorgey and contributors, in Haskell on Brick, since 2021.
swarm.page:
You have crash-landed on an alien planet with a toxic atmosphere, so you
stay inside your robotic base and send robots out instead. You program
them in a small functional language: move, grab, build, scan, and later
loops, conditions, recursion and whole fleets of robots running their own
programs. Every resource they bring back lets you craft better devices,
which give your robots new abilities and new language features, which let
them gather more.

Start with the Tutorial from the main menu; it teaches the language one
idea at a time. Then try Classic or Creative games on a generated world, or
the challenges: Sokoban, mazes, Towers of Hanoi, ranching, bridge building
and more. Progress and achievements are saved automatically.

## Controls

- Type commands at the prompt and press **Enter** to run them, for example
  `move` or `build {move; grab}`; **Ctrl+C** or **Esc** stops a program
- **Alt+W**, **Alt+E**, **Alt+R**, **Alt+T**: focus the world, robot,
  prompt and info panels; the mouse works too
- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: scroll the world view
- **F1**: help, **F2**: robots, **F3**: recipes, **F4**: commands,
  **F5**: messages, **F6**: structures
- **Ctrl+G**: show the current goal
- **Ctrl+P**: pause, **Ctrl+X** and **Ctrl+Z**: double and halve the speed
- **Ctrl+Q**: quit

## Options

- `--scenario NAME`: start a scenario directly, e.g. `Tutorials/move`
- `--seed N`: world seed for generated worlds
- `--autoplay`: watch a scenario's built-in solution
- `--speed N`: starting game speed
- `swarm keybindings`: list every key binding

## History

Brent Yorgey started Swarm in 2021, written in Haskell with the Brick
terminal UI library, and it has grown into a community project with more
than thirty contributors. This edition has one small change: it
finds its data folder next to the program, so it runs straight
from the install folder.

## Credits

- Game: [Brent Yorgey and the Swarm contributors](https://swarm-game.github.io/)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: BSD-3-Clause

tarts.title: tarts
tarts.description: Terminal art in motion: Matrix rain, a spinning donut, plasma, fire, flocking boids and more
tarts.provenance: tarts (Terminal Arts) is by oiwn and contributors, in Rust, since 2022.
tarts.page:
Twelve classic terminal effects in one program, shown one after another:
the Matrix's digital rain, the spinning ASCII donut, electric plasma, a
crackling fire, flocking boids, pipes that wind across the screen,
Conway's Game of Life, a rotating cube, drifting constellations, crabs
and butterflies, and a maze that builds itself. Each one fills your
window and keeps going for twenty seconds before the next takes over.

## Controls

- **n**, **Space** or **Right**: next effect
- **p** or **Left**: previous effect
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

To run one effect on its own, start it from a terminal by name, for
example `tarts donut`; `tarts pocketworld` grows a little world with
drifting continents, rivers and weather, and `tarts --help` lists them
all.

## Credits

- tarts: [oiwn and contributors](https://github.com/oiwn/tarts)
- Asciiverse edition: the tour
- License: MIT

termcraft.title: Termcraft
termcraft.description: Punch a tree, survive the night, then dig your way to the Nether and the dragon beyond: a whole block world drawn in terminal pixels, with up to eight friends along
termcraft.provenance: Termcraft is Sebastian Pagel's 2D survival sandbox in Rust from 2026, after Minecraft.
termcraft.page:
The sun is going down and you own nothing but your fists.

Punch a tree. Turn the wood into planks, the planks into a crafting table,
the table into a pickaxe. Dig into the hillside before the zombies come
out, light it with a torch, and listen for the creeper you did not see.
Termcraft is the whole survival loop of a block world, turned on its side
and drawn in terminal pixels: lit caves, rain and snow, rooms cut away so
you can see inside, and every creature with its own silhouette.

Then keep going. Smelt iron, find diamonds, raise a farm and breed the
animals that wander into it. Trade glances with villagers, raid dungeons,
build a portal of obsidian and step through into the Nether, where ghasts
spit fire and blazes guard the fortresses. Craft the Eyes of Ender, follow
them to the stronghold, and at the end of everything the Ender Dragon is
waiting.

You do not have to do it alone. One command hosts a world and drops you
into it; up to eight friends join from their own terminals, on the same
network or through SSH, with their own inventories, shared building, chat
and, if you leave it on, PvP.

Short on time? **Lantern Run** is a compact challenge route: cross a
broken trail, take back a ruin from its guards, raid the supply chest,
bridge the chasm and relight the signal.

## Controls

- **A** / **D** or **Left** / **Right**: walk; double-tap and hold to
  sprint (needs a terminal that reports key releases, such as kitty,
  Ghostty, foot or WezTerm)
- **W**, **Up** or **Space**: jump, swim up, climb ladders
- **Left mouse**: mine and attack; **right mouse**: place and use;
  **F**: use the block under the pointer
- **E**: inventory and crafting (the recipe book is on the left)
- **1** to **9**: hotbar; **V** / **Shift+V**: drop one or the stack
- **F4**: cycle the Detail, Overview and Wide views; **+** / **-**: zoom
- **T**: chat in co-op, commands in solo; **O**: settings (difficulty and
  game rules); **F3**: diagnostics
- **Q** or **Esc**: close a screen, or save and quit

The game autosaves. It plays at any size, best at 120x40 or larger.

## Options

- `termcraft trial`: play Lantern Run
- `termcraft host`: host a co-op world and play in it (**T** shows the
  address); friends run `termcraft client ADDRESS --player NAME`
- `termcraft join USER@HOST --player NAME`: join through an SSH account
- `termcraft world list`: your saved worlds; `termcraft world play ID`
  opens one

Everyone in a co-op game needs the same version. The full guides
(multiplayer, hosting, saves) are in the `docs` folder of the install.

## Credits

- Termcraft: Sebastian Pagel
  ([github.com/pagel-s/termcraft](https://github.com/pagel-s/termcraft)),
  2026, written in Rust
- License: AGPL-3.0-only

terminal-parrot.title: terminal-parrot
terminal-parrot.description: The party parrot, dancing in your terminal in every colour, forever
terminal-parrot.provenance: terminal-parrot is by John Hobbs and contributors, in Go, since 2016.
terminal-parrot.page:
The party parrot, the dancing kakapo of a thousand chat rooms, in ASCII
art in your terminal: it bobs and spins in a loop, changing colour every
frame, for as long as you let it.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `-delay 25` makes it a fast parrot (the default is 75
milliseconds a frame), `-orientation aussie` turns it upside down, and
`-loops 5` stops after five dances. `-path` points at a folder of your own
`.animation` files, and `terminal-parrot <name>` plays one of them.

## Credits

- terminal-parrot: [John Hobbs and contributors](https://github.com/jmhobbs/terminal-parrot)
- The parrot: a jp2a rendering of the Party Parrot, after Sirocco the
  kakapo
- Asciiverse edition: the parrot only, any key quits, a clean exit on
  SIGTERM
- License: MIT

terminal-pong.title: terminal.pong
terminal-pong.description: Pong in the terminal: against the computer, with a friend, or watch two AIs play
terminal-pong.provenance: terminal.pong is IshmamR's Pong in Rust and Ratatui (2025).
terminal-pong.page:
The classic, in your terminal. Play against the computer, take on a
friend on the same keyboard, or lean back and watch two AIs rally. Each
side has a handful of power shots that send the ball flying, and the
court grows and shrinks with your window, even mid-game.

## Controls

- **Player 1**: **Up** and **Down** (or the mouse wheel), **/** for a power shot
- **Player 2**: **W** and **S**, **Space** for a power shot
- **P**: pause; in the pause menu, **D** cycles the colour themes
- **Esc**: back to the menu

Difficulty for each mode, and the default theme, are in Settings.

## Credits

- terminal.pong: [IshmamR](https://github.com/IshmamR/terminal.pong)
- Asciiverse edition: a frame-rate cap
- License: MIT

terminal-rain-lightning.title: Terminal Rain
terminal-rain-lightning.description: Rain falls down the terminal, and in a thunderstorm forked lightning cracks across it, with the sound of rain and thunder if you like
terminal-rain-lightning.provenance: Terminal Rain is by rmaake1, in Python on curses, from 2025 to 2026, with slow motion by plasma and rain and thunder sounds contributed from Pixabay.
terminal-rain-lightning.page:
Rain streams down the terminal in cyan strokes and dots. Switch on the
thunderstorm and it pours harder and brighter, and now and then a bolt of
lightning forks down from the sky, flares and fades. With sound on, the
rain patters along and thunder rolls in a moment after each strike.

## Controls

- **t**: thunderstorm on or off (Asciiverse starts in the storm)
- **s**: speed: fast, medium, slow
- **m**: sound on or off (needs `ffplay` from FFmpeg)
- **v**: volume: quiet, normal, loud
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

From a terminal: `terminal-rain --sound` starts with sound,
`--rain-color` and `--lightning-color` take black, red, green, yellow,
blue, magenta, cyan or white, and `--speed` and `--volume` set where they
start. `terminal-rain --help` lists them all.

## Credits

- Terminal Rain: [rmaake1](https://github.com/rmaake1/terminal-rain-lightning)
- Slow motion: plasma (xXBlackPlasmaXx)
- Rain and thunder sounds: Pixabay sound effects contributed to the
  project, cut and varied by rmaake1
- Asciiverse edition: the script ported to Rust, one program for Linux,
  macOS and Windows, with the same rain, lightning, keys and sounds
- License: MIT

termsuji.title: termsuji
termsuji.description: Go in the terminal on a proper wooden board: play GNU Go on 9x9, 13x13 or 19x19, at ten strengths and with handicap stones
termsuji.provenance: termsuji is lvank's terminal client for online-go.com, in Go with tview (2022).
termsuji.page:
Go, the board game, in the terminal, on a board that looks like one:
lines and star points on wood, black and white stones on the points, as
big as the terminal allows. Play GNU Go, which comes with the game, on a
9x9, 13x13 or 19x19 board, as Black or White, at any of its ten
strengths, with up to nine handicap stones for Black.

GNU Go thinks while you look at the board, a cursor shows where you are
and the last stone played is marked. Take back a move whenever you like.
Two passes end the game and GNU Go counts it. Leave in the middle and the
game is waiting under Continue the next time, saved as an SGF file that
any Go program can open.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the cursor; **Enter**: play a stone there
- **p**: pass; **u**: take back your move and GNU Go's answer
- **t**: change the board's look; **q**: back to the menu (the game is
  saved)
- **n**: a new game once the game is over
- In the menus: **Up**, **Down** or **Tab** to choose, **Enter** to go on

## Credits

- termsuji: lvank ([github.com/lvank/termsuji](https://github.com/lvank/termsuji)),
  2022, written in Go with tview and tcell
- GNU Go 3.9.1: the GNU Go authors
  ([gnu.org/software/gnugo](https://www.gnu.org/software/gnugo/)),
  GPL-3.0-or-later, shipped beside termsuji with its licence and source
- Asciiverse edition: play against GNU Go, saved games and the classic
  board
- License: MIT (termsuji), GPL-3.0-or-later (GNU Go)

ternimal.title: Ternimal
ternimal.description: A glowing lifeform creeps and coils around the terminal along an endless path of arcs
ternimal.provenance: Ternimal is by Philipp Emanuel Weidmann, one Rust file with no dependencies, from 2017.
ternimal.page:
A lifeform made of light creeps around the window: its body stretches and
contracts as it crawls along a path of circular arcs that never ends and
never repeats, glowing white along its spine and fading to blue and violet
at its edges. Leave it running and watch it coil.

Ternimal draws with half blocks in 24-bit colour, so the body is smooth at
twice the vertical resolution of the text.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, everything about the creature can be changed with
`name=value` arguments: `length=100 thickness=1,4,1,0,0 radius=6,12` makes
a long snake, `length=200 thickness=0,4,19,0,0` a swarm, `speed=` and
`fps=` set the pace, `gradient=0:#666600,0.5:#00ff00,1:#003300` the
colours, and `true_color=false` falls back to 256 colours. Without
`fit=true` it draws a 60 by 20 arena below the prompt, as the original
does. The README lists the examples and the source lists every parameter.

## Credits

- Ternimal: [Philipp Emanuel Weidmann](https://github.com/p-e-w/ternimal)
- Asciiverse edition: quits on any key, and fills the window with `fit=true`
- License: GPL-3.0-only

tintin.title: TinTin++
tintin.description: The classic console MUD client, with a scripting language, PCRE triggers, and a mapper
tintin.provenance: TinTin++ grew from Peter Unold's TinTin III (1992); Bill Reis and then Igor van den Hoven continued it, and Igor maintains it today.

upstream.name: Peter Unold, Bill Reis and Igor van den Hoven

tintin.page:
TinTin++ is the console MUD client many players have used for decades:
connect to any MUD, then make it yours with its own scripting language,
triggers and aliases, a mapper that draws the rooms you walk through, and
split screens.

## Getting started

- `#session <name> <host> <port>`: connect, for example `#session bat batmud.bat.org 23`
- `#help`: the built-in manual
- `#end`: quit

## Credits

- TinTin++: Peter Unold, Bill Reis and Igor van den Hoven
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, no code changes
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

tinyfugue.title: TinyFugue
tinyfugue.description: The classic programmable MUD client: triggers, macros, hooks and several worlds at once
tinyfugue.provenance: TinyFugue is Ken Keys' MUD client; 5.0 beta 8 (2007) was its last release.
tinyfugue.page:
TinyFugue, "tf" to its players, has been a MUD client since the early
1990s. It connects to several worlds at once, and its macro language,
triggers and hooks let you shape every line the MUD sends and every
command you type. This edition has the patches Debian has kept it
building with.

## Getting started

- `tinyfugue <host> <port>`: connect straight away
- `/connect <host> <port>`: connect from inside tf
- `/help`: the built-in manual
- `/quit`: quit

## Credits

- TinyFugue: Ken Keys
- Debian patches: Russ Allbery, Chris Lamb
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

tristam-island.title: Tristam Island
tristam-island.description: Stranded on a small Atlantic island, explore it and find out why it is empty
tristam-island.provenance: Hugo Labrande wrote Tristam Island in 2020, in the style of a 1980s Infocom adventure and for the same Z-machine version 3.
tristam-island.page:
You wash up on the south beach of a small island in the Atlantic, a needle in a haystack with no chance of being rescued. A steep forested hill rises to the north and a boulder sits up the beach. An old-school adventure of exploring, mapping and puzzling, written in 2020 for the same Z-machine that ran Infocom's games.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/tristam-island`.

## Credits

- Tristam Island: Hugo Labrande, 2020
- License: Released as open source under CC0 1.0 by the author in 2023
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

trsr.title: Treasure
trsr.description: Two-player minesweeper: take turns digging for treasure, against the computer or a friend
trsr.provenance: abakh wrote Treasure for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
trsr.page:
Minesweeper turned around, for two. Treasure is hidden under the field,
and two sides, Percent (**%**) and Square (**#**), take turns opening
cells. A cell without treasure shows how many of its eight neighbours
hold some, found or not, and a cell with none around opens its
neighbours too. Find treasure and you score it and dig again, a few
times in a row at most. Whoever finds more than half of the treasure
wins; there is always an odd number of it, so there is no draw.

In the game's own words: *Like Mines but you need to find stuff instead
of avoiding them. Try to trick the AI into doing useless stuff.*

At the start it asks who plays each side. Press **Enter** twice to play
Percent against the computer, which plays Square; you go first. Press
**Enter** and then **h** for two players taking turns at one keyboard,
or **c** and then **Enter** to watch the computer play both sides.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: dig the cell
- **Mouse**: click to dig
- **PgUp**, **PgDn**, **<**, **>**: scroll a field bigger than the
  terminal
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit; at the end, **y** plays again and **n** or
  **q** quits

## Field size

Started from a shell, Treasure takes the size and the amount of
treasure, for example `trsr -w 30 -l 20 -m 75`: `-w` is the width,
`-l` the length (height) and `-m` the number of treasures; without `-m`
an eighth of the cells hold one. The default field is 15 by 15, or 20
by 15 on a terminal narrower than 45 columns.

## History

Treasure is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games.

tugow.title: Tug of War
tugow.description: Tug of war by typing: key in the digits on screen faster than the other side pulls
tugow.provenance: abakh wrote Tug of War for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
tugow.page:
Two figures pull on a rope. Under **Type!** is a row of digits: type the
first one and the rope moves a step your way, while the other side keeps
pulling it back at a steady pace. Pull the other side up to the line in
the middle and you go up a level, where they pull faster and every digit
is worth more. If you are dragged to the line yourself, the game is
over and your score goes into the high score table.

The digits make it practice for the number keys or the numpad. Press
**h** during a game to switch to the home row instead: **a** to **l**,
**;** and **'**.

## Controls

- **0** to **9**: type the next digit (in home-row mode, the next key)
- **h**: home-row mode, home-row keys instead of digits
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **q**: end the game; at the end, **y** plays again and **n** or **q** quits

## History

Tug of War is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a
collection of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the
classic BSD games.

typespeed.title: Typespeed
typespeed.description: Type the words before they fly off the screen: Unix commands, code keywords or a dozen languages
typespeed.provenance: Typespeed is by Jani Ollikainen and Jaakko Manelius, later maintained by Tobias Stoeckmann; 0.6.5 (2008) was its last release.

upstream.name: Jani Ollikainen, Jaakko Manelius and Tobias Stoeckmann

typespeed.page:
Words drift across the screen from left to right. Type one and press
Enter before it reaches the edge; let ten get away and the game is over.
The faster you type, the faster they come. Pick a word list first: Unix
and DOS commands, programming keywords, or words in English, Finnish,
French, German, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Spanish or Thai.

## Controls

- **Type** a word and press **Enter**
- **Esc**: end the game
- In menus: the numbers, **Up**, **Down** and **Enter**

Your high scores are kept in `~/.typespeed/score`.

## Credits

- Typespeed: Jani Ollikainen and Jaakko Manelius, with later work by
  Tobias Stoeckmann
- Debian patches: Dafydd Harries, Sudip Mukherjee, Helmut Grohne
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

umoria.title: Umoria
umoria.description: The original Moria: go down through the mines below the town, deeper and deeper, to the Balrog, who waits from level 50 down
umoria.provenance: Robert A. Koeneke wrote Moria at the University of Oklahoma from 1981 to 1986, James E. Wilson made it Umoria for Unix from 1987 to 1994, and Michael R. Cook restored it as Umoria 5.7.

upstream.name: Robert A. Koeneke, James E. Wilson, Michael R. Cook

umoria.page:
The original Moria. Below a small town of six shops lies a mine that
goes down level after level, each one new every time you enter it, and
somewhere past the 49th level waits the Balrog. Roll a character from
eight races and six classes, buy what you can afford in town, and go
down: fight what you meet, find gold, armour, weapons, potions,
scrolls, wands and staves, most of which you will not know until you
try them, and come back up to spend your gold. Death is final.

## Controls

- **1 to 9** (the number keys or the keypad): move, 5 stays put; **.**
  and a direction runs
- Walk into a monster to fight it
- **o** and a direction: open a door, **c** close, **T** tunnel
- **i** inventory, **e** equipment, **w** wear or wield, **t** take off
- **E** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **a** aim a wand, **u** use a
  staff, **f** fire or throw
- **m** cast a spell, **p** pray, **G** learn new spells
- **R** rest, **s** search, **l** look, **C** your character
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up; walk onto a number in town to shop
- **?**: all the commands, **=**: options, among them the roguelike keys
- **Ctrl-X**: save and quit, **Ctrl-K**: quit for good

## Options

- `-r`: roguelike keys (hjkl to move)
- `-n`: start a new game even if one is saved
- `-d`: show the score table

## Saving

**Ctrl-X** saves your character to your data folder, and starting
Umoria again carries on where you left off. If the terminal is closed
mid-game, the game saves itself first.

## History

Robert A. Koeneke wrote Moria at the University of Oklahoma, after
playing Rogue there, and released it in 1983 for VAX/VMS. James E.
Wilson rewrote it in C for Unix as Umoria from 1987, and Umoria 5.x
became the Moria most people played; it was released under the GPL in
2008. Michael R. Cook restored and modernised it as Umoria 5.7. This
edition keeps saves and scores in your own data folder.

## Credits

Robert A. Koeneke (Moria), James E. Wilson (Umoria), David J. Grabiner
and many others (Umoria 5.x), Michael R. Cook (Umoria 5.7). GPL-3.0 or
later.

unnethack.title: UnNetHack
unnethack.description: NetHack with more of everything: more randomness, more levels, more challenges, down to the Amulet of Yendor
unnethack.provenance: Patric Mueller started UnNetHack in 2009 as a fork of NetHack 3.4.3, the DevTeam's game, to be NetHack as it would look had its releases gone on; he and contributors still develop it.
unnethack.page:
NetHack's big variant. You go down through the Dungeons of Doom for the
Amulet of Yendor, as in NetHack, but the dungeon has more in it: Angband
style towns, the Ruins of Moria, a black market, an Advent Calendar
portal, Sheol, an icy branch of Gehennom, the Convict role, and many
smaller changes that make each game less predictable and harder. New
players can press **T** at the start for a tutorial.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift**, run
- **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T**
  take off, **P** put on, **R** remove, **a** apply
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors; **s**: search; **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **#**: extended commands, such as `#pray`
- **?**: help, **;**: what is that symbol, **Ctrl-P**: earlier messages
- **S**: save and quit

## Saving and options

**S** saves the game to your data folder (`~/.local/share/unnethack`),
and starting UnNetHack again carries on from there. Your options go in
`~/.unnethackrc`, or in `unnethackrc` in that folder, as `OPTIONS=` lines;
`OPTIONS=windowtype:curses` switches to the curses interface, and
`OPTIONS=role:Valkyrie,name:Freya` skips the questions at the start.

## History

UnNetHack is Patric Mueller's fork of NetHack 3.4.3, started in January
2009, meant to show "how NetHack would look today if the DevTeam didn't
stop releasing". It gathered patches from the NetHack community and its
own new levels and branches, and it is played on public servers. This
edition is built for Linux and macOS, keeping
everything it writes in your own data folder. The succubus and incubus
seduction scene is left out, with upstream's own build option.

## Credits

- Game: Patric Mueller and the UnNetHack contributors, after NetHack by
  the NetHack DevTeam
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: NetHack General Public License

urogue.title: UltraRogue
urogue.description: Herb Chong's Rogue of 1985 to 1995: ten character classes, a flea market at the start, and unique artifacts deep in the Dungeons of Doom
urogue.provenance: Herb Chong wrote UltraRogue in 1985 and 1986 from Rogue 3.6 and an early Advanced Rogue, gave its source to Nicholas J. Kisseberth in 1992 and worked on it with him to 1995.

upstream.name: Herb Chong (1985 to 1995); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

urogue.page:
Herb Chong's long-grown Rogue. Pick one of ten classes, from fighter,
paladin and ranger to druid, illusionist, assassin and ninja, spend
your gold at Friendly Fiend's Flea Market, and go down. The monsters
come in both cases and many kinds, and unique artifacts lie deep in the
dungeon for the bravest to bring back.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way, **m** and a direction to step without picking up
- **f** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand or
  staff
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring, **A**: use an
  artifact
- **c**: cast a spell or say a prayer, **a**: affect the undead,
  **^**: set a trap, **D**: dip something in a pool
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>`: stairs down
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder (press Return to take the name
offered). To carry on, start it from a shell as `urogue -r`; a saved
game is deleted once it is restored. Characters you choose to keep at
the start are stored there too.

## History

Herb Chong wrote UltraRogue in 1985 and 1986, from Rogue 3.6 and an
early Advanced Rogue. In 1992 he gave the source to Nicholas J.
Kisseberth (Yendor), its first restoration, and the two kept working on
it until 1995; the Roguelike Restoration Project released it as 1.0.7
in 2005. This edition keeps your files in your data folder and fixes
saving so that a saved game can be restored. It is part of the
Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Herb Chong, after Rogue by Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold and
Advanced Rogue by Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka; restoration by Nicholas
J. Kisseberth. BSD licence with clauses on the names UltraRogue and
urogue.

vms-empire.title: VMS Empire
vms-empire.description: One continent-spanning war against the computer, with armies, fleets and planes: the 1970s ancestor of Civilization
vms-empire.provenance: Walter Bright wrote Empire in the early 1970s; Chuck Simmons wrote this C version in 1987, and Eric S. Raymond has maintained it since around 1990.
vms-empire.page:
A full-scale war between two emperors, you and the computer, on a randomly
generated world of continents and oceans. There is only room for one.

You start with a single city and a map you have never seen. Cities build
armies, fighters, patrol boats, destroyers, submarines, troop transports,
carriers, battleships and satellites. Explore, take the unclaimed cities,
ship armies across the sea, and destroy the other side. The computer plays
by exactly the same rules.

The game saves itself every 10 turns and picks up where you left off the
next time you start it.

## Controls

Keys work in upper or lower case. **h** shows help for the mode you are in,
and **Ctrl+L** redraws the screen.

In command mode, between rounds:

- **a**: automove, the normal way to play a round
- **z**: the whole world, zoomed out
- **s**: save the game
- **q**: quit

In move mode, when the cursor sits on one of your pieces:

- **q w e / a d / z x c** or the **arrow keys**: move one square
- **Space**: leave the piece where it is
- **y**: send an army to attack the nearest target by itself
- **g**: explore unknown territory
- **s**: sentry, park a piece until something comes near
- **b**: change what a city builds
- **o**: go back to command mode after this round

## Options

- `-w N`: percentage of the world that is water, 10 to 90 (default 70)
- `-s N`: how smooth the coastlines are (default 5)
- `-g WxH`: world size
- `-t`: wrap the map round at the edges
- `-d N`: how long, in milliseconds, each message stays at the top of the screen (default 2000)
- `-S N`: autosave every N turns (default 10)
- `-f file`: use another save file

## History

Walter Bright wrote Empire in the early 1970s as a student at Caltech. It
spread to DEC's VAX/VMS, which gave it the name VMS Empire; Craig Leres
added terminal support and Ed James converted parts to C with curses. In
1987 Chuck Simmons at Amdahl rewrote it completely in C with a new
computer strategy, pieces and map generator, and Eric S. Raymond has
maintained it since around 1990, adding colour in 1994. Its line leads
to Civilization (1990) and Master of Orion (1993).

This edition adds a small patch that lets it build and save games on
Windows.

## Credits

- Original game: Walter Bright
- C version: Chuck Simmons
- Maintainer: [Eric S. Raymond](http://www.catb.org/~esr/vms-empire/)
- Windows console support: [PDCurses](https://pdcurses.org)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

warp.title: Warp
warp.description: Larry Wall's real-time space war: fly an Enterprise and a Base at once through a wraparound universe where blasts spread and enemies never wait
warp.provenance: Larry Wall wrote Warp from 1983 (version 7.0 is from 1986), before he wrote Perl; NetBSD added it to its games in 2020.
warp.page:
Warp is a space war in real time: the enemies keep moving and shooting
whether you act or not. You command an Enterprise and a Base at the same
time, in a universe that wraps around at every edge, against Klingons,
Romulans, Gorns, Tholians, space amoebas, planet crushers and homing
torpedoes. Things that blow up damage what is near them, and a dense
universe can go up in a chain reaction.

Each wave ends when your Enterprise and Base are both gone or every
enemy is destroyed, and the waves get harder. Besides phasers and photon
torpedoes you have tractor beams and a cloaking device, and the shape of
each universe's star field changes how you have to fight.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: steer the current ship (diagonals on yubn)
- **Shift** with a direction: fire a photon torpedo that way
- **Ctrl** with a direction: fire phasers that way
- **%** or **Delete**: torpedoes in every direction
- **i** or **w**: Enterprise in impulse or warp mode, **p**: switch to
  the Base, **o**: the other vessel
- **c** and **v**: cloak and uncloak
- **s**: stop all torpedoes, **S** or **0**: stop the Enterprise
- **?**: command summary, **^R**: redraw, **q**: quit (it asks), **Q**:
  quit at once

## History

Larry Wall wrote Warp from 1983, years before he wrote Perl, and
version 7.0 came out in 1986. NetBSD added it to its games in November
2020, under the NetBSD Foundation's BSD licence.

The Asciiverse edition builds it for Linux and macOS, fixes three
overflows that crashed a second game in one run, and keeps its saved
games and scoreboards in the player's own data folder. Warp is part of
BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

wolfpack-empire.title: Wolfpack Empire
wolfpack-empire.description: The Internet's long-running multiplayer wargame: build a nation sector by sector against other players on a live server
wolfpack-empire.provenance: Empire is Peter Langston's game; this line of the code comes from Dave Pare (UCSD, 1986) through Chainsaw and Empire 3 to Wolfpack, who have kept it going as Empire 4 since 1996.
wolfpack-empire.page:
Empire is a war game played over the Internet since the 1980s. You run a
country on a shared world: explore the land around your capital, designate
sectors as farms, mines, factories and harbours, grow your population,
research technology, and build ships, planes and armies. Then deal with
your neighbours, who are real people, through trade, alliances,
telegrams and war. The world moves on whether you are logged in or not: updates
happen on a schedule, and a game runs for weeks.

This is the Empire client. It connects straight to Wolfpack Fever, the
game the Wolfpack team keeps running all year: no registration, grab a
country and go.

## Getting started

At the prompts, use one of the countries **1** to **8**, with the same
number as the password. Countries start in sanctuary, safe from attack;
the `break` command ends it, and breaking sanctuary counts as a promise to
play the game. Using more than one country is not allowed.

To look around first, log in as country `visitor` with any password and
read the message of the day (`motd`) and the newspaper (`newspaper`).

## Commands

Type commands at the `Command :` prompt. A few to start with:

- `nation`: your country at a glance
- `map #`: the map around you
- `census *`: your sectors
- `explore c 0,0 5 gh`: move 5 civilians from 0,0 west and claim land
  (directions `y u g j b n`, `h` to stop)
- `designate 2,0 m`: make a sector a mine
- `read`: your telegrams; `wire` for announcements, `newspaper` for the news
- `declare` and `relations`: alliances and war
- `info`: the built-in manual, and `info <command>` for any command
- `quit`: log out; your country stays in the game

## Options

- `empire COUNTRY PASSWORD`: log in without the prompts
- `-s host:port`: play on another Empire server
- `-u`: UTF-8 output
- `-2 file`: keep a log of the session

## History

Empire goes back to Peter Langston's game of the late 1970s and early
1980s. Dave Pare's reimplementation at UCSD in 1986 started the open line
of code, carried on through BSD Empire, KSU, Chainsaw and Empire 3 to
Wolfpack, who have developed it as Empire 4 since 1996. Wolfpack still hosts games and the code is still
developed.

This edition is the client, unchanged except that it connects to
Wolfpack Fever by default.

## Credits

- Empire: Peter Langston, Dave Pare, Jeff Bailey, Thomas Ruschak, Ken
  Stevens, Steve McClure, Markus Armbruster and [Wolfpack](http://www.wolfpackempire.com/)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

worm.title: Worm
worm.description: Steer a growing worm to the numbers and see how long it can get before it runs into a wall or itself
worm.provenance: Michael Toy wrote Worm at UC Santa Cruz around 1980, and it shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov added colour and some grass for looks in 2016 for his bsd-games.
worm.page:
The classic growing worm. Your worm is a line of `o`s with an `@` for a
head, and it never stops moving. Somewhere on the field is a digit: eat
it and the worm grows by that many segments, and a new digit appears.
The game ends when the worm runs into the wall or into itself.

The longer the worm, the harder it is to find a way through, and every
digit you eat adds the worm's growth to your score. Fill one eighth of
the screen with worm and you have won. The blue grass is only there to
look at; you can crawl straight over it.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: turn
- **q**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `worm 20` starts with a worm 20 segments long
instead of 7.

## History

Michael Toy wrote Worm at UC Santa Cruz around 1980, and it shipped with
BSD Unix among Berkeley's games for the video terminals of the day. Mike
Sharov's bsd-games, the modern Linux port, draws it in colour and added
the grass in 2016.

worms.title: Worms
worms.description: Coloured worms wander the screen, turning at random and bouncing off the edges: the BSD screen piece from 1980
worms.provenance: Eric P. Scott wrote worms at Caltech High Energy Physics in October 1980, a Unix version of the DEC-2136 program of the same name, and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on.
worms.page:
Eight worms crawl across the screen, each in its own colour and
character, with a head that looks different from its body. They turn at
random, slide along the edges and cross each other's paths, and whatever
they leave behind them is wiped clean as they go.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `worms` takes more: `-n` sets the number of worms,
`-l 10` or `-l 5-40` their length, `-r` random lengths, `-t` a trail of
dots, `-f` a field of WORM letters for them to eat, `-d` the pause between
moves in milliseconds, and `-C` and `-H` colour and heads (Asciiverse
starts it with `-C -H -n 8`).

## History

Eric P. Scott wrote worms at Caltech High Energy Physics in October
1980, a Unix version of the DEC-2136 program of the same name, and it
has shipped with BSD Unix ever since. This edition quits on any key. It
is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

- worms: Eric P. Scott, from [NetBSD's source tree](https://github.com/NetBSD/src/tree/trunk/games/worms)
- License: BSD-3-Clause, copyright The Regents of the University of California

wump.title: Hunt the Wumpus
wump.description: Track the Wumpus through a cave of twenty rooms by smell, dodging bottomless pits and giant bats, and shoot it with a crooked arrow
wump.provenance: Hunt the Wumpus was first presented in People's Computer Company in 1973; Dave Taylor of Intuitive Systems wrote this version for BSD Unix in 1989.

upstream.name: Dave Taylor, Intuitive Systems (1989), after Hunt the Wumpus (1973)

wump.page:
One of the oldest computer games there is. You are in a cave of twenty
rooms, each joined to three others by tunnels, and somewhere in it lives
the Wumpus. You cannot see it, but you can smell it up to two rooms
away. You can also feel the draft from a bottomless pit next door and
hear the bats that, disturbed, will carry you off to another part of the
cave.

Each turn you either move to a neighbouring room or shoot one of your
five crooked arrows, giving it a path of up to six rooms to fly
through. Hit the Wumpus and you win. Miss, and it may wake up and move;
give the arrow an impossible path and it flies off at random, maybe
straight back into you. Some tunnels only go one way.

## Controls

The game is typed: enter a command and press **Enter**.

- **m** and a room number, such as `m6`: move to that room
- **s** and a list of rooms, such as `s8 4`: shoot an arrow along that path
- **?**: the instructions
- **q**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, wump builds other caves: `-r` sets the number of
rooms (20), `-t` the tunnels from each room (3), `-p` the pits (3), `-b`
the bat rooms (3) and `-a` the arrows (5), as in `wump -r 30 -a 3`.

## History

Hunt the Wumpus was first presented in the pages of People's Computer
Company in 1973. This version was written for BSD Unix by Dave Taylor of
Intuitive Systems in 1989, and Mike Sharov's bsd-games, the modern Linux
port, prints its instructions directly and highlights the important
words in bold.

xrogue.title: XRogue
xrogue.description: Robert Pietkivitch's Rogue of 1989 to 1992, grown from Advanced Rogue 7.7: nine classes, over 200 monsters, and a shop on level 0
xrogue.provenance: Robert Pietkivitch wrote XRogue for the AT&T UNIX PC between 1989 and 1992 from Advanced Rogue 7.7, and restored it with Nicholas J. Kisseberth from 1996.

upstream.name: Robert Pietkivitch (1989 to 1992); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

xrogue.page:
The last of the Bell Labs Rogue line. You share out your attribute
points, choose one of nine classes (fighter, ranger, paladin, magician,
cleric, thief, assassin, druid or monk) and begin on level 0 in Friendly
Fiend's Equipage, a shop full of arms, armour and magic, before taking
its stairs down. More than 200 monsters live below, many of them
intelligent, and the game sets you a quest for one unique item.

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **z**: zap a wand or staff
- **i**: inventory, **P**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off
- **C**: cast a spell, **p**: pray, **c**: chant, **a**: affect the
  undead, **D**: dip something in a pool
- In the shop: **$** price, **#** buy, **%** sell
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit (type yes)

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `xrogue -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Robert Pietkivitch wrote XRogue between 1989 and 1992 for the AT&T UNIX
PC, building on Advanced Rogue 7.7. He sent the source to Nicholas J.
Kisseberth (Yendor) in 1996 and worked with him to bring it back; he
died in 2002, before sending the enhancements he had made in 2000.
Kisseberth's Roguelike Restoration Project released 8.0.1 to 8.0.3, and
rogueforge carries it on. This edition keeps your files in your data
folder and fixes saved games that
would not restore and a score file that crashed on 64-bit machines. It
is part of the Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Robert Pietkivitch, after Advanced Rogue by Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka
and Rogue by Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by
Nicholas J. Kisseberth. BSD licence.

zork1.title: Zork I: The Great Underground Empire
zork1.description: Explore the Great Underground Empire for its treasures, starting by a white house
zork1.provenance: Infocom released Zork I in 1980; Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels and Tim Anderson wrote it.

developer.name: Infocom (Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels, Tim Anderson)

zork1.page:
You stand west of a white house, with a mailbox and a boarded front door. Somewhere below lies the Great Underground Empire, and nineteen treasures for whoever is brave, clever and careful enough to bring them back. Watch out for the thief, and keep your lamp lit: it is pitch dark, and you are likely to be eaten by a grue.

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take lamp**, **open mailbox**, **put sword in case**
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/zork1`.

## Credits

- Zork I: Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels and Tim Anderson; Infocom, 1980
- Released under the MIT license by Microsoft, with Xbox and Activision, in 2025
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
