ztrack.title: Ztrack
ztrack.description: Pseudo-3D driving down an endless three-lane road at 150 mph, dodging traffic you can only half see
ztrack.provenance: Russell Marks wrote Ztrack in C on curses (1995, version 1.0 in 1996).
ztrack.page:
Get as far as you can down an endless three-lane road full of stupid but
dangerous traffic. You score more the faster you go, and the top speed is
150 mph. Run into the back of a car, or swerve into a lane that is
occupied, and you lose one of your three cars.

You see the road from behind the wheel, over your bonnet. Cars level with
you are out of sight, but your wing mirrors light up with a blob when a lane
beside you is taken, so check them before you change lanes.

You don't hold a pedal: you set a mode. Accel keeps speeding up, decel keeps
slowing down, and cruise holds your speed exactly.

## Controls

- **Up** or **q**: accel mode
- **Down** or **a**: decel mode
- **Space** or **Tab**: cruise at the current speed
- **Left** or **o**: move left a lane
- **Right** or **p**: move right a lane
- **Esc** or **X**: end the game

On the title screen, **Space** starts a game and **Esc** or **q** quits.
The high score lasts until you quit.

## History

Russell Marks wrote Ztrack 1.0 in October 1995, loosely after a Casio
LCD driving game he remembered as "Turbo Drive", and put it in the public
domain; it was uploaded to sunsite.unc.edu (now ibiblio) in 1996. FreeBSD still
carries it in its ports collection.

This edition reads the keyboard through curses rather than straight from
the terminal device. That makes the cursor keys steer (in the original they
ended the game) and lets the game run in the Windows console. It also fixes
an out-of-bounds read when drawing the title logo. The gameplay is
unchanged.

## Credits

- Game: Russell Marks
- Windows console support: [PDCurses](https://pdcurses.org)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: public domain

prince-of-braille.title: Prince of Braille
prince-of-braille.description: Port of the 1989 Apple II Prince of Persia from Mechner's source, prince in Braille
prince-of-braille.provenance: Asciiverse ported Jordan Mechner's Prince of Persia (Apple II, 1989), written from the source code Mechner released.
prince-of-braille.page:
A faithful port of Jordan Mechner's 1989 Apple II Prince of Persia, built from the source code he released, with the prince drawn in Braille.

Run, climb, leap and hang across the palace, and dodge spikes, loose floors and closing gates.

## Status

The first playable cut: all 14 original levels, the kid's movement and the traps. Guards are not in yet.

tetrix.title: Tetrix
tetrix.description: Six fields. Nine dirty tricks. One survivor! The late-90s LAN-party block buster legend is back: clear lines, grab specials, and Quake, Bomb and Switch your friends into oblivion!
tetrix.provenance: Asciiverse made Tetrix in Rust in 2026, after St0rmCat's TetriNET, the late-90s multiplayer falling-block game with attack blocks. Its rules follow TetriNET 1.13, and the rotation table and core rules are ported from Andrew Church's tetrinet 0.11.
tetrix.page:
**SIX FIELDS. NINE DIRTY TRICKS. ONE SURVIVOR.**

Remember the late 90s? Six friends, six fields, blocks falling faster and faster, and somebody across the room laughing a little too hard. That was TetriNET, and it's back in your terminal!

Clear lines and your field coughs up specials: lettered blocks that drop straight into your arsenal. Then pick a victim. Hit them with a Blockquake and watch every row in their field lurch sideways! Set off a Block Bomb and blow their O pieces to bits! Shove junk lines up from below until they're gasping at the ceiling! And when your own field is about to bury you? Switch Fields, and hand them the mess with a smile.

Clear two, three or four lines at once and everyone else eats one, two or four junk lines. Classic rules, classic cruelty.

- **Up to six players in one brawl!** Host a game and it simply appears on everyone's menu across the network. No addresses to type, no internet needed.
- **Nine specials**, from the sneaky Add Line to the life-saving Nuke Field.
- **Nobody else awake?** Ada, Blitz, Cobol, Dvorak and Emacs are always up for a game, from easy all the way up to brutal.
- **Bigger terminal, bigger boards.**

It's the one you play with five friends at a LAN party until somebody spills a drink. **WHO'S STILL STANDING?**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: move
- **Up** or **x**: rotate clockwise; **z**: counter-clockwise
- **Down**: soft drop; **Space**: hard drop
- **1** to **6**: fire your front special at that player (your own number for the ones meant for yourself)
- **d**: discard the front special
- **s**: the landing shadow on or off
- **?**: the keys, and what every special does

Tetrix needs a terminal of at least 92 columns by 28 rows.

## The specials

- **A** Add Line: a junk line pushed up from the bottom
- **C** Clear Line: removes your bottom row (use on yourself)
- **N** Nuke Field: empties your field (use on yourself)
- **R** Random Clear: knocks out ten random cells
- **S** Switch Fields: swap fields with the target
- **B** Clear Specials: the target's specials turn into plain blocks
- **G** Gravity: every column collapses, filling the holes (use on yourself)
- **Q** Blockquake: every row shifts sideways
- **O** Block Bomb: every O block in the target's field explodes

## Options

- `--solo`, `--host`, `--join`: straight to a way of playing
- `--bots N`, `--skill N`: how many bots, and how good
- `--name`, `--level N`, `--seed N`
- `--classic-delay`, `--slide`, `--no-classic`, `--noshadow`: rule and display tweaks; `tetrix --help` explains each

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Rules after St0rmCat's TetriNET 1.13
- Piece rotation and core rules ported from Andrew Church's tetrinet 0.11
- Networking: iroh

sleighride.title: Sleighride
sleighride.description: Second day of Christmas, Santa's asleep and the elves have found the keys! Grab a sleigh, a reindeer or a broomstick and race like mad, before Santa fires up the snowplough and comes for the ringleader!
sleighride.provenance: Asciiverse made Sleighride in Rust in 2026, out of the Christmas folklore of Julbocken, La Befana, the Yule Cat, the Yule Lads, Ded Moroz and Snegurochka.
sleighride.page:
**SECOND DAY OF CHRISTMAS. SANTA'S ASLEEP. THE ELVES HAVE FOUND THE KEYS.**

Every present is delivered. Santa is snoring in his armchair by the workshop fire. And every last one of his helpers has grabbed anything with runners and gone for a joyride!

Bob takes the big sleigh. Holly and Juniper saddle up the reindeer. Sprocket fires up the workshop snowmobile, Pip grabs a toboggan, Nutmeg straps on racing skis, Tomte rides Julbocken, the straw Yule goat, and Befana? Befana takes her broomstick. Pick your racer and floor it!

But come lap two... SANTA'S AWAKE! He's in the one thing they left behind: the snowplough. He's got a list, he's checking it twice, and whoever is out in front is clearly the ringleader. Take the lead and he's coming for YOU, a mitten the size of a sack swinging in for a good clip round the ear. YOU'RE ON THE NAUGHTY LIST!

Drift through the bends until your sparks burn frost blue, then gold, then aurora, and let them rip for a boost! Fly off the kickers and throw a barrel roll! Smash open present boxes for snowballs, homing tinsel and peppermint boosts, or hold out a sprig of mistletoe on a stick: any rival who gets too close gets kissed and stops dead in a cloud of hearts!

- **Ten courses!** A frozen lake, a lake of eggnog flecked with nutmeg, black ice full of holes (SPLASH!), a candy cane forest, a gingerbread village with a cottage right in the road (jump it!), Santa's own workshop with its conveyor belts, a glacier split by crevasses, a birch wood where Ded Moroz lays frost on the road, the clifftops of a fjord, and a Christmas night market where the crowd throws presents.
- **Hazards straight out of Christmas folklore:** the Icelandic Yule Cat, the prankster Yule Lads, snow tornadoes, blizzards, and a line of penguins waddling across the road with a polar bear lumbering after them, never quite fast enough. Plough into a penguin and it belly-slides away across the snow. Penguins like that.
- **Real hills and jumps,** carved in voxels, right in your terminal.
- **Up to eight players** on the local network, on keyboard or gamepad.

Ten courses, eight racers, one very cross Santa. **CAN YOU WIN WITHOUT GETTING CAUGHT?**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **A** and **D**): steer
- **Up** or **W**: gas; **Down** or **S**: brake and reverse
- **Space** or **Shift**, held while steering: drift
- **X**, **E** or **Ctrl**: use your item; with brake held, drop a present behind you as a trap
- **P**: pause, **R**: restart, **Esc**: back
- **F1** or **H**: help, with the drifting, items, Santa and the hazards
- **F8**: sound on or off, **M**: music on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad to steer, A gas, B brake, right shoulder drift, X, Y or left shoulder item

On terminals without the kitty keyboard protocol, Up latches the gas on, Down turns it off, and Space toggles a drift.

## Options

- `--race`: straight into a race
- `--course N`: pick the course, 1 to 10
- `--as NAME`: race as Bob, Holly, Sprocket, Pip, Juniper, Nutmeg, Tomte or Befana
- `--host`, `--join`, `--name NAME`: races on the local network
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Folklore: Julbocken, La Befana, the Yule Cat, the Yule Lads, Ded Moroz and Snegurochka, from Christmas traditions across Europe
- Networking: iroh

panzer.title: Panzer
panzer.description: It is time to make a stand in toyland! Toy tanks - real ricochets! Bank your shells off the walls, plant your mines, and outfox nine enemy tanks with nine nasty tricks, all the way to the Last Stand!
panzer.provenance: Asciiverse made Panzer in Rust in 2026, after Wii Play's Tanks (Nintendo, 2006).
panzer.page:
**TOY TANKS. REAL RICOCHETS.**

Twenty missions. One little tank. And a whole toy box of enemy tanks that want you scorched off the map!

Every shell you fire bounces off the walls, and so does every shell they fire. Bank a shot round a corner! Shoot their shells clean out of the air! Drop a mine behind a crate and back away very, very slowly. You get five shells and two mines at a time, and one hit is all it takes. For them, and for you.

Meet the opposition:

- **Tinpot** can't move. It just sweeps its turret, waiting for the bounce.
- **Plodder** wanders about. Thump. Thump. Thump.
- **Hornet** hangs back and fires rockets twice as fast as your shells.
- **Skitter** dashes about in a nervous panic, sowing mines as it goes.
- **Rascal** comes straight for you, three shells at a time.
- **Sniper** never moves, and never misses the angle you forgot.
- **Viper** banks its shots, dodges yours and lays the odd mine.
- **Ghost** is invisible. Its tread marks are not. And it hums.
- And **Onyx**? The big black one. It will not stop coming.

Listen closely! Every enemy has its own engine voice, and the battle march picks up a new instrument for every kind of enemy on the field: a woodblock for the Tinpot, a tuba for the Plodder, a kazoo for the Hornet, timpani for the Onyx. Hear a theremin but see nobody? That's a Ghost. Lose a tank and you get a sad trombone.

- **Twenty missions,** from First Shot to Last Stand, with a spare tank every five.
- **Two-player co-op** on the local network, one machine each. The spare tanks are shared, and friendly fire is very much on.
- **Keyboard and mouse, or a twin-stick gamepad.**

**GOOD LUCK, COMMANDER.**

## Controls

- **W A S D** or the **arrow keys**: drive
- **Mouse**: aim (or **I J K L** for eight ways, **Q** and **E** to turn slowly)
- **Left click** or **Space**: fire (five shells at most)
- **Right click** or **F**: drop a mine (two at most)
- **P** or **Esc**: pause, **H**: help
- **M**: music on or off, **F8**: all sound on or off
- **Gamepad**: left stick drives, right stick aims, right trigger fires, left trigger or A drops a mine

Panzer needs a truecolour terminal. 160x50 is playable, 200x60 or more is comfortable: the arena scales to fit.

## Options

- `--mission N`: straight into mission N
- `--host`, `--join`: co-op on the local network
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- After Wii Play Tanks (Nintendo, 2006), with original names, maps, art and music
- Music and sound synthesised in the game
- Networking: iroh

rusty-pinball.title: Rusty Pinball
rusty-pinball.description: Physics pinball with nine tables in Braille vector graphics, after Vector Pinball
rusty-pinball.provenance: Asciiverse ported Brian Nenninger's Vector Pinball for Android, written from its source code.

sigpipe.title: SIGPIPE
sigpipe.description: The data is already on its way! Lay pipe as fast as your fingers allow: loop it, split it, buffer it, and pray it never hits an open end. cat: write error: Broken pipe!
sigpipe.provenance: Asciiverse made SIGPIPE in Rust in 2026, after the pipe-laying puzzle games of the late 1980s.
sigpipe.page:
**THE DATA IS COMING. LAY PIPE. FAST.**

A process has started. Somewhere on the board, `cat` is about to start writing, and its data has nowhere to go. Yet.

You have seconds. Grab pieces from the queue and slam them down across the grid: straights, corners, crossovers, tees. Then the countdown hits zero, the modem chirps, and the green data starts creeping down your pipe, one segment at a time, each one a note higher than the last...

Keep laying. Stay ahead of it. Because the moment it reaches an open end, it's all over:

`cat: write error: Broken pipe`
`[exit 141]`

- **Loop it!** Send the stream back through a crossover for +500. Five loops in one level? That's a 5000 bonus.
- **Split it!** A tee sends the data down both arms at once, and suddenly you're racing two fronts.
- **Buffers** soak up the flow, **valves** let data through one way only, and the `nul` sink swallows whatever you feed it.
- **Press F when you're feeling brave:** fast flow, double points.
- **Endless levels,** each one longer, faster and more cramped than the last.
- **Versus on the local network:** race a rival on an identical board, and every three segments you pipe locks a cell on theirs.

Pause and you're `[1]+ Stopped`. Pass and it's `[exit 0]`. Fail and... well, you know the signal. **DON'T BREAK THE PIPE.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **W A S D** or **H J K L**: move the cursor
- **Enter** or **Space**: lay the next piece (or replace one, at a small cost)
- **Mouse**: point and click to lay
- **F**: fast flow (during the countdown, starts the data at once)
- **P**: pause, **M**: sound on or off, **Esc**: back, **Q**: quit
- On the title: **V** hosts a versus match, **C** joins one
- **Gamepad**: d-pad moves, bottom button lays, left or top button or right trigger for fast flow, Start pauses

SIGPIPE fits an 80x24 terminal. At 144 columns or wider, your rival's board shows live beside yours in versus.

## Options

- `--level N`: start at level N
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Sound synthesised in the game
- Networking: iroh

tty-rex.title: tty-rex
tty-rex.description: Chrome's offline T-Rex runner, recreated faithfully from Chromium's source
tty-rex.provenance: Asciiverse recreated Chrome's offline T-Rex runner, written from Chromium's own source: the same rules, timings, sprites and sounds.

uxo.title: uXo
uxo.description: BOOM! Drop bombs, chain the blasts and blow your way through the Orchard, or grab three friends and blast each other sky-high in Battle! Kick them, punch them, throw them, and watch out for the skull!
uxo.provenance: Asciiverse made uXo in Rust in 2026, a love letter to the 90s bomb-arena games.
uxo.page:
**DROP IT. RUN. BOOM!**

Bombs. Lots and lots of bombs. Drop one, run, and BOOM: the blast rips out in a cross and flattens everything in its path. Line them up right and one sets off the next, and the next, and the next... a chain reaction that tears the whole arena apart. Caught in your own blast? That one's on you.

Kick bombs down the lanes. Punch them over the hedges. Pick them up and hurl them. Lay a whole row in one go, or set them off by remote at exactly the wrong moment for somebody else.

Out in the Orchard, duds lie everywhere, bombs that never went off, every one of them waiting for a spark. Set them all off, blast the baddies that have moved in, and fight your way to the Bramblehog, a great ball of brambles that rolls at anything that moves.

Beat a Hopper or a Ram and it might leave an egg behind. Hatch it, climb on, and it's yours: the Hopper hops you clean over blocks, the Ram charges. And when a blast catches you, your mount takes the hit instead.

- **Adventure, alone or with a friend:** nine stages through the Orchard, from Windfall Lane through the Hedge Maze, where the hedgehogs pretend to be hedges, past the Cider Press and the Crow Tree, all the way to the Bramblehog.
- **Battle for up to four:** six arenas, from the Ice Rink, where you slide until something stops you, to the Warp Garden and the Catacombs. Blown up? Ride the edge and lob bombs back in for revenge. Let the clock run down and the walls start closing in.
- **Eighteen power-ups, and the dreaded skull.** Catch a disease and you might drop bombs nonstop, run backwards, never stop walking, or turn invisible. Bump into a rival and it's theirs instead.
- **Every gamepad is a player,** and two can share the keyboard.

Every bomb on the grid is unexploded ordnance. For now. **IF YOU SEE ME RUNNING, TRY TO KEEP UP!**

## Controls

- **Move**: stick, d-pad, **W A S D** or the **arrow keys**
- **Bomb**: A or X on a pad, **Space** (W A S D player) or **Enter** (arrows player); press again standing on your bomb with the line bomb to lay a row
- **Ride** (your mount's hop or charge): Y, **E** or **.**
- **Action**: B, **F** or **/**: throw what you carry, else punch the bomb ahead, else pick up the bomb underfoot, else set off your oldest remote bomb
- **Start** or **P**: pause, **+** and **-**: zoom (**0**: automatic), **Esc** or Select: back to the title

- Game: Asciiverse
- A love letter to the 90s bomb-arena games

brickspire.title: Brickspire
brickspire.description: The stars are going out! The Mason has walled up the Lamplighter at the top of his tower. Five towers, fifty floors, one ball: smash your way up before the last star fades!
brickspire.provenance: Asciiverse made Brickspire in Rust in 2026: a brick breaker after the great arcade and 16-bit ones, played up a turning tower in the manner of the late-80s tower climbers.
brickspire.page:
**THE STARS ARE GOING OUT.**

Every night the Lamplighter climbs into the sky and lights the stars. But not any more. The Mason has walled the Lamplighter up at the very top of his tower, the Brickspire, and now, one by one, the stars are going dark.

Five towers stand between you and the top. Fifty floors. One ball. Smash your way up!

Clear a floor and the whole tower turns, swinging the next one round to face you. Up through the Old Keep, where a Gargoyle spits fire from its balcony and a Storm Cloud rumbles over the roof. Up through the Ivy Tower, where vines slide along their rows and a giant crow guards its twig nest. On through the Bell Tower, where clockwork bricks tick back into place and the Great Bell sends shock rings rolling across the roof. Then the Sea Tower, lashed by storms, with a serpent rising beside the balcony and the Weathercock whirling on top. And every tower you climb, there are fewer stars left in the sky...

Here's the twist: your paddle changes its path as you climb! On the floors it runs straight. On the balconies it swings along an arc. On the roofs it circles the whole arena, and every angle you thought you knew goes out of the window.

Catch the capsules as they fall: a Plank for a longer paddle, Mortar to catch the ball, Chisels to fire, an Hourglass to slow things down, a Flock of three balls, a Spare life, or a Stair straight up to the next floor.

- **Five towers, fifty floors, ten bosses,** each tower with its own look and its own trick brick.
- **Two looks:** chunky pixel art, or pipe graphics drawn in box lines. Press G to switch.
- **Keyboard, mouse or gamepad.**

At the top, the Mason is still laying bricks, as fast as you can break them. Break through, free the Lamplighter, and light up the sky again. **HURRY, BEFORE THE LAST STAR FADES!**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **A** and **D**, **H** and **L**), or the **mouse**: move the paddle
- **Space**, **Enter** or **Up**: launch the ball, fire Chisels, let go of a caught ball
- **P**: pause, **R**: restart, **Q** or **Esc**: quit
- **G**: pixel art or pipe graphics, **M**: sound on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad moves (the stick aims round the roof), bottom or right button or right trigger fires, Start pauses

## Options

- `--floor N`: start on floor N (1 to 50)
- `--glyphs`: start in pipe graphics
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Sound synthesised in the game

kaiku.title: Kaiku: Echoes Home
kaiku.description: A savage blast hurls you deep into enemy territory, where no human has ever flown! Fight through two hostile fleets, decode the lost voices of Earth, and find the one gate that leads home. Can you make it back alive?!
kaiku.provenance: Asciiverse made Kaiku in Rust in 2026. The echoes are NASA mission audio and John F. Kennedy's speeches; Gates of Zendocon (Epyx, 1989), ZType and Typespeed inspired it.
kaiku.page:
**THE WAR IS RAGING. AND YOU'RE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF IT.**

An intergalactic war burns across the stars, and you're right in the thick of it. Then, out of nowhere, a savage blast rips through your ship and hurls you off course, far beyond the front line, deep into enemy territory where no human has ever been!

No charts. No backup. No way back. Just the Amber and Jade fleets closing in from every side, and a receiver crackling in the dark...

*...the eagle has landed... houston, we've had a problem... godspeed, john glenn...*

Earth's old transmissions, bouncing through space for decades! Broken, garbled, half lost in the static, and they're your only map home. The clearer the echo, the nearer home!

Interceptors flash out of nowhere! Lancers charge down their deadly lines! Jammers scramble the very voices you need to hear! Every sector is a gauntlet, and at the end of every one wait three gates. Only one leads closer to Earth.

- **Fight with your guns, decode with your fingers!** Type each echo clear, letter by letter, with enemy fire all around you.
- **Choose your gate!** Pick wrong and you're thrown off the path. Pick right and Earth gets closer.
- **Snatch power-ups by typing their words:** spread shot, rapid fire, shields, smart bombs, an escort drone, even slow time!
- **The real words of Apollo, Mercury, Gemini and President Kennedy**, waiting to be pulled out of the static.
- **Two players, one ship!** Plug in a gamepad: one flies, one decodes.

You're alone, outgunned and light-years from home. **CAN YOU MAKE IT BACK?!**

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **Ctrl+h/j/k/l**: fly
- **Space** (hold): fire
- **a-z**: lock onto an echo or a power-up's word, and decode it
- **Backspace**: drop the lock (progress is kept)
- **Tab**: dash, a burst of speed you can't be hit in
- **Enter**: smart bomb; on the map, fly on
- **Esc**: pause; **F1**: the controls; **F8**: sound and music on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad to fly, bottom face button to fire, right face button to bomb, left face button to dash

Terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty) give exact key presses and releases.

## Options

- `--skip-intro`: straight into sector 1
- `--sector N`: start in a later sector
- `--demo`: the game plays itself; any key quits
- `--credits`: the credits on their own
- `--mute`, `--no-music`: no sound, or effects only

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Echoes: NASA mission audio (Mercury, Gemini, Apollo) and John F. Kennedy's speeches
- Inspired by Gates of Zendocon (Epyx, 1989), ZType and Typespeed
- Sound and music synthesised in the game

ceres.title: Ceres
ceres.description: Ceres Mountain: three thousand metres of ice, spikes and wind. Jump, dash and wall-kick your way to the summit, and try not to read the memorial on the way up!
ceres.provenance: Asciiverse restored Celeste Classic (Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry, PICO-8, 2015), from Noel Berry's C# port and checked against the original.
ceres.page:
**3000 METRES. ONE GIRL. ONE DASH.**

At the foot of Ceres Mountain stands a stone. *This memorial to those perished on the climb*, it says. Ceres reads it, ties her boots a little tighter, and starts up anyway.

Thirty-one screens of ice, spikes and howling wind stand between her and the summit, a hundred metres at a time. Jump! Dash through the air in any of eight directions! Cling to the rock and kick off again! When her hair turns red, the dash is spent: land, catch your breath, and go again.

Bounce off springs. Snatch a balloon for a fresh dash in midair. Race across snow that crumbles under your feet, and ride the moving platforms over the spikes. Hunt down the cherries hidden off the beaten path, though some of them flap away the moment you dash. Find the key, open the chest. And somewhere up there, past the Old Site, a golden sun-seed is waiting to give you a second dash...

You will fall. A lot. Every fall puts you straight back at the start of the screen to try again, and when you plant the flag at the summit, the mountain tells you exactly how many times.

- **Super-tight platforming, true to the frame:** 31 levels from 100 m to the summit, and every jump, dash and wall-kick plays exactly as in the original PICO-8 classic, checked frame by frame against it.
- **All-new art and an all-new soundtrack.**
- **Keyboard or gamepad,** on a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others).

The summit is waiting. **HOW MANY TIMES WILL YOU FALL?**

## The original

In 2015, Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry made a hardcore little platformer for the PICO-8 fantasy console in just four days. They filled the cart almost to the last byte: 8186 of 8192 code tokens, the entire sprite sheet, the entire map and 63 of 64 sounds. That game was Celeste Classic, and it grew into the acclaimed Celeste (2018). Ceres restores it for the terminal, their code and their levels, with new art and new music.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **W A S D**: move
- **Z**, **C**, **N** or **Space**: jump
- **X**, **V** or **M**: dash, in any of eight directions
- **Esc** or **P**: menu, **R**: restart, **Q**: quit
- **K**: screen shake on or off, **A**: square pixels or sharp ones, **F8**: sound on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad moves, bottom or top button jumps, the other face buttons or the triggers dash, Start opens the menu

## Options

- `--level N`: start at level N (1 to 31; 31 is the summit)
- `--no-shake`: no screen shake
- `--sharp`: exact 1:1 pixels
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Original game: Celeste Classic by Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry (PICO-8, 2015)
- Code and levels: from Noel Berry's C# port, MIT licence
- Restoration, art and music: Asciiverse

marble-recovery.title: Marble Recovery
marble-recovery.description: They say you've lost your marbles. They're right: twelve of them, rolled off into places that should not exist. Roll, tilt and tumble through strange worlds to bring every one of them home!
marble-recovery.provenance: Asciiverse made Marble Recovery in Rust in 2026, after Marble Madness (Mark Cerny, Atari, 1984), with twelve levels of its own.
marble-recovery.page:
**THEY SAY YOU'VE LOST YOUR MARBLES.**

They're right. Twelve of them, rolled off into places that should not exist. Time to go and get them back, one at a time.

No jump button. No fire button. Just a marble, gravity and your nerve. Ease it down the slopes, coax it along the ledges and keep it rolling, because one hard landing and it shatters.

The first worlds are almost reasonable: grey checkered terraces and blue cliffs, and a little slime that doesn't chase you, it just waits for you to stop. Then come the Gulpers, who mean no harm; they simply can't tell a marble from a snack. A tide that keeps its own time. Iron bully marbles, heavy, proud and not very bright, who come straight at you without looking where they're going.

And then the madness sets in. Ice where nothing holds you back. Floors with opinions, rising and falling beneath you. Springs that throw you somewhere higher. A world where falling takes its time. Physics that shouldn't work, does!

- **Twelve hand-built levels in three acts:** Losing It, The Madness, and Recovery.
- **Race your own ghost:** your best run on every level rolls right beside you.
- **Grab a gamepad** and the stick feels like an arcade trackball. Keyboard and mouse work too.

Twelve marbles, every one of them out there somewhere. **GO AND GET THEM BACK!**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **W A S D** or **H J K L**: roll
- **Mouse**: hold a button and push toward the pointer, like a trackball
- **Gamepad**: the stick rolls
- **Enter** or **Space**: go on, **R**: restart the level, **Esc**: back, **Q**: quit
- **N** and **P**: next or previous level, **+** and **-**: zoom

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- After Marble Madness (Mark Cerny, Atari, 1984); every level here is a new design

moraen.title: Moraen
moraen.description: The ice is gone, and the dwarves' treasure lies buried in the rubble it left behind. Dig in, gather the gems and bring the clan's treasure home, before the stone trolls awake!
moraen.provenance: Asciiverse made Moraen in Rust in 2026, a love letter to the 1984 cave-digging classic.
moraen.page:
**THE ICE IS GONE. THE TROLLS ARE STIRRING.**

When the great ice came down from the north, the dwarves sealed their treasure halls and fled. For ten thousand years the glacier lay over the mountain, and the stone trolls who guard its depths froze where they stood.

Now the ice has gone. All that's left is the moraine: rock, rubble, and somewhere underneath, the gems of the old halls. You're the youngest of the clan, sent back to bring the treasure home. And deep in the mountain, the trolls are starting to thaw...

Dig through the rubble and gather the gems. Collect enough and the old hall doors swing open. Mind the boulders: the moraine is still settling, and one careless dig brings a hillside down on your head. Drop a stone on a firefly and it bursts into flames; crush a butterfly and it scatters into gems. The old dwarf rune-stone still works after ten thousand years, turning every boulder that falls through it into treasure. And something green is creeping through the halls, filling every gap: trap it and it turns to gems, let it grow and it turns to stone.

But watch the boulders closely. Some of them blink.

A sleeping stone troll looks like any other rock, until you get close and it starts to blink. Come any closer, or let the thaw reach it, and it wakes: too heavy to climb, it stomps along the ground hurling stones at you, down from above or straight across the cave. Its touch is death. But drop a boulder on a troll and... OOF! Just another rock. And when the hall doors open, daylight floods in, and every troll turns back to stone.

- **Twenty caves and five bonus intermissions** across the land the ice left behind, from First Thaw to the troll-haunted Bergschrund.
- **Five levels of difficulty,** every cave reshuffled for each.
- **Faithful to the 1984 cave-digging classic,** down to the tick, plus trolls of our own.
- **Chunky pixel art or crisp character graphics,** keyboard or gamepad.

The clock is the thaw, and the trolls are waking. **DIG FAST!**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **W A S D**: move and dig
- **Shift** with a direction, or **Space** / **Enter** held: grab or dig the next cell without moving
- **P**: pause, **Esc**: back
- **G**: pixel art or character graphics, **+** and **-**: zoom, **0**: automatic zoom
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad moves, any face button grabs, Start pauses

## Options

- `--cave N`: start at cave N (1 to 25)
- `--level N`: difficulty 1 to 5
- `--glyphs` or `--pixels`: the look to start in

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- A love letter to the 1984 cave-digging classic: a faithful engine for its rules, with our own caves, hero and creatures

ohm.title: Ohm's Workshop
ohm.description: The old master's workshop is yours now. Fix the town's gadgets with real circuits and watch them glow, click and blink... or smoke, pop and bang!
ohm.provenance: Asciiverse made Ohm's Workshop in Rust in 2026, in the family of SHENZHEN I/O, Retro Gadgets and Turing Complete, with a real circuit solver at its heart.
ohm.page:
**THE OLD MASTER'S BENCH IS YOURS NOW.**

Welcome to Ohms Verkstad, the little electronics repair shop the whole town still calls Ohm's. It's the early eighties, you're the new apprentice, the old master's notebook is on the shelf, and the inbox is already filling up.

Mrs Berg's bike lamp eats batteries. Elsa, who is eight, wants every room of her doll's house lit. Café Ohlsson wants a sign in the window, Mr Holm needs a lighthouse flasher down at the harbour, and Mr Nilsson's model railway needs a level crossing that actually works.

Pull open the parts drawers, lay the copper, drop in a resistor... and watch. The circuit is alive while you build it: current ripples through the traces, LEDs glow, relays click and capacitors slowly fill. And get it wrong? That's a show too! Resistors glow red, then smoke. LEDs flare and die. A capacitor in backwards goes BANG. One key puts the burnt parts back.

Then the test bench has its say: fresh batteries and tired ones, a bright day and a dark night. Pass, and the gadget goes home to its owner. Then see if you can match the old master himself: as cheap as his build, and lasting as long on a battery.

- **A real circuit solver underneath:** real volts, real milliamps, real parts, real kronor. What works here works on a breadboard.
- **From a bike lamp to your first chip:** resistors, capacitors, relays, diodes, transistors and logic, one customer at a time.
- **The Master's Notebook:** a page for every idea, each with a live circuit you can switch and measure.
- **A multimeter and a scope** that read whatever you point at, and a sandbox to build anything you like.
- **No timer, no pressure.** Poke, measure, think, and try again.

The whole town is counting on you. **DON'T LET THE MAGIC SMOKE OUT!**

## Controls

Mouse and keyboard work together: point at a part with the mouse and press a key to act on it.

- **Arrow keys**, **W A S D** or **H J K L**: move the cursor; with **Shift**: lay copper behind it
- **Mouse**: drag to lay copper, click to place a part, right click to erase, click a switch to flip it, the wheel turns a knob
- **Space**: place the selected part, **R**: rotate, **X** or **Del**: erase
- **Tab** or **1** to **9**: pick a drawer, **E**: operate the part under the cursor
- **T**: run the test bench, **U** or **Ctrl+Z**: undo, **Ctrl+Y**: redo, **Esc**: back
- **F1** or **?**: help, anywhere
- **Gamepad**: d-pad moves, hold A to lay copper, B erases, X rotates, Y operates, the shoulders change drawer

## Options

- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Every electronics fact checked against a real datasheet or standard, listed on its Notebook page

terminal-orbit.title: Terminal Orbit
terminal-orbit.description: The aliens are already here! Fly real Newtonian orbits across the solar system in a starfighter drawn in Braille, from the Moon to the rings of Saturn and all the way out to Pluto.
terminal-orbit.provenance: Asciiverse ported Steve Belczyk's ORBIT, a 1999 OpenGL space combat simulator, from its original C source. The original campaign is all here, and the first part of Episode Two is new.
terminal-orbit.page:
**THE ALIENS ARE ALREADY HERE.**

It started with a strange alien construction, quietly gathering energy. They towed it to the Mars Science Station for study. Then the alien fighters came for it.

You fly a small starfighter, and out here nothing is faked: real Newtonian physics, real gravity, real planets at their real distances. Point your nose at a target and you'll sail straight past it! Learn to thrust, brake and coast, swing into orbit, match speeds and dock, and then do it all again with alien fighters on your tail.

Train between the Earth and the Moon. Defend the Mars Science Station. Pull the truth out of an alien data store: the whole alien presence at Saturn was a deception, and the real invasion is heading for Jupiter. Hunt a hidden communications station in the Cassini Division of Saturn's rings, then take the war out past Uranus, all the way to Neptune and Pluto.

- **Steve Belczyk's whole 1999 ORBIT campaign,** 28 missions from Earth orbit to Pluto, ported from his own C source.
- **Episode Two: Open Skies,** a new campaign: the aliens are gone and the science missions fly again, with salvager pirates and the breakaway Jovian Combine in the way. Its first part is here.
- **Space drawn in Braille:** ships, planets with real surface maps (press T), 2000 real stars from the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, and constellation lines (press B).
- **An orbit autopilot** (press G) that swings you into a perfect equatorial orbit, with the classic starship-in-orbit camera shots.

The solar system needs a pilot who understands orbits. **ARE YOU THAT PILOT?**

## Controls

- **W** / **S** or **Up** / **Down**: thrust forward and back
- **A** / **D** or **Left** / **Right**: yaw, **I** / **K**: pitch, **J** / **L**: roll
- **X**: warp engines, **H**: hold still (needed to dock)
- **Space**: fire, **U**: lock the nearest enemy, **Y**: next target, **F**: next weapon
- **G**: orbit autopilot, **C**: camera (in orbit: the two orbit shots and the cockpit)
- **T**: planet surfaces, **B**: constellation lines, **N**: names, **O**: the orrery, **Z**: dense star field
- **M**: recall the last mission message, **P**: pause, **Q** or **Esc**: back to the title (progress is saved)

## Credits

- ORBIT: Steve Belczyk, 1999, released as freeware
- Terminal port and Episode Two: Asciiverse
- Stars: the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, from ORBIT's own source

braillestorm.title: Braillestorm
braillestorm.description: Your terminal is in a storm! Wildcard globs, rogue cursors and runaway forks swarm the screen, and you're the last prompt standing. Twin-stick fury in glorious Braille, over a grid that ripples with every blast!
braillestorm.provenance: Asciiverse made Braillestorm in Rust in 2026, inspired by Mark Incitti's freeware GridWars (2005); no code, art or sound is taken from it.
braillestorm.page:
**YOU ARE THE LAST PROMPT STANDING.**

Something has gone badly wrong in your terminal. The globs have broken loose and tumble everywhere. Block cursors blink awake and come hunting. Forks multiply: shoot one and it splits into two quick children. And they just keep coming, wave after wave, faster every time.

You're a lone shell prompt, `❯`, with a twin stream of fire and three bombs. Move with one stick and shoot with the other, in any direction, all at once. Every shot dents the glowing grid beneath you, every burst sends it rippling, and every bomb rings the whole field like a bell.

- **Waves that never stop,** each announced in big glowing letters, each bigger and faster than the last. From the tenth, every fifth wave is a rush: cursors from every corner at once.
- **Three bombs** that blast the field clear around you when it gets too close.
- **Drawn in glorious Braille:** thin, glowing vector lines of dots, sixty frames a second.
- **Gamepad, mouse or keyboard.** Clear a wave without losing your ship for a bonus, earn an extra life and bomb every 25,000 points, and chase your own best score.

How long can you hold back the storm? **JUST ONE MORE WAVE...**

## Controls

- **WASD**: move
- **Arrow keys**: fire; or hold the **left mouse button** to fire at the pointer
- **Space** or **right click**: bomb
- **P** or **Enter**: pause; **Space** or **Enter**: play again after game over
- **Q** or **Esc**: quit
- **Gamepad**: left stick to move, right stick to fire, A or a shoulder button to bomb, Start to pause

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others), or with a gamepad or the mouse. Elsewhere the arrows fire sticky: the last arrow keeps firing until you press the opposite one.

## Options

royal-ur.title: Royal Game of Ur
royal-ur.description: The oldest board game with known rules: race your pieces past the rosettes of a 4,500-year-old board, in four reconstructions
royal-ur.provenance: Asciiverse made Royal Game of Ur in Rust in 2026. The rules are Irving Finkel's reconstructions from a Babylonian tablet of 177 BC, and R. C. Bell's from 1960.
royal-ur.page:
**THE OLDEST BOARD GAME WE CAN STILL READ THE RULES OF.**

Somewhere around 2600 BC, someone in the city of Ur was buried with their favourite board game. It was dug up in the 1920s, all shell and lapis lazuli, and for most of a century nobody knew how to play it. Then a museum curator found the rules on a clay tablet that had been filed under bird omens.

Two players, seven pieces each, a path of fourteen squares. Throw the lots, move, and pray. Land on an enemy in the shared middle row and it goes all the way back to the start. Land on a rosette and you throw again. That middle rosette has been the most fought-over square on Earth for forty-five centuries.

Pick your rules:

- **Finkel 2017**: the one most people play today
- **British Museum 1990s**: five pieces and no safe rosette, a meaner race
- **R. C. Bell 1960**: a betting game; pieces enter only on a five, and a rosette makes your opponent pay
- **The Babylonian tablet**: five different birds, knucklebones you dare to throw, and the scribe's own fortunes ("You will draw fine beer")

Play the computer at three strengths, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Space** or **Enter**: throw
- **Arrows** or **Tab**: choose a piece; **Enter**: move it
- **D**: dare the ox bone (tablet rules)
- **Mouse**: click a lit piece
- **F1**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit

senet.title: Senet
senet.description: The Egyptian game of passing through the netherworld, played for three thousand years, with every honest reconstruction of its lost rules
senet.provenance: Asciiverse made Senet in Rust in 2026. No ancient rules survive; it plays Timothy Kendall's reconstruction in two forms and R. C. Bell's.
senet.page:
**PLAY YOUR WAY THROUGH THE NETHERWORLD.**

For three thousand years, Egypt played Senet. Pharaohs played it, scribes played it, and in time the dead played it too: the board became the soul's journey through the netherworld, and sets were buried with their owners, Tutankhamun among them.

Throw the four sticks, count the light sides, and race your pieces along the S-shaped track and off the board. Guard your pieces in pairs, block with three in a row, swap places with a lonely enemy. The House of Beauty must be landed on. The House of Water must not. And the last three houses each want an exact throw, and the gods are not in a hurry.

Nobody kept the rules, only thirty squares, a handful of sticks and a lot of tomb paintings of people having a great time. So choose your reconstruction:

- **Kendall, five pieces**: the rules on most sets sold today
- **Kendall, seven pieces**: the 1978 original, where falling into the House of Water stalls your whole side until you fish the piece out
- **R. C. Bell 1960**: ten men each, a long die, and capture by landing

Play the computer at three strengths, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **Tab**: choose a move; **Enter**: make it
- **R**: rescue a piece from the water (Kendall, seven pieces)

mehen.title: Mehen
mehen.description: Race your pharaohs up the coiled snake by guessing marbles in a fist, and set lions on the other team: one of Egypt's oldest games, reconstructed in 2024
mehen.provenance: Asciiverse made Mehen in Rust in 2026. No ancient rules survive; it plays James F. R. Masters' 2024 reconstruction.
mehen.page:
**RACE YOUR PHARAOHS UP THE COILED SNAKE. MIND THE LIONS.**

Five thousand years ago, Egyptians played a game on a snake: a serpent coiled round its own head, its body cut into squares, with little lions, lionesses and marbles. Then everyone stopped playing it, and the rules went with them. This is a 2024 reconstruction, built from the old boards, pieces and tomb pictures of clenched fists and open hands.

Your pharaoh is a marble at the snake's tail. Hide one to five marbles in your fist, and your opponent guesses how many. Guess wrong, and your pharaoh slithers forward that far. Guess right, and theirs moves instead, and they may set a lion on yours!

A pharaoh held by a lion goes nowhere until the lion is dead, and killing a lion is another guessing game, with smaller numbers and worse odds. Land on an enemy and you swap places. Two right guesses in a row bring a dead lion back. The first team to get every pharaoh to the head is reborn, and wins.

Play one against one, or teams of two or three. The computer bluffs with the mix game theory says is safest, and on hard it notices that you always hide five. Two people at one keyboard get a look-away screen while the other hides.

## Controls

- **1** to **5**, or **arrows** and **Enter**: hide or guess
- **Arrows** and **Enter**: choose a pharaoh
- **Y** or **N**: set a lion loose
- **Mouse**: click numbers, pharaohs and answers
- **F1**: the rules and what is known; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit

hnefatafl.title: Hnefatafl
hnefatafl.description: The Viking game of the king: twenty-four attackers, one king and his guard, and five rule sets from Copenhagen to Lapland
hnefatafl.provenance: Asciiverse made Hnefatafl in Rust in 2026. No Norse rules survive; it plays today's reconstructions as the World Tafl Federation and Aage Nielsen give them, and R. C. Bell's Tablut of 1960.
hnefatafl.page:
**ONE KING. TWENTY-FOUR VIKINGS WHO WANT A WORD WITH HIM.**

Before chess reached the north, the Vikings played tafl. In the middle of the board sits a king with his small guard. All round the edges wait twice as many attackers, and they would very much like a word with him.

The king wants out. His guards want to get him out. The attackers want to box him in. Every piece slides like a rook, so walls go up and come crashing down fast. Sandwich an enemy between two of yours to take it; the throne and the corners bite too. Get the king to safety and the defenders win. Surround him, and it's over.

The Norse rules are lost, so choose your reconstruction:

- **Copenhagen 11x11**: the tournament game, with shield walls along the edge and the exit fort
- **Fetlar 11x11**: the Shetland rules, no shield wall and no fort
- **Brandubh 7x7**: the quick Irish game, a king and four princes against eight Viking invaders
- **Tablut 9x9, Linnaeus**: written down by Linnaeus in Lapland in 1732, the only tafl game anyone recorded while it was still played
- **Tablut 9x9, Bell 1960**: the same game as an 1811 mistranslation left it, where the king can only be taken from all four sides. It is not fair, and it is fun

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

fox-and-geese.title: Fox and Geese
fox-and-geese.description: One fox, a whole gaggle of geese, and a cross-shaped board: the medieval hunt game, as R. C. Bell gives it
fox-and-geese.provenance: Asciiverse made Fox and Geese in Rust in 2026. The rules are R. C. Bell's (1960), with thirteen or seventeen geese.
fox-and-geese.page:
**ONE FOX. A WHOLE GAGGLE OF GEESE. SOMEBODY GETS EATEN.**

One fox, thirteen geese (or seventeen, if you'd like the geese to stand a chance), and a board shaped like a plus sign.

The fox jumps geese like a draughts piece and takes them off the board, several in one move if they're careless. The geese can't take anything at all. All they can do is waddle, one step at a time, and close in until the fox has nowhere left to go.

Play the fox and it's a hunt: find the gap, wait for the slip, pick the gaggle apart. Play the geese and it's a siege: hold the line, never leave a goose with an empty point behind it, and squeeze. Get the fox down to three geese and he wins, because three can never trap him.

Hunt games like this are old in the north: a medieval saga mentions one, and an English king's household bought silver-gilt foxes and hounds for one in the 1460s.

- **Thirteen geese**: the older form; geese step any way along a line, and the fox has the better of it
- **Seventeen geese**: more geese that never step back; played well, the geese should win

Play the computer at three strengths, as fox or geese, or a friend at the same keyboard.

mancala.title: Mancala
mancala.description: Seeds, pits and a lot of counting: the sowing games of Africa, Asia and Europe, from Ghana's Oware to Toguz Kumalak of the steppe, each with its own rules
mancala.provenance: Asciiverse made Mancala in Rust in 2026. Each of its nine games follows a source: the Oware Society's tournament rules, R. C. Bell (1960), E. W. Lane's account of Cairo (1836), W. J. Champion's Kalah patent (1955), M. Hellier on Malay congkak (1907), Mrs H. G. Durai on Pallanguli (1928), the Kazakh competition rules of 2013 and Fritz Jahn (1917).
mancala.page:
**SEEDS, PITS, AND A LOT OF COUNTING.**

Two rows of pits, a pile of seeds, and one move: lift every seed from a pit and sow them one at a time into the pits that follow. Where the last one lands decides everything.

That's mancala, and it isn't one game but hundreds, played from West Africa to the Philippines. They all sow; after that they argue about nearly everything. Here are nine of them:

- **Oware (Abapa)**: the Ghanaian tournament game; capture twos and threes on the other side, but never take every last seed
- **Wari**: the same family, where taking everything is simply not allowed
- **Mankal'ah, the game of the ignorant** and **the game of the wise**: the coffee-house game of 1830s Cairo, played with 72 pebbles set out by hand. Don't like how they were set out? Turn the board round, and give up the first move
- **Kalah**: the American game most people call Mancala
- **Congkak**: the Malay game on a boat-shaped board, where the sowing runs on and on from every loaded hole
- **Pallanguli**: the Tamil game, where four seeds in a hole make a cow for its owner
- **Toguz Kumalak**: nine holes of nine stones from the Kazakh steppe, where three stones in an enemy hole make it yours for good
- **Bohnenspiel**: the bean game found in a Baltic manor house in 1908

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

- **Mouse**: click a pit

morris.title: Morris
morris.description: Three in a row takes a man: Nine Men's Morris and its family, from the Roman game boards to Morabaraba of South Africa
morris.provenance: Asciiverse made Morris in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow R. C. Bell (1969), the World Mill Association's rules, Ralph Gasser (1996) and Mind Sports South Africa's Morabaraba rules.
morris.page:
**THREE IN A ROW TAKES A MAN.**

Place your men one at a time on the points of the board, then slide them along the lines. Three of yours in a row is a mill, and a mill takes one of your opponent's men. Every move either builds a mill, blocks one, or sets up the next. Bring your opponent down to two men, or leave them no move, and you've won.

It's been scratched into Roman bricks, cut into an oak board buried with a Viking ship, written down by a Spanish king in 1283, and it's still played the world over as the mill, merels and morris. Six forms of it:

- **Nine Men's Morris, today's rules**: the tournament game; down to three men, yours fly to any empty point
- **Nine Men's Morris after Bell**: the older game, no flying
- **Morabaraba**: South Africa's game of twelve men, with diagonals at the corners
- **Six Men's Morris**: two squares and six men each
- **Three Men's Morris**: three men each on a small square, where a mill wins outright
- **Three Men's Morris, placing only**: four counters each and no moving

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

mu-torere.title: Mū tōrere
mu-torere.description: Four men each on an eight-pointed star and one empty point: the Māori blocking game of New Zealand's East Coast
mu-torere.provenance: Asciiverse made Mū tōrere in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Elsdon Best's Games and Pastimes of the Maori (1925), as Tuta Nihoniho of Ngāti Porou explained the game to him, and the rule most often played today.
mu-torere.page:
**FOUR MEN EACH. ONE EMPTY POINT. NOWHERE TO HIDE.**

An eight-pointed star drawn round a centre, like an octopus. You have four men, your opponent has four, and there's always exactly one empty point. Move a man into it, if it's joined. Nothing is ever taken: the side that can't move has lost. It sounds simple, and it's a knife-edge.

Mū tōrere was played on the East Coast of New Zealand's North Island, on a star marked in charcoal on a plank or on bark, sometimes just scratched in the earth, and written down in 1925 from Tuta Nihoniho of Ngāti Porou.

- **The pūtahi beside an enemy**: today's common rule; a man may step into the centre only from beside an enemy man
- **Mū tōrere after Best**: the rule as first written, where it holds only for the opening move, and the side that moves second can win at once; the game shows you how

The game is small enough to be solved, and the program solves it when it starts: on hard, the computer plays perfectly.

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

konane.title: Kōnane
konane.description: Black and white stones, every hollow full, and every move a jump: the Hawaiian game Cook's expedition saw in 1779
konane.provenance: Asciiverse made Kōnane in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Michael Ernst (1995), after Kenneth Emory (1924) and Peter Buck (1957), and the National Park Service at Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau; its largest board is the one James King described in 1779.
konane.page:
**EVERY MOVE IS A JUMP. RUN OUT OF JUMPS AND YOU LOSE.**

Every hollow of the board starts full, black and white in turn. Two stones are lifted out, and from then on every move is a jump: leap one of your opponent's stones into the empty hollow beyond and take it, and keep jumping along the same line if you can. The first player who can't jump has lost.

Kōnane was played all across Hawaiʻi on boards cut into lava stone, with pebbles of coral and lava for stones. An officer on Captain Cook's third voyage saw it in 1779 on a board of 238 squares and thought it "much more intricate" than draughts. King Kamehameha, the story goes, sometimes beat his opponent in a single move.

- **Kōnane after Ernst**: the classic, 8 by 8, with jumps that may run on in a straight line
- **Modern Kōnane**: the same, but one jump a move
- **Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau**: 9 by 11, like the old stone board there
- **King's papamū**: the great board of 238 squares, 14 by 17

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

seega.title: Seega
seega.description: Fill a square of holes with your kelbs, then step and trap: the Egyptian game Lane saw cut into the top of the Great Pyramid
seega.provenance: Asciiverse made Seega in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Edward William Lane's Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836), which gives them in full.
seega.page:
**FILL THE BOARD. THEN THE TRAPPING STARTS.**

A square of holes, every one filled but the centre, two kelbs at a time. Then someone steps into that empty centre, and the game cracks open. Move a kelb so that an enemy lies trapped between it and another of yours, and you take it; as long as you can take, you keep moving. Box your opponent in completely, and they must give up a kelb just to open a way.

In the 1830s, an Englishman living in Cairo watched Egypt's farmers play seega in holes made in the ground, and saw seega boards cut into the stones on top of the Great Pyramid by the guides who took travellers up it.

- **Seega of five**: 5 by 5, twelve kelbs each
- **Seega of seven**: 7 by 7, twenty-four kelbs each
- **Seega of nine**: 9 by 9, forty kelbs each

alquerque.title: Alquerque and Fanorona
alquerque.description: Leap and take on the lined board of Alfonso X's Book of Games, or sweep whole lines away in Madagascar's Fanorona
alquerque.provenance: Asciiverse made Alquerque and Fanorona in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Alfonso X's Book of Games (1283, in Sonja Musser Golladay's translation), R. C. Bell (1969), W. Montgomery's account of Fanorona (1886) and Schadd and colleagues (2008).
alquerque.page:
**LEAP AND TAKE, OR SWEEP WHOLE LINES AWAY.**

Points joined by lines along every row, column and diagonal. In alquerque, your men leap enemies like draughts pieces and can keep on leaping. In fanorona, the national game of Madagascar, you capture by moving towards an enemy or away from one, and the whole unbroken line of enemies in that direction is swept off the board at once!

Alquerque's first rules are in the Book of Games a Spanish king had made in 1283. Fanorona was being played "everywhere, in-doors and out of doors" in 1886, its lines scratched on rocks and on the paving outside the palace. Its board is two alquerque boards side by side, and in 2008 it was proved that fanorona, played perfectly, is a draw. Nobody plays perfectly.

- **Alquerque de doze, after Alfonso X**: 5 by 5, twelve men each, taking not compulsory
- **Alquerque after Bell**: the stricter game; taking compulsory, and no man steps backwards
- **Fanorona, today's rules**: 9 by 5, twenty-two men each, approach and withdrawal
- **Fanorona after Montgomery**: the rules as first written down, in 1886
- **Vela**: the handicap game the winner must play after a defeat
- **Fanoron-dimy**: fanorona on the little board of five by five

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

tabula.title: Tabula
tabula.description: The Roman ancestor of backgammon: fifteen men, three dice, and the one game position that survives from antiquity
tabula.provenance: Asciiverse made Tabula in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow the reconstructions of Louis Becq de Fouquières (1869), R. G. Austin (1934), R. C. Bell (1969) and H. J. R. Murray.
tabula.page:
**THE GAME THE EMPEROR LOST.**

Fifteen men each, three dice, and a race round the board and off it. Each die moves one man. Two of your men together close a point; a single man is hit when an enemy lands on him, and must start all over again. The first to bear off all fifteen wins. If that sounds like backgammon, it should: this is its Roman ancestor.

The Romans left boards by the hundred, dice towers, a tavern wall at Pompeii showing two players quarrelling over a throw, and exactly one recorded game: a poem tells how the emperor Zeno lost with a throw of 2, 5 and 6. Play it here, and the program finds the poet was right: that throw leaves Zeno only one play, and it ruins him.

- **Tabula, the colours opposite**: the sides run against each other, as in backgammon
- **Tabula, the colours the same way**: both run the same way round, so every point is contested from the start
- **Ludus duodecim scriptorum**: the older game of three rows of twelve

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

pachisi.title: Pachisi and Chaupar
pachisi.description: Four colours round a cross of four arms, thrown with six cowrie shells or three long dice: the game that became Ludo
pachisi.provenance: Asciiverse made Pachisi and Chaupar in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Rajendralala Mitra's account printed by Edward Tylor (1879), Edward Falkener (1892, reprinted by R. C. Bell) and Abu'l-Fazl's Ain-i Akbari (about 1590).
pachisi.page:
**THE GAME THAT BECAME LUDO, AS EMPERORS PLAYED IT.**

A cross of four arms, four colours of four men, partners sitting opposite. Each man leaves the middle, runs right round the cross and comes home again: 84 steps. Land on a lone enemy man and he goes back to the start, unless he's safe on a castle. The partnership with all eight men home first wins.

At the emperor Akbar's court, around 1590, games could last three months, and a player who lost patience had to drink a cup of wine. The name comes from the best throw of the cowrie shells, twenty-five: pachis. The English took it home in the 1880s, and called it Ludo.

- **Pachisi after Tylor**: six cowries, the rules as recorded from Calcutta in 1879
- **Pachisi after Falkener**: the rules of 1892
- **Chaupar after Abu'l-Fazl**: three long dice and no castles, the game of Akbar's court

shatranj.title: Shatranj
shatranj.description: Chess before the queen and the bishop, as the masters of Baghdad played it, and the Indian chaturanga they wrote down
shatranj.provenance: Asciiverse made Shatranj in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow H. J. R. Murray's A History of Chess (1913), from the books of al-'Adli and as-Suli, and al-Biruni's account of India (about 1030).
shatranj.page:
**CHESS BEFORE THE QUEEN.**

This is chess as it was a thousand years ago. The king, knight and rook move as they do today. But the counsellor steps only one square diagonally, the elephant leaps exactly two, and a pawn that reaches the far row becomes a counsellor. No castling, no double step. Win by mate, by stripping away every enemy man but the king, or by leaving the enemy king without a move.

The masters of Baghdad played it at the caliph's court in the 9th and 10th centuries, and wrote it down, with over 1,600 problems that survive to this day. It came from India by way of Persia, and went on to Europe, where in time the counsellor and the elephant became the queen and the bishop.

- **Shatranj**: the Baghdad masters' game; stalemating the enemy shah wins
- **The Medinese victory**: whoever first strips the other's king bare wins at once
- **Chaturanga, the Indian rules**: where a stalemated shah wins
- **The elephant in the corner**: the Indian game, its elephant leaping along the ranks and files
- **Al-Biruni's elephant**: "the trunk and the four feet", one more old elephant

patolli.title: Patolli
patolli.description: Five black beans, a cross painted on a mat, six stones each: the Aztec game that players staked themselves on
patolli.provenance: Asciiverse made Patolli in Rust in 2026. Its rules are R. C. Bell's suggested rules (1969), on the equipment Diego Durán describes (about 1579).
patolli.page:
**THE AZTEC GAME PLAYERS STAKED THEMSELVES ON.**

A cross painted on a mat, six stones each, and five black beans, each with a single white hole. Cast the beans: the holes showing count one to four, and all five count ten. Bring your stones in, take them once round the cross and off. The pinched squares cost you forfeits; the rounded ends give you another throw. The first with all six stones off wins the pool.

A Spanish friar in Mexico described patolli around 1579: the mat, the stones, the beans, the god of the beans, and the gamblers who, with nothing left, staked themselves, and became slaves for ever if they couldn't buy themselves back. The authorities tore up the mats and burned the beans, and nobody wrote the rules down. What you play here are the rules a games historian suggested in 1969, on the friar's equipment.

Play the computer at three strengths, or a friend at the same keyboard.

nard.page:
**THE OLDEST GAME IN THE BAZAAR. THE TOUGHEST OPPONENT IN TOWN.**

Fifteen men a side, two dice, and the oldest name the backgammon family still answers to: *nard*, as the game is called from Iran to Russia.

The board is dressed like an inlaid tavla set from a bazaar: a brass wall, ivory and crimson points, a rim of Braille inlay, and on a big terminal, a ground of eight-pointed stars all around it.

And across the table sits a real opponent: bgsage, a neural-network backgammon engine. On **easy** it's friendly, picks among the plays close to the best, and never doubles. On **normal** and **hard** it thinks one and two moves ahead, and it doubles, takes and passes like a player who means it. Push your luck too far and it will gammon you.

Money play with the doubling cube, gammons and backgammons, and the score kept across the session. Or hand the other side to a friend at the same keyboard. **YOUR ROLL.**

dominos.title: Dominos
dominos.description: Clack! Ivory tiles on green baize: the Block game, the Draw game and All Fives, against a sly computer or your friends round the table on the local network.
dominos.provenance: Asciiverse made Dominos in Rust in 2026. Rules after pagat.com's Block, Draw and All Fives.
dominos.page:
**IVORY TILES. GREEN BAIZE. CLACK!**

Pull up a chair. Three games, two to four players, and nobody minds if you count on your fingers.

- **The Block game**: the purest one. Match an open end or pass; the first to go out, or the lowest hand when everyone is stuck, takes everyone else's pips.
- **The Draw game**: the same, with a boneyard to draw from whenever you like, even when you could play, until only two tiles are left there. More tiles, more choices, more pips to be caught holding.
- **All Fives**: the first double becomes the spinner and the line grows four arms. Every time the open ends add up to a multiple of five, you score on the spot. First to 200 wins, the moment it's reached.

Play the computer, or open a table on the local network: your friends find it by themselves, take the open seats, and the computer fills the rest. At four, play partners, sitting opposite and scoring as a side. Everyone only ever sees their own hand, so no peeking.

The computer comes in three strengths, and in All Fives the hard one is sly: it remembers which numbers you couldn't play, and leaves you ends you can't match. **SHUFFLE UP.**

## Controls

- **← →** or **h l**: choose a tile from your hand, or click it
- **Enter** or **Space**: play it; where it fits two ways, **← →** choose the end
- **D**: draw from the boneyard
- **?** or **F1**: the rules of the game you are playing
- **Q** or **Esc**: back to the menu

## Options

- `--rules block|draw|fives`: the game the menu starts on
- `--demo`: the computer plays every seat
- `--seed N`: the same deal again
